article_title: Speaking to Write: Examining Language Learners' Acceptance of Automatic Speech Recognition as a Writing Tool
citation: Johnson, C., & Cardoso, W. (2021). Speaking to write: examining language learners’ acceptance of automatic speech recognition as a writing tool. In N. Zoghlami et al. (Eds), CALL and professionalisation: short papers from EUROCALL 2021 (pp. 167-171). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2021.54.1327
title: Use ASR-based writing to lift the burden of error-free form so learners can attend to content and other aspects of writing
description: Because ESL students often focus on linguistic form at the expense of content, context, genre, and process, the article proposes ASR dictation as a way to redirect attention: "Using ASR, a technology that converts speech to text, may remove some of the burden of producing error-free form, allowing students to pay attention to other aspects of writing such as content." The tool is free, accessible, and meets Chapelle's CALL criteria, including attention to meaning and authentic use. The article frames this as pedagogically promising but not yet tested for effectiveness.
requirements: Training on the ASR tool before use
Learners' speech intelligible to the technology
constraints: Pedagogical effectiveness not yet assessed; the authors state studies are needed to determine its true pedagogical potential and best practices for classroom implementation
target_learners: adult ESL writers in academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: attention to content, context, genre, and writing process rather than form alone
examples: Participants wrote authentic academic texts with ASR and reported focusing on getting the meaning of their ideas into texts without focusing on form
key_sources: Johnson, C., & Cardoso, W. (2021). Speaking to write: examining language learners’ acceptance of automatic speech recognition as a writing tool. In N. Zoghlami et al. (Eds), CALL and professionalisation: short papers from EUROCALL 2021 (pp. 167-171). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2021.54.1327

article_title: Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes
citation: Julie Bruch, Jasmine Forde, Ijun Lai, Veronica Sotelo Muñoz. (2022). Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/menu-of-measures-high-quality-measures-of-middle-years-math-student-outcomes
title: Assess measure quality with explicit criteria plus context-fit questions before adopting a measure
description: When choosing a measure of student outcomes, apply a set of quality criteria and then ask context-specific questions to judge fit. The resource "includes a set of criteria that can be used to assess measure quality, as well as context-specific questions to help readers determine if a specific measure is a good fit for their unique circumstances." Quality and fit are treated as distinct checks.
requirements: A defined set of measure-quality criteria
Context-specific questions about the adopting setting
constraints: Fit judgments depend on the reader's unique circumstances, so criteria alone do not guarantee fit
target_learners: middle grades math students
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable measurement of math outcomes
examples: The menu pairs its curated measure list with quality criteria and context-specific fit questions for educators, district leaders, researchers, and funders
key_sources: Julie Bruch, Jasmine Forde, Ijun Lai, Veronica Sotelo Muñoz. (2022). Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/menu-of-measures-high-quality-measures-of-middle-years-math-student-outcomes

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use
title: Ask the right questions and use data aligned with district goals
description: The brief's second key recommendation is to "Ask the right questions and use the correct data to support district goals." It observes that many districts do not know what questions to ask or what data to use, so question formulation and data selection are treated as capacities districts must deliberately develop. The recommendation ties data analysis directly to district improvement goals.
requirements: Districts need clarity on their goals so that questions and data selection can support them
target_learners: school district staff and administrators
target_learning_goals: formulating answerable questions and selecting appropriate data to support district goals
examples: The brief suggests ways districts can overcome challenges associated with this recommendation, drawing examples from the strategic data use initiative evaluation
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use

citation: Kristin Hallgren, Cassie Pickens Jewell, Celina Kamler, Jacob Hartog, Andrew Gothro. (2013). Companion Document for the Strategic Data Project and Education Pioneers Year 1 Report: Laying the Groundwork for Data-Driven Decision Making. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Assess agency data practices across collection, use, analysis, and reporting when laying groundwork for data-driven decision making
description: The study's interview protocol addressed agencies' efforts in four areas: "data collection, use, analysis, and reporting efforts." This suggests that groundwork for data-driven decision making should be assessed across these distinct practice areas rather than a single measure, since each agency's experience was profiled along these dimensions.
requirements: Interviews or assessments covering collection, use, analysis, and reporting
target_learners: school district and education agency staff
target_learning_goals: data-driven decision making
examples: Interviews in the implementation study addressed agencies' data collection, use, analysis, and reporting efforts

article_title: Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? (Journal Article)
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2011). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Researchers should assess statistical power for mediator-outcome linkage analyses before relying on them to interpret RCT results
description: Because the article develops power formulas specifically for exploratory analyses linking teacher practice outcomes to student achievement outcomes in clustered school-based RCTs, it implies that researchers should evaluate power for these analyses when designing studies. The simulated power analysis exists to inform such assessments, indicating that typical RCTs may face power limitations for linking impacts on teacher practice and student achievement.
requirements: Access to the article's power formulas and design parameters for the planned RCT
constraints: Applies to clustered school-based RCT designs using OLS or IV estimators
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators
target_learning_goals: Designing adequately powered analyses of teacher practice mediators
examples: The article conducts a simulated power analysis to illustrate power for these linkage analyses in typical RCTs
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2011). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/ja-do-typical-rcts-of-education-interventions-have-sufficient-statistical-power-for-linking-impacts

article_title: Trauma-Informed Planning Strategies to Help Students Transition Back to School in the Era of COVID-19, Fact Sheet
citation: Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic. (2020). Trauma-Informed Planning Strategies to Help Students Transition Back to School in the Era of COVID-19, Fact Sheet. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/trauma-informed-planning-strategies-to-help-students-transition-back-to-school-in-the-era-of-covid-19
title: Assess-plan-build capacity-implement-reassess cycle for school crisis response
description: This pattern names the five recurring phases the fact sheet prescribes for trauma-informed reopening: "assessing, planning, building capacity, implementing, and reassessing." Because the strategy is iterative, the reassessing phase feeds back into assessing and planning, making the cycle repeatable across the school year rather than a one-time checklist.
requirements: Schools initiate the cycle before the start of the school year
constraints: Derived from crisis response guidance for COVID-19 reopening
target_learners: K-12 school communities, including students and staff
target_learning_goals: Sustaining a trauma-informed learning environment through iterative improvement
examples: The fact sheet presents the five steps as the structure schools should follow when developing their trauma-informed reopening plans.

article_title: Six insights regarding test-taking disengagement
citation: Steven Wise. (2021). Six insights regarding test-taking disengagement. Educational Research and Evaluation, 26(5-6), 328-338. https://www.nwea.org/research/
title: Assessment programs should attend to test-taking disengagement when interpreting scores
description: This principle holds that operators of assessment programs, particularly international assessment programs, should consider disengaged test taking when making and defending inferences from scores. The article's stated purpose is to discuss "six important insights yielded by this research and their implications for assessment programs", grounding the recommendation in evidence that disengagement distorts individual and aggregated scores and therefore the validity of country-level attainment inferences.
requirements: Assessment programs need methods for measuring disengagement to act on it
target_learners: Students in international and large-scale assessment programs
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of assessment scores at individual and aggregate levels
examples: The article derives implications for assessment programs from six research insights on disengagement
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2021). Six insights regarding test-taking disengagement. Educational Research and Evaluation, 26(5-6), 328-338. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/six-insights-regarding-test-taking-disengagement/

article_title: Unlocking the Potential of Technology Innovations: A Vision for Supporting Multilingual Learners
citation: Danae Kamdar, Tiffany Leones, Amanda LaTasha Armstrong, Shelton Daal & Ximena Dominguez. (2025). Unlocking the Potential of Technology Innovations: A Vision for Supporting Multilingual Learners. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Asset-based, culturally and linguistically responsive design pattern for MLL edtech
description: This pattern treats multilingual learners' languages, cultures, and communities as assets to design around rather than obstacles, moving beyond simple translation. The report recommends that "efforts that move beyond simple translation and consider issues of cultural and linguistic sensitivity are needed." Interview exemplars include a studio that prioritized creating a product in Spanish first for Puerto Rican and Mexican communities before translating to English, recognizing that language and culture are interconnected, and recruiting a native speaker of the community as narrator so the community's language is authentically reflected.
requirements: Design teams must meaningfully include voices of MLLs, families, communities, and educators early and often throughout product development
Cultural and linguistic specificity must be addressed, since Spanish-speaking populations vary widely in cultural traditions and vocabulary
constraints: Interviewees noted that diversity among Spanish-speaking populations makes standardized best practices difficult and that addressing power dynamics among diverse team members takes time
target_learners: Young multilingual learners ages 3-8 and their families and communities
target_learning_goals: Engagement, comprehension, and enjoyment of learning content
Identity affirmation and authentic cultural and linguistic representation
examples: One studio developed a product for Spanish-speaking communities by designing in Spanish first, then translating to English; another recognized the need for a community native speaker as narrator during design
key_sources: Danae Kamdar, Tiffany Leones, Amanda LaTasha Armstrong, Shelton Daal & Ximena Dominguez. (2025). Unlocking the Potential of Technology Innovations: A Vision for Supporting Multilingual Learners. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/f37dc670-36a6-4f6e-a6c4-bf312be4fac0

article_title: Teacher’s Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning
citation: Judi Fusco, Sarah DiMaria, Beverly Yeadon, Linette Victor, Sarah Hampton, Janet Kolodner, London Jenks, Susan Yoon. (2024). Teacher's Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Use an asset-based approach to classroom culture to balance status relationships and help students feel valued
description: Drawing on Bielaczyc and colleagues (2013) and Webb (2009), the primer recommends fostering a safe, supportive classroom culture by helping each student recognize the strengths and assets they bring to collaboration. As the primer explains, "an asset-based approach that highlights how each student plays an important role during collaboration helps balance status relationships among students by raising awareness of the multiple skills needed to accomplish the group task." Teachers should frequently discuss the importance of multiple abilities, comment on contributions of students who may be perceived as less important, and emphasize that no one person is best at every ability. The goal is a place where students feel valued and comfortable taking risks and sharing ideas.
requirements: Teachers must discuss the importance of multiple abilities and stress that all students bring important skills
constraints: The primer ties this to establishing trust through strong teacher-student relationships, which research links to engagement, attendance, grades, and lower dropout rates
target_learners: K-12 students in collaborative groups, including students perceived as less important to their groups
target_learning_goals: Willingness to take risks, share ideas, and work together during collaborative learning
examples: The primer cites Webb (2009) on teachers discussing multiple abilities and commenting on contributions of students perceived as less important to the group
key_sources: Judi Fusco, Sarah DiMaria, Beverly Yeadon, Linette Victor, Sarah Hampton, Janet Kolodner, London Jenks, Susan Yoon. (2024). Teacher's Roles in Supporting Collaborative Learning. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/6dc71c9f-b523-4c36-9da8-d98b364e17e0

article_title: Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide
citation: Culturally Responsive Assessment Collaborative. (2025, November). Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/276/
title: Design assessment as a coherent system aligned with learning goals and equity outcomes
description: When assessment is defined as a system rather than a single test, the guide's coherence principle requires that all components—from individual items to high-stakes policy measures—align with contemporary models of learning and the equity outcomes of the broader curriculum and program context. In CRA, this means externally developed instruments must be intentionally designed to support the culturally responsive teaching and learning occurring in the local environment. No single test can be the sole driver of equity and improvement; the system's role is to complement broader instructional, community, and aspirational goals.
requirements: All components of the assessment system must align with contemporary models of learning and the desired learning goals and equity outcomes of the overarching curriculum
constraints: Externally developed assessment instruments require intentional design to fit the local culturally responsive context
target_learners: assessment developers and graduate measurement students
target_learning_goals: design coherent assessment systems that support culturally responsive teaching and equity
examples: The guide cites Evans et al. (forthcoming), Glaser et al. (2001), and Marion et al. (2024) on coherence in assessment systems
key_sources: Culturally Responsive Assessment Collaborative. (2025, November). Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/276/

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: ASSISTments
citation: ASSISTments evidence summary. (2020). https://www.assistments.org
title: Dual-content homework design: textbook-linked problem sets plus mastery-oriented skill practice
description: ASSISTments organizes its homework content along two complementary types: "the first is linked to existing textbook homework problems and provides teachers the flexibility to assign suitable problem sets and the second is intended for mastery-oriented skill practice." This pattern lets homework both follow the enacted curriculum and provide repeated practice toward mastery, with the platform returning assessment information to teachers.
requirements: existing textbook homework problems to link content to
a problem bank supporting mastery-oriented practice
constraints: as evaluated, the pattern applied to grade 7 math homework in middle school settings
target_learners: middle school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: math homework completion with assistance and mastery of math skills
examples: Teachers assigned suitable problem sets linked to their textbook while also drawing on mastery-oriented skill practice content
key_sources: ASSISTments evidence summary. (2020). https://www.assistments.org

article_title: Structuring Out-of-School Time to Improve Academic Achievement
citation: Beckett, M., Borman, G., Capizzano, J., Parsley, D., Ross, S., Schirm, A., & Taylor, J. (2009). Structuring out-of-school time to improve academic achievement: A practice guide (NCEE #2009-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Assess OST program performance and use results to improve program quality
description: Program improvement depends on articulating goals and expectations, effective management, and staff performance and experience. "Recommendation 5 presents strategies for schools and districts to use to identify programs that are most likely to result in academic improvement and to monitor existing programs to ensure that the highest-quality services are being provided to students." Action steps are to develop an evaluation plan, collect program and student performance data, analyze the data and use findings for program improvement, and conduct a summative evaluation.
requirements: An evaluation plan
Collection of program and student performance data
Analysis of data and use of findings for program improvement
A summative evaluation
constraints: The level of evidence for this recommendation is low
target_learners: students served by school, district, and program administrators evaluating OST services
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of OST program quality and academic services
examples: The checklist lists developing an evaluation plan, collecting program and student performance data, analyzing data for program improvement, and conducting a summative evaluation.

article_title: Developing a Stealth Assessment System Using a Continuous Conjunctive Model
citation: Jiaqi Yu, Wenchao Ma, Jewoong Moon, Andre R. Denham. (2022). Developing a Stealth Assessment System Using a Continuous Conjunctive Model. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 11–31. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7639
title: Implement evidence-based assessment models at the early stage of educational game development to enable task-specific stealth assessment
description: The article argues that stealth assessment should be built into a game from the start rather than retrofitting analytics onto pre-existing games. It notes it is "hard to track players' mastery of content knowledge due to the lack of task-specific data across the game levels" when using pre-existing games, and that researchers have promoted "implementing evidence-based assessment models at the early stage of game development". The Nomads was designed with task-specific tracking and a CCM so that randomly generated items could yield diagnostic skill profiles.
requirements: Game tasks mapped to skills via a Q-matrix determined by subject experts
An event-based logging system recording each completed item's skills, correctness, timing, and scaffold use
constraints: Building a DGBL application with a learning analytics system from scratch is costly and time-consuming, per the article
target_learners: K-12 students playing educational mathematics games
target_learning_goals: Unobtrusive measurement of skill mastery during gameplay
Diagnostic skill profiles that inform learning support
examples: The study's team designed and developed The Nomads from scratch with nine task types, embedded scaffolds, and log parameters aligned to five attributes before collecting data.
key_sources: Jiaqi Yu, Wenchao Ma, Jewoong Moon, Andre R. Denham. (2022). Developing a Stealth Assessment System Using a Continuous Conjunctive Model. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 11–31. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7639

article_title: Integrating Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)
citation: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/
title: Use existing staff and time more strategically before adding new SEAD programs or positions
description: The guide's asset-mapping principle holds that schools should inventory and realign all resources—staff, time, technology, space, community assets, and budget—around their vision before purchasing new programs. It argues that traditional add-on approaches are "insufficient because it rarely attends to the classroom teachers that comprise over 80% of a typical school's budget," and that "Identifying opportunities to use existing staff and time more strategically should come before making additional investments." Resource equity means allocating by need rather than giving every student the same thing.
requirements: A full asset map of resources inside and outside the school, including community assets such as after-school care, health centers, and nonprofits
constraints: New positions created through trade-offs may lack content-team colleagues and need district professional-learning support
target_learners: All students, with resource decisions based on need
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to social, emotional, and academic development supports
examples: Rogers' school eliminated teaching assistant positions and hall monitors to fund a floating science teacher and expanded planning time
key_sources: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/

article_title: Cost and Cost Effectiveness of ASSISTments Online Math Support: Analysis from a Randomized Controlled Study in Middle School
citation: Feng, M., Weiser, G., & Collins, K. (2024). Cost and cost effectiveness of ASSISTments online math support: Analysis from a randomized controlled study in middle school. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: ASSISTments online math homework platform
description: ASSISTments is a free, web-based platform used in the study as an online tool for math homework, with many teachers also using it for classwork. It "provided students with instant feedback on their math work, while teachers received real-time data and progress reports on student learning." The platform contains textbook-based problems from schools' existing curricula plus prebuilt content, and developers built teacher-created practice problems into it on request. No specialized hardware or software was required beyond existing devices.
requirements: Teachers are expected to assign ASSISTments assignments for 20-30 minutes at least twice a week and regularly review data reports of student work
constraints: The platform itself is free, but effective implementation in the study required professional development, a local coach, and modest technology support for account setup
target_learners: seventh-grade middle school math students
target_learning_goals: middle school mathematics achievement
examples: In the North Carolina RCT, intervention teachers implemented ASSISTments over two consecutive school years with 2-day summer professional development and coaching visits averaging three per teacher per year
key_sources: Feng, M., Weiser, G., & Collins, K. (2024). Cost and cost effectiveness of ASSISTments online math support: Analysis from a randomized controlled study in middle school. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655721

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Quality instruction for English learners promotes asset-based teaching, learning, and assessment grounded in funds of knowledge and identity
description: The brief's second feature holds that students' knowledge, experience, and sensibilities are critical assets for gaining new knowledge and skills. Asset-based instruction prioritizes what students can do rather than what they can't yet do, rooted in students' funds of knowledge—abilities passed down through generations—and funds of identity. Teachers build instruction around student-specific funds (interests, talents, passions) and community funds (collective histories, activities, norms, values).
requirements: Teachers must develop an understanding of their students' families, communities, cultures, and interests in ways that establish and sustain relationships.
constraints: The brief notes this sociocultural focus is particularly important for learners from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, who may otherwise experience a sociocultural disconnect from classroom activities and settings.
target_learners: English learners and their non-English learner peers
target_learning_goals: Meaningful, culturally responsive learning that leverages students' rich experiences as a catalyst for developing learning
examples: Teachers can gather evidence by asking students to journal and write stories about their families in their first language and in English, bring in collections of significant items, make videos, take photographs, and draw self-portraits.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673602

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments Companion Report: Implementation Analysis of the ASSISTments Intervention
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments companion report: Implementation analysis of the ASSISTments intervention. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: ASSISTments platform with the four steps of formative assessment
description: ASSISTments is "a free, web-based formative assessment platform for teachers and students in grades 3 through 12" that delivers immediate feedback, hints, explanations, and step-by-step scaffolds while generating color-coded class- and student-level reports. Its use is standardized into four steps of formative assessment: Assign standards-aligned problem sets, Practice with immediate feedback, Assess reports to identify patterns and errors, and Review selected problems using anonymized projected data. The intervention paired the platform with a virtual professional learning community to train rural middle school teachers.
requirements: Teachers need initial training and ongoing support to use the platform effectively following the four steps
constraints: Home internet or device access limits out-of-school use, so the study found in-class use more equitable
target_learners: middle school students in grades 6–8, particularly in rural and underresourced schools
target_learning_goals: middle school mathematics achievement
formative assessment practices
examples: Teachers assigned regular assignments and Skill Builders, with 70% of assignments being regular assignments rather than Skill Builders
key_sources: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments companion report: Implementation analysis of the ASSISTments intervention. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677784

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments Companion Report: Implementation Analysis of the ASSISTments Intervention
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments companion report: Implementation analysis of the ASSISTments intervention. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Virtual professional learning community (vPLC) for ASSISTments teacher training
description: The vPLC is a virtual professional learning model designed to connect rural and geographically isolated teachers with peers and learning opportunities. It consisted of eight 75-minute virtual facilitated sessions during the school year, supplemented by asynchronous activities, led with three core goals: supporting effective ASSISTments use following the four steps, engaging teachers in analysis-of-practice, and modeling NCTM norms of excellent math teaching. Teachers responded positively: most (87%) participated fully, and about half rated the vPLC as comparable to or better than other professional development they had experienced.
requirements: Trained facilitators, a facilitation guide, and session structures such as breakout-room discussions with peer teachers
constraints: Designed for teachers with limited access to in-person PLCs; rural vPLCs are more effective when flexible, interactive, relevant, and ongoing, per the article's cited research
target_learners: rural middle school math teachers and teachers lacking peer networks or in-person professional learning access
target_learning_goals: effective use of ASSISTments and the four steps of formative assessment
data-informed math instruction
professional community building
examples: Session themes included using ASSISTments data and common wrong answers to inform instruction and framing mistakes as part of learning
key_sources: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments companion report: Implementation analysis of the ASSISTments intervention. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677784

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments: Evaluation Final Report
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: ASSISTments platform: student-facing independent practice with immediate feedback and mastery-based Skill Builders, plus teacher-facing real-time reports
description: ASSISTments is an online math platform with a student-facing interface and teacher-facing tools. Students complete regular assignments built from OER curriculum problems (Illustrative Math, EngageNY) and mastery-oriented Skill Builders, receiving "immediate feedback on the correctness of answers"; they "cannot proceed to the next problem until they have correctly solved the current one". Teachers view real-time grid-format reports showing per-question accuracy, common wrong answers, and individual student responses, which they use to target instruction and form groups.
requirements: Students need technology access allowing internet-based classwork and homework, an eligibility condition the study states for participating teachers' students.
constraints: Full credit is awarded only for independent solving; partial credit is given when students use hints or require multiple attempts.
target_learners: Middle school students in grades 6-8
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement, including conceptual understanding, procedural skill/fluency, and application
examples: In the study treatment condition, teachers were asked to assign prebuilt content at least three times per week for 17 weeks using a combination of regular assignments and Skill Builders.
key_sources: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677852

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments: Evaluation Final Report
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Assign grade-level problem sets aligned to learning goals that yield actionable data, balancing conceptual understanding, procedural fluency, and application
description: Drawing on NCTM norms for effective mathematics instruction adapted for ASSISTments, the vPLC encouraged teachers to "assign grade-level problems that align with a learning goal and yield actionable data" and to "assign problem sets with a balance of focus on conceptual understanding, procedural skill/fluency, and application". Teachers were also to support students in identifying appropriate target scores based on their current level and to assign high-leverage problem sets with multiple entry points for all learners.
requirements: Teachers need access to prebuilt OER problem sets and Skill Builders within ASSISTments so assignments can align with grade-level standards and produce report data.
constraints: The recommendations were developed specifically for use with ASSISTments, adapting NCTM norms to that platform.
target_learners: Middle school math teachers serving grade 6-8 students, including in high-expectations-for-all-learners settings
target_learning_goals: High expectations for all learners and actionable data generation from independent practice
examples: Session 1 of the vPLC covered upholding high expectations while assigning a problem set, practiced within ASSISTments.

article_title: Technology-Based Support Shows Promising Long-Term Impact on Math Learning: Initial Results from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Middle Schools
citation: Feng, M., Huang, C.-W., & Collins, K. (2023). Technology-based support shows promising long-term impact on math learning: Initial results from a randomized controlled trial in middle schools. WestEd. https://osf.io/exqpn
title: Four-step formative assessment loop for technology-supported math homework
description: The ASSISTments intervention is organized around "a four-step loop that can be readily integrated into day-to-day instructional practices." Teachers (1) find and assign standards-aligned content, (2) students work with instant feedback and support, (3) teachers examine performance data to inform instructional decisions, and (4) teachers share and review data with students, discussing common misconceptions. Teachers were expected to assign 20–30 minutes of assignments at least twice a week and regularly review data reports.
requirements: Teachers need systematic professional development and ongoing coaching to implement the loop; teachers were trained to encourage students to rework problems they initially got wrong and to discuss commonly missed questions.
constraints: Developed and evaluated for middle school math homework support aligned to a state curriculum.
target_learners: Grade 7 and 8 middle school math students
target_learning_goals: Grade 7 and 8 mathematics proficiency on state standards
examples: Intervention teachers assigned ASSISTments homework twice weekly with a local coach visiting classrooms three times per school year.

article_title: Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems
citation: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Assessment continuum from standardized tests to student-designed investigations
description: The paper presents assessment strategies as a continuum (Figure 2) running from "Standardized, multiple-choice tests of routine skills" through standardized tests with performance tasks, systems of performance items, multi-week performance tasks, to "Longer, deeper investigations (2-3 months) & exhibitions, including graduation portfolios". Along the continuum, "tasks become more complex, measuring progressively larger and more integrated sets of knowledge and skill". The student's role shifts "from passively receiving and responding to external questions" to "taking increasing initiative for finding and making sense of information".
requirements: Tasks are scored based upon a set of pre-determined criteria, usually codified in a rubric; when comparability is needed, scorers are trained and often moderated
constraints: The paper notes multiple-choice and close-ended items "cannot measure higher level thinking skills or the ability to apply them"
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: deeper learning skills including communication, meta-cognitive and learning-to-learn skills, and resilience
examples: MARS and BAM tasks, SCALE/CCSSO Performance Assessment Resource Bank tasks, NY Performance Standards Consortium portfolios, IB and AP assessments
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L. (2017). Developing and Measuring Higher Order Skills: Models for State Performance Assessment Systems. Council of Chief State School Officers. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606777

article_title: Teaching for Powerful Learning: Lessons from Gateway Public Schools
citation: Cook-Harvey, C. M., Flook, L., Efland, E., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2020). Teaching for powerful learning: Lessons from Gateway Public Schools. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-gateway
title: Design assessment to support learning rather than competition or labeling, using mastery-oriented grading and shared rubrics
description: The report presents Gateway's assessment approach as a design principle: "Assessment at Gateway is designed to support learning rather than competition or labeling." Mastery-oriented grading makes standards, expectations, and goals clear and consistent across teachers, and staff-created shared rubrics are used by students to evaluate their progress, set expectations, choose their level of challenge, and continuously improve their work. Students can show what they know in multiple ways and revise work products until they reach proficiency.
requirements: Shared rubrics created by staff, clear and consistent mastery-oriented grading standards across teachers, and opportunities for revision
constraints: Described as practiced at one school; the report presents it as a promising practice rather than a tested intervention
target_learners: middle and high school students in inclusive classrooms
target_learning_goals: deep learning and continuous improvement of work
self-assessment against clear standards
examples: Performance assessments and exhibitions make learning visible and authentic and provide opportunities for public feedback
key_sources: Cook-Harvey, C. M., Flook, L., Efland, E., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2020). Teaching for powerful learning: Lessons from Gateway Public Schools. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/social-and-emotional-learning-case-study-gateway

article_title: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families
citation: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org/
title: Use asset-framing in assessment reports so results acknowledge system responsibility and student strengths rather than deficit labels
description: The brief holds that "asset-based language and beliefs are fundamental to strong assessment reporting." Asset-framed reports explicitly acknowledge system-level responsibility for providing supports, highlight students' strengths and capabilities, and avoid deficit language such as "student cannot" in favor of phrases like "has yet to demonstrate" or "may need support in." The brief illustrates this with Massachusetts' report language assigning the school a role in determining assistance, contrasted with Delaware and Idaho language it says places the onus on the student.
requirements: Reports must emphasize system-level action rather than faulting individual students, and avoid language reinforcing deficit mindsets
constraints: The brief states asset-framing is not about hiding achievement gaps or lowering expectations for students
target_learners: K-12 students and their families, particularly those from historically underserved backgrounds
target_learning_goals: families' accurate understanding of assessment results and appropriate actions to support grade-level learning
examples: Massachusetts' score report states the school, in consultation with the parent/guardian, should determine the coordinated academic assistance the student needs; New Mexico's use of the label "novice" is cited as a stigmatizing counterexample
key_sources: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED658190

article_title: Design Principles for Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528
title: Assessments must be experienced as a value-add that outweighs their implementation burden
description: The report argues that for assessments to support instruction, "the benefits of engaging in the assessment itself as well as the information yielded significantly outweigh the burden of implementation." Educators identified value-add elements including transparent access to high-quality tasks, student work and educative rubrics, classroom- and school-level reporting focused on instructional shifts, opportunities-to-learn data alongside results, and professional learning for making sense of rich student information such as scoring performance tasks.
requirements: Assessments consistent enough with what teachers already do to be valid measures while providing enough new information to warrant implementation effort
constraints: The compelling benefits differ by context depending on access to high-quality materials, workforce strength, professional learning structures, and historical and cultural elements
target_learners: K-12 students, teachers, and families
target_learning_goals: Instructionally useful assessment information
Educator learning from assessment implementation
examples: Educators named scoring student work on performance tasks as a valuable professional learning opportunity
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528

article_title: Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems: What Is the Role of Performance Assessments?
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469
title: Signaling function of large-scale assessments as a driver of instructional experiences
description: The report describes signaling as the mechanism by which large-scale assessments shape instruction: rich performance tasks provide concrete examples and direct experiences of the kinds of learning opportunities students should have, signaling to educators and leaders the instruction needed to prepare students to complete such tasks. It argues assessment systems frequently make their biggest mark on instruction through this signaling function, influencing what gets taught and what success looks like. The cascade of signals grows as districts adopt predictive interim assessments and item banks mirroring state questions.
requirements: Assessment tasks must model instructional shifts and sophisticated performance expectations for the signal to point toward deeper learning
constraints: The report presents signaling as an authors' interpretation of how assessments influence instruction, not a tested causal result
target_learners: K-12 students in state and district assessment systems
target_learning_goals: deeper learning
disciplinary practices
higher-order thinking and problem-solving
examples: Performance tasks in large-scale programs signal features of effective learning environments and, when curriculum-embedded, provide actual classroom experiences
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Pennsylvania
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Pennsylvania. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: Pennsylvania's Aspiring to Educate program: multiple pathways into teaching with financial supports and district-preparation partnerships
description: Aspiring to Educate is Pennsylvania's Grow Your Own-style investment providing "multiple pathways to high school students, adults, paraprofessionals, and college students to become teachers" with financial supports for preparation. It includes a $500K investment in partnerships between districts and teacher preparation programs, and a "Youth Pathway for Aspiring Educators" giving high school juniors a dual-enrollment path into a partnering institution of higher education with upwards of 30 credits available. The brief rates the state green on GYO support, teacher academies/dual enrollment, and district-preparation partnerships.
requirements: State funding, guidance, and public support for Grow Your Own programs that attract candidates of color
target_learners: High school students, adults, paraprofessionals, and college students
target_learning_goals: Pathways into the teaching profession, particularly for aspiring teachers of color
examples: In June 2022, an additional $1 million of state PAsmart funds went to supporting the next Aspiring to Educate pilot with a focus on diversifying the STEM teacher pipeline.

article_title: Designing assessments in the generative AI era: A tailored assessment framework for ICT tertiary education
citation: Ahangama. (2026). Designing assessments in the generative AI era: A tailored assessment framework for ICT tertiary education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00582-0
title: Assessment Design Matrix (ADM) linking graduate competencies, assessment strategies, and assessment methods
description: The ADM is a tripartite structure that integrates graduate competencies, assessment strategies, and assessment methods into a practical guide for assessment designers. The article states it "provides a practical, hands-on guide for assessment designers to craft integrity-focused assessments that assess ICT graduate competencies", with competencies informing strategy selection, strategies guiding method choice, and methods generating evidence of competency attainment.
requirements: Competencies must be identified before selecting strategies and methods
constraints: Tailored to the ICT discipline

target_learning_goals: ICT graduate competencies including problem-solving, ethics, teamwork, and communication
examples: The matrix demonstrates how competencies inform strategy selection, strategies guide method choice, and methods generate valid evidence of competency attainment

article_title: What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue
citation: Russell Scheinberg, Ameeta Agrawal, Tetyana Sydorenko, Kalab Kahsay, Nina Vyatkina, Griet Boone. (2026). What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22225
title: Transcript-based pipeline for measuring interactional fluency and direction-sensitive uptake from diarized ASR output
description: A reusable analysis pipeline that operationalizes interactional fluency and direction-sensitive linguistic uptake for spoken AI practice "using metrics extractable from diarized ASR output without manual linguistic annotation." The fluency component extracts seven features from word-level timestamps (conversation length, turn count, mean turn duration, words per turn, response latency, floor ratio, within-turn pause ratio). The uptake component tracks lexical adoption via a global timeline with a first-use, first-source-wins rule, and syntactic uptake via four German morphosyntactic template types parsed with the Stanza UD pipeline, with correctness checked against a 91,270-noun gender lexicon. The authors provide it as "a reusable analysis pipeline for rapid, scalable evaluation of conversational AI in educational settings."
requirements: Diarized, timestamped ASR transcripts with verified speaker labels; a baseline monologue preceding each dialogue to establish learner-specific vocabulary baselines
constraints: Transcript-based analysis excludes prosody, pronunciation, stress, intonation, and segmental accuracy
NLP pipelines trained on Standard German may degrade on disfluent L2 speech; word-level ASR errors were not systematically corrected
target_learners: second- and third-year university L2 German learners
target_learning_goals: measuring interactional fluency and linguistic uptake in L2 spoken dialogue practice
examples: Applied to 78 AI dialogues and 39 human-human conversations from four sites, with three AI transcripts' speaker label swaps corrected via a disfluency-rate classifier
key_sources: Russell Scheinberg, Ameeta Agrawal, Tetyana Sydorenko, Kalab Kahsay, Nina Vyatkina, Griet Boone. (2026). What Changes When the Interlocutor Is an AI? Interactional Fluency and Linguistic Uptake in L2 Spoken Dialogue. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22225

article_title: ASR Technology in College English Speaking Instruction: The Role of Feedback Internalization and Metacognitive Strategies
citation: Chen D, Zeng L, Ou W and Zhong S (2026) ASR technology in college English speaking instruction: the role of feedback internalization and metacognitive strategies. Front. Psychol. 17:1847238. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1847238
title: Integrated model of ASR features, metacognitive strategies, and oral proficiency outcomes with language proficiency as moderator
description: The article proposes "a comprehensive theoretical framework that examines the dynamic relation -ships between ASR technology, learner characteristics, and pedagogical outcomes." It positions four ASR features (recognition accuracy, usage frequency, corrective feedback quality, reflection task design) as inputs, reflective behavior and intrinsic motivation as psychological mediators that transform external feedback into internalized learning, and language proficiency as a moderator of the mediator-to-outcome paths. The framework integrates metacognitive strategies with ASR-assisted second language learning and was tested via structural equation modeling.
requirements: Measurement of the four ASR features, the two mediators, proficiency, and oral proficiency improvement via validated questionnaire items
constraints: Tested with self-report questionnaire data from undergraduates at one Chinese university; proficiency classified from self-reported CEFR levels and CET band scores
target_learners: college English learners
undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: oral English proficiency
feedback internalization
self-regulated reflective learning
examples: The model was operationalized as a 34-item questionnaire and estimated with EFA, CFA, and multi-group SEM on 325 valid responses
key_sources: Chen D, Zeng L, Ou W and Zhong S (2026) ASR technology in college English speaking instruction: the role of feedback internalization and metacognitive strategies. Front. Psychol. 17:1847238. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1847238

article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: ASE-26: a twenty-one-module undergraduate curriculum for agentic software engineering
description: ASE-26 is a comprehensive undergraduate curriculum deposited on Zenodo under CC BY-ND 4.0, organising agentic software engineering into twenty-one modules across four parts plus a closing module. Part 1 covers the discipline, Part 2 the environment, Part 3 the engineering (Modules 10 through 18, the largest part), and Part 4 the market, with Module 21 teaching practitioners to keep their mental model of the field fresh. The article states the structure "follows the order in which a practitioner builds capability rather than the order in which the literature was published," and the full text with reference lists is deposited as the canonical reference.
requirements: Students are expected to already have foundational knowledge of computer science and some experience with software engineering
constraints: The curriculum is designed to be revised; Module 21 distinguishes durable principles from contingent capabilities tied to current model and ADE features
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students with foundational computer science knowledge
target_learning_goals: framing and specifying agentic projects
context engineering
verification gate design
multi-agent workflow design
code review against the MRP standard
security and governance of agentic systems
examples: Module 11 covers context engineering; Module 12 covers safety with Git as the primary safety layer; Module 14 introduces five multi-agent workflow patterns from Anthropic's engineering writing

article_title: ASTRA: A Scalable Next-Generation ATCO Training Simulator with Autonomous Simpilots
citation: Ethan Chew, Enjia Wu, Iruss Eng, Ian Lim, Ranen Sim, Brandon Koh, Kaleb Nim, Caden Toh, Wei Dong Soin, Darius Koh, Galen Tay, Prannaya Gupta, Jonathan Koong, Yong Zhi Lim. (2026). ASTRA: A Scalable Next-Generation ATCO Training Simulator with Autonomous Simpilots. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18319
title: ASTRA: an end-to-end ATCO training simulator automating the simpilot role
description: ASTRA is a training simulator that automates the human simpilot role by transcribing ATCO trainee speech, interpreting instructions, and generating pilot and controller responses. It implements "an end-to-end speech-to-speech pipeline to respond to input commands from ATCO trainees with appropriate responses", built on Unity with Cesium Ion geospatial visualization and an instructor-facing interface for configuring and monitoring scenarios.
requirements: Localizes ASR and TTS models to the Singaporean operational context, since frontier models trained on American and British English fail on Singaporean-accented speech
constraints: Higher-order competencies such as planning ability and conflict resolution are outside the evaluation framework's scope
target_learners: Air traffic control operator trainees
target_learning_goals: Radiotelephony communication proficiency
Air traffic control command skills
examples: The paper's five pipeline stages are ASR, Controller Instruction Understanding, Response Generation, Text-to-Speech, and Simulation of Aircraft Movement, modeled after Lin et al. (2021)
key_sources: Ethan Chew, Enjia Wu, Iruss Eng, Ian Lim, Ranen Sim, Brandon Koh, Kaleb Nim, Caden Toh, Wei Dong Soin, Darius Koh, Galen Tay, Prannaya Gupta, Jonathan Koong, Yong Zhi Lim. (2026). ASTRA: A Scalable Next-Generation ATCO Training Simulator with Autonomous Simpilots. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18319

article_title: ASTRA: A Scalable Next-Generation ATCO Training Simulator with Autonomous Simpilots
citation: Ethan Chew, Enjia Wu, Iruss Eng, Ian Lim, Ranen Sim, Brandon Koh, Kaleb Nim, Caden Toh, Wei Dong Soin, Darius Koh, Galen Tay, Prannaya Gupta, Jonathan Koong, Yong Zhi Lim. (2026). ASTRA: A Scalable Next-Generation ATCO Training Simulator with Autonomous Simpilots. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18319
title: Two scenario modalities: open-ended Free-for-All traffic and instructor-authored event-driven Story Mode
description: ASTRA structures training scenarios into two modalities. "In Free-for-Allmode, pre-loaded aircraft create an open-ended environment where trainees manage traffic reactively, suited for advanced users.", while Story Mode lets instructors design event-driven scenarios with a node-based tool in which nodes are aircraft profiles connected by triggers. Each scenario node defines an Event Trigger, an Event Type (the simulation condition to listen for), and an Event Handler (the actions to run), enabling dynamic sequencing that adapts to trainee actions without further intervention.
requirements: Story Mode requires instructors to author node-based scenarios defining aircraft profiles, event triggers, event types, and event handlers
target_learners: Air traffic control operator trainees, from novice to advanced
target_learning_goals: Reactive traffic management
Handling structured event-driven ATC scenarios
examples: Story Mode triggers respond to conditions such as AfterReportingWaypoint, with parameters like Waypoint Name

article_title: From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs
citation: Yi Zhang & Julia Rayz. (2026). From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08009
title: Assess LLM educational control beyond execution correctness before deploying models as educational tools
description: The article argues that excelling at execution benchmarks shows a model can be a proficient problem solver without being an effective educator, and that optimizing solely for functionally correct solutions can cause an "illusion of learning". It recommends that "when deploying LLMs as educational tools, we should look beyond valid problem-solving and actively assess whether a model can recognize educational frameworks, adjust cognitive complexity, and intentionally mutate tasks for different learners." The Bloom-aligned framework provides a concrete evaluation for this.
requirements: Evaluation against an established learning-objective taxonomy rather than pass-or-fail execution metrics alone
constraints: Findings establish a comparative baseline on two Qwen3-Next models; broader validation across additional model families, scales, and training recipes remains an important next step
target_learners: novice programming learners
target_learning_goals: keeping AI-generated tasks within learners' zone of proximal development
examples: The framework revealed that both evaluated models readily synthesize additional cognitive complexity but struggle to produce lower-level mutations for novice-oriented learning
key_sources: Yi Zhang & Julia Rayz. (2026). From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08009

article_title: Evaluation of pre-trained models for pedagogical assessment of novel AI-assisted educational questions
citation: Michael Lawrence Castanares, Princess Ventures, and Allan Tan. (2026). Evaluation of Pre-trained Models for Pedagogical Assessment of NovelAI-Assisted Educational Questions. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27749
title: Asyncform (AF) dataset of 863 teacher-labeled AI-generated educational questions
description: The Asyncform (AF) dataset is an out-of-distribution corpus of AI-assisted educational questions created by the authors to test Bloom-level classifier transfer. The article states: "we generated 863 AEQ covering subjects in English, Mathematics, and Science. AF dataset was labeled with corresponding Bloom Taxonomy level by three K-12 teachers who taught the subjects." Each question received a single Bloom label due to limited staff, and annotation included subject, grade level, learning objectives, and question text.
requirements: Bloom labels supplied by subject-matter K-12 teachers with content information (subject, grade level, learning objectives, question) presented during annotation
constraints: Only a single Bloom label was provided per question due to limited staff
target_learners: K-12 students in English, Mathematics, and Science
target_learning_goals: Bloom Taxonomy cognitive-level alignment of AI-generated educational questions
examples: Used as an OOD test set for TFPOS-IDF ML, DistilBERT, and LLM Bloom classifiers, and for retraining experiments

article_title: Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction
citation: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23177
title: Asymmetric miscalibration account of cognitive offloading to AI (the speedup illusion framework)
description: The article proposes that offloading decisions require calibration — an accurate mental model of one's own and the tool's capabilities — and that for LLMs this calibration is asymmetric: people are "accurate in their prediction of the completion time" for independent work but systematically underestimate AI-assisted time. Grounded in the metacognitive access argument, it holds that people lack privileged access to an LLM's internal workings, and that effort-time conflation sustains the illusion. The framework positions calibration as both a subject and a mechanism for studying AI use.
requirements: Applies to simple cognitive tasks completable under 5 minutes with current LLM assistants; the article notes the complexity level at which AI genuinely saves time is an open question
constraints: Based on between-subjects aggregates with crowdsourced participants; the prediction and completion samples were not completely disjoint
target_learners: US adult Prolific participants completing simple cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: Accurate calibration of when AI assistance saves time versus effort in cognitive offloading decisions
examples: The study operationalized calibration as the gap between predicted and actual completion times across 24 tasks in four categories of LLM use at two difficulty levels.
key_sources: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23177

article_title: CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education
citation: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140
title: AST-based structural command representation using bashlex parse trees, tree metrics, and TF-IDF weighted n-grams
description: A structural representation pipeline that parses Linux/bash commands into abstract syntax trees using bashlex and extracts features from the trees. The article explains that "each command is additionally represented by the multiset of ordered pairs(parent_label, child_label)extracted from the AST," alongside ten numeric tree metrics (node count, depth, max width, leaf count, branching factor, pipelines, operators, redirects, commands, subshells) and TF-IDF weighted n-grams (n = 1 to 4) over the DFS preorder node-kind sequence. This abstracts away lexical content such as file names and arguments, retaining structural relationships that determine command behaviour.
requirements: Valid Linux/bash commands parseable by bashlex; standard scaling of numeric metrics
constraints: Purely syntactic analysis cannot distinguish commands with identical syntax but different operational semantics, such as structurally identical L1 and L2 commands
target_learners: computing education researchers and instructors classifying commands
target_learning_goals: automatic assignment of taxonomy levels from command syntax
key_sources: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140

article_title: DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging
citation: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. Companion Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Systems, Programming, Languages, and Applications: Software for Humanity (SPLASH Companion '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3837729.3840500
title: Assess the debugging process, not only the final patch, because identical final code can hide different debugging competence
description: Classroom assessment that considers only the submitted code and pass/fail test result creates a process-visibility gap: the intermediate steps of reproducing, narrowing, hypothesizing, and verifying leave no durable record. The article argues that "the final code can look identical even when the underlying debugging competence differs", so feedback that ignores the process misses what the exercise was meant to assess. Recording the reproduce-observe-hypothesize-edit-verify chain makes that process reviewable.
requirements: A lightweight, structured record of the debugging process that is cheap to produce, cheap to read, and bounded to the task at hand
constraints: Screen recording and live observation capture the process faithfully but do not scale to large cohorts, are intrusive, and collect far more data than a review task requires; commit history is too coarse and easily rewritten
target_learners: Novice programmers in classroom debugging exercises
target_learning_goals: Systematic debugging investigation rather than lucky guessing or repeated edit-and-test flailing
examples: The article contrasts two students who both submit a passing solution: one may have followed an evidence-based debugging process while the other edited and tested repeatedly until the suite turned green
key_sources: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. article_title: Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship
citation: Shen, N., Lee, L. S., and He, A. (2026). Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1956939
title: Differentiated framework of assistive versus content-generative AI use
description: The article's organizing analytical distinction separates two modes of student engagement with generative AI. As the authors state, "AI mayfunctionasassistivesupportwhenstudentsuseitforideation, referencegathering,processmanagement,reﬁnement,ortechnique learning. It may function diﬀerently when it contributes directly to the content of the ﬁnal work." Assistive use scaffolds students' own creative decisions, while content-generative use enters the authorship of the work itself. The framework is operationalized through two questionnaire indicators, ai_help_pct and ai_content_pct, capturing augmentation-oriented versus substitution-oriented usage.
requirements: AI use must be measured as a mode of participation in the creative process rather than as generic adoption, frequency, or perceived usefulness.
constraints: The two indicators are students' self-estimates of perceived AI involvement rather than precise behavioral measurements or system log data.
target_learners: undergraduate art students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: distinguishing process support from content substitution
visible creative decision-making
examples: The questionnaire asked students to report the perceived proportion of AI assistance in the creative process and the perceived proportion of the final output directly generated or substantially shaped by AI.

article_title: Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics
citation: Zachery Quince and Emily Faulconer. (2026). Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00651-w
title: Design assessments so that task demands, not policy labels, shape which GenAI functions students use
description: The article argues that a purpose-specific or open-use policy label defines what is permitted but cannot determine how students use GenAI; the assessment itself creates the demand. It concludes that "assessment design shapes which GenAI functions become meaningful": tasks rewarding polished communication elicit language and structure uses, while problem-solving tasks elicit checking, clarification, and verification uses. Assessment design that rewards understanding and requires student judgement aligns with the markers of evaluative judgement, keeping constructive alignment intact in the GenAI era.
requirements: Assessment tasks that require application of concepts to real-world scenarios and student judgement
constraints: The study is a single case with limited generalisability and does not establish a causal link between policy and outcomes; confounds include learning progression, tool familiarity, and task complexity
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: maintaining constructive alignment and evaluative judgement when GenAI is available
examples: A1's presentation task made planning, language, and structure support relevant; A2's workbook and A3's quiz made checking, clarification, and verification relevant
key_sources: Zachery Quince and Emily Faulconer. (2026). Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00651-w

article_title: Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI
citation: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3
title: Assessment twins: two deliberately linked assessment components addressing the same outcomes through different modes of evidence
description: The article names and substantively describes assessment twins as a redesign approach for the GenAI era. Twins are conceptualised as "two deliberately linked components that address the same learning outcomes through different modes of evidence, scheduled closely together to allow for cross-verification". The pairing lets instructors triangulate evidence across formats so that validity can be checked even when one format is vulnerable to generative AI misuse.
requirements: The two components must address the same learning outcomes and be scheduled closely together to allow cross-verification.
constraints: The authors acknowledge challenges including resource intensity, equity concerns, and the need for empirical validation.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: course learning outcomes assessed through GenAI-vulnerable formats
examples: The article proposes pairing pedagogically valuable yet GenAI-vulnerable assessment formats so evidence can be triangulated across the twin tasks.
key_sources: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3

article_title: Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI
citation: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3
title: Assessment twin implementation challenges: resource intensity, equity concerns, and pending empirical validation
description: The article identifies a set of implementation challenges accompanying the assessment twin approach. As printed, the authors acknowledge "the challenges, including resource intensity, equity concerns, and the need for empirical validation". These challenges qualify the approach's readiness: designing and marking linked task pairs demands additional resources, may affect students unevenly, and the approach has not yet been empirically tested.
requirements: Adopters should plan for the additional resourcing that designing and marking two linked assessment components requires.
constraints: The approach currently lacks empirical validation, per the authors' own acknowledgement.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of learning outcomes under generative AI availability
examples: The article lists resource intensity, equity concerns, and the need for empirical validation as acknowledged challenges of the twin approach.
