article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Design assessment so that integrity is enacted through transparent, justified decision-making rather than inferred from technological absence
description: The paper's central design principle: assessment should be reconceptualized as the primary site where educational integrity is enacted, shifting attention "from whether GenAI was used to how academic choices were made and responsibility exercised". Assessment structures that foreground decision-making, transparency, and justification render integrity visible within hybrid human-GenAI work and scaffold accountability instead of relying on surveillance.
requirements: Assessment tasks must explicitly require justification, verification, and articulation of decision-making
Educators need shared criteria and professional calibration to interpret articulated judgement consistently
constraints: The paper notes these designs may become performative, with learners aligning discourse to expectations without internalizing commitments
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: accountable ethical reasoning and evaluative judgement in GenAI-augmented work
examples: The paper distinguishes integrity-oriented assessment from authentic assessment: authenticity asks whether a task mirrors real-world practice, whereas integrity-oriented design asks whether learners can justify decisions
key_sources: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model
citation: Vega-Baudrit JR and Rivera Álvarez A (2026) Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model. Front. Educ. 11:1918707. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1918707
title: Make verification an assessed activity, not merely a recommendation
description: This principle holds that verification of GenAI outputs should be built into assessment so that chemical judgment, not fluent production, is the assessed construct. The review states that "Verification should be assessed, not merely recommended" and that student reasoning should remain visible through prompt logs, annotated outputs, drafts, calculations, oral defense, and revision histories. Verification must be operationalized through chemistry-specific checks such as conservation, units, valence, electron flow, stereochemistry, spectral consistency, data provenance, experimental feasibility, and safety.
requirements: Assessment tasks must require students to identify AI errors, defend corrections, or explain why a generated answer should be rejected
Evidence of thinking such as prompt logs, intermediate calculations, and revision histories must be preserved
constraints: A generic recommendation to verify AI output is insufficient without chemistry-specific checks
target_learners: University chemistry students
target_learning_goals: Chemical judgment and verification skills
Independent reasoning in AI-supported tasks
examples: The review describes verification-centered assessment in which students identify an AI error, defend a correction, compare alternative representations, reproduce reasoning without AI, or explain why a generated answer should be rejected
key_sources: Vega-Baudrit JR and Rivera Álvarez A (2026) Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model. Front. Educ. 11:1918707. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1918707

article_title: Tracing GenAI Literacy: Student-AI Interaction Patterns in Academic Writing
citation: Angxuan Chen, Jiyou Jia. (2026). Tracing GenAI Literacy: Uncovering Student-AI Interaction Patterns in Academic Writing through Epistemic Network Analysis. First International Workshop on Advancing AI Literacy with Learning Analytics (AI-LIT) @ LAK26, April 2026.
title: Assess GenAI literacy in situ from prompt patterns rather than relying only on pre-tests
description: The authors argue that because ENA of interaction logs distinguishes literacy groups, "literacy can be assessed in situ": educational systems could analyze prompt patterns to estimate a learner's literacy level dynamically instead of relying on pre-tests. This positions process data as a complement to self-reported or static literacy instruments.
requirements: Requires systems that log and analyze student prompts in real time.
constraints: Findings are preliminary results from one abstract-writing task with 162 students.
target_learners: university students using GenAI tools
target_learning_goals: GenAI literacy assessment
examples: The study compared ENA-projected scores of high- and low-literacy groups classified by a validated GenAI Literacy Test.

article_title: Teaching Intro AI When the Tools Can Do the Homework: A Course Redesign and a Student Bill of Rights
citation: Yusuf Pisan. (2026). Teaching Intro AI When the Tools Can Do the Homework: A Course Redesign and a Student Bill of Rights. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05175
title: Assessment without examinations: weight moved to in-class exercises, reflective writing, and a defended team project that resist unattributed automation
description: This pattern rebuilds grading around tasks a language model cannot quietly ghost-write, on the bet that "an assessment a model can silently complete is a weak assessment." The Spring 2026 grade comprised in-class exercises done in the room in a fixed hour (20 percent), weekly projects that may be reflection, programming, or a mix (40 percent), and a team project (40 percent), with no midterm or final. Reflective writing carries a first-person account of the student's own process, and in-class exercises were graded complete-or-incomplete on submission with AI scores advisory only.
requirements: In-class exercises require a fixed scheduled hour in the room and produce an artifact on the spot
Reflective writing must be required to be in the student's own voice
constraints: The author's own students, asked to design fair grading for such a course, mostly reinvented proctored or handwritten assessment, the strongest internal challenge to this structure
The author makes no causal or learning-outcome claims for the structure
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: artificial intelligence fundamentals
engineering judgment and supervision of AI tools
reflective practice
examples: The Spring 2026 CSS 382 grade was in-class exercises 20 percent, weekly projects 40 percent, and team project 40 percent, with the syllabus stating there was no final exam
key_sources: Yusuf Pisan. (2026). Teaching Intro AI When the Tools Can Do the Homework: A Course Redesign and a Student Bill of Rights. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05175

article_title: RACES: reward-aligned consistent essay scoring with large language models
citation: Zhenxin Zhang, Ziyu Ding, Mengyun Liu and Haiwei Sang. (2026). RACES: reward-aligned consistent essay scoring with large language models. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00607-8
title: ASAP 2.0 dataset of argumentative student essays with 1–6 human-assigned scores
description: The ASAP 2.0 dataset (Crossley et al. 2024) is the public AES benchmark used to evaluate RACES. It "contains approximately 24,000 argumentative essays written by students, covering diverse topics and writing styles", with about 17,000 used for training and the rest for validation and testing. Each essay carries a human-assigned score from 1 to 6 based on strict evaluation criteria, serving as the only human-assigned labels in the experiments.
requirements: Used here with a 1–6 score scale; results are interpreted within this benchmark setting
constraints: The article states results should not be read as evidence of cross-dataset or cross-domain generalization
target_learners: student writers whose argumentative essays populate the dataset
target_learning_goals: automated scoring of argumentative writing quality
examples: RACES and its baselines were trained and evaluated on this dataset with QWK as the agreement metric

article_title: 'Problem-Based Learning and the Structural Conditions for Productive AI Integration'
citation: Michael Rowe. (2026). Problem-based learning and the structural conditions for productive AI integration. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/haet3_v1
title: Assessment should move toward evidence of engagement and away from artefact quality as the primary indicator of learning
description: The essay recommends reorienting assessment from products to making engagement visible and taking it seriously as evidence, because engagement proxies retain meaningful resistance to AI substitution while artefact proxies have become trivially gameable. It states: "Assessment must move toward evidence of engagement and away from reliance on artefact quality as the primary indicator of learning." Proposed alternatives each carry limitations the essay names.
requirements: A deliberate account of what engagement looks like and how to observe it systematically; institutional infrastructure for programmatic assessment
constraints: Assessing engagement at scale remains an open problem; portfolios are resource-intensive, oral examinations raise equity concerns, reflective accounts can be performed, and scalability is unresolved
target_learners: higher education students in professional programmes
target_learning_goals: valid evidence of learning and professional development
examples: The essay lists portfolios, oral examinations, observed clinical practice, reflective accounts, and programmatic assessment as partial answers with real limitations

article_title: Ask Me Anything: Exploring Children's Attitudes Toward an Age-tailored AI-powered Chatbot
citation: Saniya Vahedian Movahed and Fred Martin. (2025). Ask Me Anything: Exploring children's attitudes toward an age-tailored AI-powered chatbot. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14217
title: Ask Me Anything (AMA): a topic-specific, age-tailored child-friendly chatbot
description: Ask Me Anything is a Python chatbot built with CustomTkinter and the ChatGPT API that "answers only topic-specific questions" in three areas: astronomy, sneakers and shoes, and dinosaurs. Its interface has a sidebar for name, grade, age range, and topic selection, and a main area for questions and answers. Prompts include topic and age variables (7-9, 9-11, 12-14) so responses are age-appropriate and on-topic. It was tested with 63 K-8 students; source code is publicly available.
requirements: Uses the OpenAI API with a prompt template carrying topic and age variables to constrain responses to the selected topic and age band
constraints: Answers only its three selected topics; off-topic queries are declined by design
target_learners: K-8 students aged 7-14
target_learning_goals: Fostering balanced and informed engagement with AI technology in educational settings
examples: Used by 63 students over two days at a partner K-8 school, with 3-10 minutes of interaction each and post-surveys

article_title: ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring
citation: Solomon Sunday Oyelere. (2026). ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring and participation-balanced collaboration in introductory programming. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100633
title: ASTRA Synthetic Benchmark Dataset: an open synthetic trace dataset for collaborative programming evaluation
description: An openly archived synthetic dataset mirroring the ASTRA logging schema, encoding a prespecified between-subjects design across three conditions (alone_tutor, pair_tutor, pair_multiagent) and a bank of 20 short Python tasks. It provides turn-level dialogue traces with speaker roles, task-level artefacts (submitted code, correctness, retries, time-to-correct, verification indicators), and a derived-metrics table with precomputed summaries. The article states it is "best interpreted as simulated evidence that supports benchmarking and method development".
requirements: Used with its data dictionary and README documenting generation assumptions and intended use
constraints: Synthetic, not observational data about real learners; results support benchmarking and method development, not causal estimates of learning effects
target_learners: Researchers and developers of trace-based evaluation methods for AI-supported collaborative programming
target_learning_goals: Measurement of interaction dynamics, participation balance, reciprocal engagement, and verification behaviours in introductory programming
examples: The dataset encodes 540 participants across three conditions, 360 sessions, and 1440 task episodes over 20 Python tasks

ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring and participation-balanced collaboration in introductory programming. article_title: ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring
citation: Solomon Sunday Oyelere. (2026). ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring and participation-balanced collaboration in introductory programming. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100633
title: ASTRA prototype: open-source multi-agent tutoring web application with JSONL trace logging
description: A Python Streamlit web application wrapping a multi-agent backend around an LLM API (gpt-4o-mini by default). It instantiates a Pedagogical Tutor Agent (PTA) for conceptual and metacognitive support and a Collaborative Group Agent (CGA) for participation balance and coordination, maintains a lightweight CASM learner-state profile inferred as JSON after each student message, and writes turn-level and solution records to JSON Lines files. The article states the implementation and logging schema are released "as open-source software (Oyelere, 2026b), enabling replication, stress-testing, and extension of trace-based analyses".
requirements: An OpenAI API key supplied via the local environment; human marker grading of final code, as the prototype does not yet execute code automatically or compute correctness without human grading
constraints: Prompt-based guardrails rather than formal safety filters; outputs not fully deterministic because no explicit decoding controls are passed
target_learners: Introductory programming learners in future ethics-approved pilots; researchers testing multi-agent tutoring
target_learning_goals: Conceptual programming support, debugging guidance, balanced participation, and verification behaviour in collaborative Python tasks
examples: The prototype includes three built-in Python tasks: summing numbers from 1 to n, debugging a factorial function, and filtering even numbers from a list

article_title: ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring
citation: Solomon Sunday Oyelere. (2026). ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring and participation-balanced collaboration in introductory programming. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100633
title: ASTRA social–cognitive framework for multi-agent tutoring
description: A framework formalising how social, cognitive, and regulatory information guides multi-agent tutoring in collaborative programming. It models a session as a partially observable multi-agent process in which "ASTRA instantiates the latent state z_t using a structured Cognitive–Affective–Social Model (CASM)" with cognitive, metacognitive, socio-emotional, and group-regulation components. Role-differentiated agents (Tutor, Facilitator, optional Coordinator) condition policies on a belief state over this latent state, and support is framed as optimising a multi-objective reward over task progress, metacognitive quality, and participation-oriented equity proxies.
requirements: Inference of the belief state from interaction traces; in the current implementation, LLM-based inference combined with lightweight trace statistics such as turn ratios and phase markers
constraints: The current prototype does not learn policies by optimising the reward; it approximates desirable behaviour via role-specific prompting and scheduling
target_learners: Novice programmers working alone or in dyads with AI agent support
target_learning_goals: Coordinated cognitive support, metacognitive regulation, and participation-oriented facilitation during collaborative programming
examples: In the multi-agent configuration the Facilitator intervenes when indicators such as participation skew cross pre-defined thresholds

article_title: A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom
citation: Kilinc, S., Aldemir, T., Misiejuk, K., Kaliisa, R., Sabanwar, V., Bicer, A., Song, D., & Yalvac, B. (2026). A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11, 100683. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100683
title: Aspen: a prompt-engineered AI chatbot peer mentor for inquiry revision
description: Aspen is a custom AI chatbot built as a prompt-engineered pedagogical agent on a general-purpose GPT model, not a fine-tuned model, with behavior shaped through system-level instructions, response-format constraints, task-specific scaffolds, and iterative testing. It was positioned as "a peer mentor for middle school agricultural research teams," using brief, friendly, task-relevant language and prioritizing questions, hints, feedback, and explanations over unrestricted answer provision. The web-based interface (Flutter Web) included a text chat window and animated 3-D avatar, with interactions logged in Firebase Realtime Database.
requirements: Task-specific grounding, iterative testing, and prompt constraints to reduce risks of hallucinated or instructionally misaligned content and answer-oriented interaction
constraints: Because Aspen relied on a general-purpose model, its responses remained subject to variability, occasional hallucination, and imperfect alignment with domain-specific instructional goals; safeguards are design measures, not independent verification of response quality
target_learners: eighth-grade students in a rural agriculture-STEM classroom
target_learning_goals: revising research questions and hypotheses against inquiry criteria
examples: Students were instructed to share Aspen's responses aloud, compare suggestions with inquiry criteria, and negotiate whether and how to incorporate them rather than adopt them automatically

article_title: A Posthumanist Approach to AI Literacy
citation: Zhaozhe Wang, Chaoran Wang. (2025). A posthumanist approach to AI literacy. Computers and Composition 76 (2025) 102933. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compcom.2025.102933
title: Assemblage and rhizomaticity as posthumanist concepts for AI-mediated literacy
description: The article deploys Deleuze and Guattari's assemblage and rhizomaticity, elaborated by Bennett, Leander and Burriss, and Sherman et al., to explain how posthumanist relationality plays out in AI-mediated literacy. An assemblage is "always temporarily formed as diverse human agents, nonhuman actants, discourses, and signs come into contact and relate to one another," and assemblages operate rhizomatically, shifting and reconfiguring in any direction. Literacy practices are conceived as forming assemblages in which AI may partake, co-producing meaning with human writers.
requirements: Analysis must attend to language as part of the assemblage, since language mediates human-AI relational dynamics and may reinforce linguistic hierarchies in multilingual contexts
target_learners: literacy researchers and educators
postsecondary writers
target_learning_goals: understanding co-produced meaning in human-AI composing
examples: The authors describe a student's ongoing dialogues with an AI chatbot in which ideas build on AI-generated texts while AI adapts to the student's inputs
key_sources: Zhaozhe Wang, Chaoran Wang. (2025). A posthumanist approach to AI literacy. Computers and Composition 76 (2025) 102933. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compcom.2025.102933

article_title: Exploring the Assistance Dilemma in Experiments with Cognitive Tutors
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Vincent Aleven. (2007). Exploring the Assistance Dilemma in Experiments with Cognitive Tutors. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9049-0
title: The assistance dilemma: balancing information giving and withholding in learning environments
description: The article names and frames the "assistance dilemma" as a fundamental open problem in instructional science: "How should learning environments balance information or assistance giving and withholding to achieve optimal student learning?" It treats results from Cognitive Tutor experiments comparing forms of interactivity as partial answers to this general question, and argues the field needs "specific conditions and parameters that indicate when and to what extent to use information giving versus information withholding forms of interaction."
requirements: Further experimental science to yield specific conditions and parameters indicating when and to what extent to use information giving versus information withholding interactions
constraints: The article states how best to achieve the balance "remains a fundamental open problem in instructional science"
target_learners: Students using intelligent tutoring systems across subject-matter areas
target_learning_goals: Optimal student learning from interactive problem-solving environments

article_title: Scientific Discovery Learning with Computer Simulations of Conceptual Domains
citation: Ton de Jong, Wouter R. van Joolingen. (1998). Scientific Discovery Learning with Computer Simulations of Conceptual Domains. Review of Educational Research. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190680v1
title: Embed assignments, questions, or games in simulations to support learning outcomes
description: Structured prompts such as investigation, specification, and explicitation assignments, guiding questions, and goal-state games support planning and focus learners' attention in simulation-based discovery. The review finds this measure "seems to have a clear effect on the learning outcome", and reports frequent voluntary use of assignments with positive effects on intuitive knowledge in several studies.
requirements: Assignments must be matched to the simulation domain, as in the investigation, specification, and explicitation types the review describes
constraints: The review notes many support studies were still in an engineering phase or combined measures so individual effects could not be traced
target_learners: Students learning conceptual domains such as physics or economics through simulation
target_learning_goals: Intuitive knowledge of the simulated domain
Planning and goal setting in discovery learning
examples: White (1984) used games asking learners to reach a specific simulation state; learners with games outperformed pure-simulation learners on qualitative problems
De Jong et al. (1995) and Swaak et al. (1996) found students used assignments frequently and assignments positively affected intuitive knowledge

article_title: Deaf Individuals’ Bilingual Abilities: American Sign Language Proficiency, Reading Skills, and Family Characteristics
citation: Freel, B. L., Clark, M. D., Anderson, M. L., Gilbert, G. L., Musyoka, M. M., & Hauser, P. C. (2011). Deaf Individuals’ Bilingual Abilities: American Sign Language Proficiency, Reading Skills, and Family Characteristics. Psychology, 2(1), 18-23. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2011.21003
title: Use well-developed ASL as a bridge when teaching English literacy to deaf learners
description: The article argues that instruction for deaf children should build on a fully developed first language rather than apply strategies designed for hearing children. It reports that "fluent ASL-English bilinguals possess grammatically-structured ASL that serves as a bridge to the acquisition of written English", and that teachers often fail to map ASL grammar onto English grammar for students. Bilingual education programs using ASL for general communication and for teaching English, reading, and writing are the recommended approach.
requirements: Teachers must clearly distinguish grammatical differences between ASL and English and teach students how to map one grammar onto the other
Comprehensive development of ASL as a first language should be a priority
constraints: The article notes deaf children often arrive at school without a developed first language, and no national research-based ASL curriculum exists
target_learners: deaf children in bilingual education programs
target_learning_goals: English literacy
reading comprehension
examples: The study's finding that native signers exhibited more proficient bilingual abilities than non-native signers supports the bridge role of early full ASL exposure

article_title: Child maltreatment and ADHD symptoms in a sample of young adults
citation: Sanderud K., Murphy S., Elklit A. (2016). Child maltreatment and ADHD symptoms in a sample of young adults. European Journal of Psychotraumatology. https://doi.org/10.3402/ejpt.v7.32061
title: Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS v1.1) six-item screening measure for probable adult ADHD
description: The ASRS v1.1 is a six-item self-report screening instrument measuring the frequency of core ADHD symptoms — concentration problems, hyperactivity, and memory problems — on a 5-point Likert scale from "never" to "all the time". Items were recoded so a symptom was present at ≥3 on the first three questions and ≥4 on the remaining three, and a binary probable-ADHD variable used a threshold of ≥4. In this study it produced a Cronbach alpha of 0.66 and classified 431 (14.5%) participants above cutoff.
requirements: Respondents answer six frequency items on a 5-point Likert scale; a probable ADHD classification requires the ≥4 threshold on the recoded binary variable
constraints: The article reports a Cronbach alpha of 0.66 in the current sample and notes the measure is a screening tool based on self-report, not a clinical diagnosis
target_learners: young adults (24-year-old cohort)
target_learning_goals: screening for attention, hyperactivity, and memory problems consistent with probable adult ADHD
examples: Used with 2,980 young Danish adults; 431 (14.5%) scored above the cutoff for probable ADHD

article_title: Game-based learning: A design-based theory of teaching–learning–assessment systems
citation: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/
title: Gordon's transactional troika: assessment, teaching, and learning as inseparable, mutually reinforcing processes
description: Gordon proposes that assessment, teaching, and learning form a dynamic, dialectical system rather than separate stages of education. He writes that he describes them "as a kind of troika or three-legged stool: each element supports and strengthens the others, and none should function independently of the whole." In this transactional view, an assessment is a two-way exchange in which the student is an active agent who interprets tasks, uses feedback, and brings identity and feeling into the interaction. The handbook series is organized around this reconceptualization, treating assessment as embedded in pedagogy rather than as an external verdict passed on learning after the fact.
requirements: Assessment must be implemented in a supportive, trustful environment so it feels like an extension of teaching rather than a judgment from on high
constraints: The authors frame this as a vision requiring institutional change; conventional high-stakes testing regimes currently operate outside this paradigm
target_learners: All learners across preK-12, higher education, workplace, and informal settings
target_learning_goals: Intellective competence and human development
examples: Gordon cites Feuerstein's instrumental enrichment tasks, which functioned as assessments and interventions at once
key_sources: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/

article_title: Game-based learning: A design-based theory of teaching–learning–assessment systems
citation: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/
title: Design assessments as learning opportunities that challenge and teach at the same time
description: The principle holds that assessments should be crafted as rich problems, projects, or simulations that both elicit evidence of learning and produce it. Gordon writes that "assessments can be designed as learning opportunities: rich problems, projects, or simulations that both challenge students to apply their knowledge and teach them something in the process." When students receive scaffolded support such as hints, feedback, and opportunities to try again, the assessment itself contributes to development, shifting it from a static checkpoint to a dynamic, educative experience.
requirements: Scaffolded support (hints, feedback, opportunities to try again) so the assessment contributes to development
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: Problem solving, inquiry skills, deeper learning
examples: A challenging science investigation that doubles as an assessment of inquiry skills and a chance for students to refine experimental reasoning
key_sources: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/

article_title: Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers
citation: Willis, Colin, Tracy Powell-Rudy, Kelsie Colley, and Joshua Prasad. 2021. Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers. Journal of Intelligence 9: 53. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence9040053
title: Assess non-social cognitive traits in a non-social manner to fairly evaluate autistic and neurotypical candidates
description: The article argues that assessing non-social cognitive traits in a non-social manner may provide a fair way to assess both autistic and neurotypical candidates' readiness for the same job. Removing socially laden demands avoids cognitive disruption that social situations cause autistic individuals, and each game used measured non-social traits found to have the smallest group differences in prior meta-analytic work. The study's results support this for a narrow set of cognitive abilities.
requirements: Assessment content must align with non-social cognitive traits shown to have minimal group differences in traditional formats
constraints: The pattern is not expected to hold for content autistic individuals typically struggle with, such as social or emotional assessments
target_learners: autistic job seekers
neurotypical job seekers
target_learning_goals: fair assessment of job-relevant cognitive ability in selection
examples: The study administered game-based packages measuring working memory, visuospatial ability, and math-based memory, finding no or small group differences
key_sources: Willis, Colin, Tracy Powell-Rudy, Kelsie Colley, and Joshua Prasad. 2021. Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers. Journal of Intelligence 9: 53. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence9040053

article_title: Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs
citation: Diego Zapata-Rivera, Carol Forsyth, Edith Aurora Graf and Yang Jiang. (2024). Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs. Leveraging Large Language Models for Next Generation Educational Technologies, CEUR Workshop Proceedings. https://ceur-ws.org
title: ASATA authoring pipeline for RegExp/LSA conversation-based assessments
description: The AutoTutor Script Authoring Tool for Assessment (ASATA) implemented earlier CBAs by converting conversation diagrams into XML scripts, using LSA and RegExp to parse student responses and determine agent reactions. Conversations included one or two virtual agents interacting with the student and lasted between 2-5 turns. The authors describe this as an expensive methodology requiring time and various expertise: "This process took weeks for conversations to go from the initial descriptions to conversation diagrams to actual script conversations implemented into ASATA and tested with user data." Automated script-based testing of regular expressions with sample responses reduced iterations and testing time but remained limited by the time needed to develop and change regular expressions.
requirements: Conversation diagrams documenting construct information, conversation paths, closing statements, and partial scoring rules
Sample responses gathered from experts, small-scale pilot studies, and crowdsourcing efforts for automated testing
constraints: Development and testing were time-consuming, requiring manual entry of possible student responses and weeks of effort per conversation
target_learners: middle-school students
target_learning_goals: science inquiry skills
examples: The 2014 scientific inquiry volcano scenario CBA with two agents, a main question, 2-5 turns, and partial score assignments was built through this pipeline

Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs. Leveraging Large Language Models for Next Generation Educational Technologies, CEUR Workshop Proceedings. https://ceur-ws.org

article_title: Are Individual Differences in Arithmetic Fact Retrieval in Children Related to Inhibition?
citation: Bellon E, Fias W and De Smedt B (2016) Are Individual Differences in Arithmetic Fact Retrieval in Children Related to Inhibition? Front. Psychol. 7:825. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00825
title: Associative-network interference account of arithmetic fact retrieval
description: The article works within the theoretical account that arithmetic facts are stored in an associative network in semantic memory, so that retrieving one fact activates competing facts that must be inhibited. It states that "arithmetic facts are particularly prone to interference" because of shared features, and that poor inhibition could yield specific errors such as answering 6 × 3 = 24. This framework motivated the study's hypothesis that cognitive inhibition would relate to fact retrieval, a hypothesis the data did not support in typically developing children.
requirements: The account presupposes that competing problem-answer associations are formed and stored in long-term memory during fact learning
constraints: The present study's data did not support the predicted inhibition–fact-retrieval association in typically developing third graders
target_learners: typically developing third-grade children learning single-digit arithmetic
target_learning_goals: automatized retrieval of single-digit arithmetic facts
examples: The study used multiplication verification items with table-related false solutions (e.g., 6 × 3 = 24) to probe competing associations
key_sources: Bellon E, Fias W and De Smedt B (2016) Are Individual Differences in Arithmetic Fact Retrieval in Children Related to Inhibition? Front. Psychol. 7:825. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00825

article_title: The contribution of executive functions to narrative writing in fourth grade children
citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2015). The contribution of executive functions to narrative writing in fourth grade children. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-015-9558-z
title: Assess a variety of low- and high-level executive functions with standard neuropsychological measures when studying developing writers
description: The authors argue that conceptualizing EF only as self-regulation strategies misses low-level EF contributions. They state "it is necessary to assess a variety of EF, including low-level EF with standard neuropsychological measures, in order to acquire more insight into the contribution of EF to writing outcome in developing writers". Their broad battery revealed direct and indirect EF contributions.
requirements: A broad test battery covering inhibition, updating, shifting, and planning
constraints: Findings are from one grade (fourth) and one genre (narrative)
target_learners: developing writers in elementary school
target_learning_goals: written composition
examples: The study administered eight EF tasks including Tea-Ch subtests, WISC-IV Digit Span, D-KEFS tasks, and Tower of London

article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: Assess and address computer anxiety before introducing students to an LMS
description: Because computer self-efficacy mediates anxiety's negative effect on perceived ease of use, the authors recommend that "prior to introducing prospective students to the LMS they should be tested for any computer anxieties they may have". Addressing anxiety as part of the e-learning experience enhances it, and reducing anxiety increases the return on e-training investment in corporate settings.
requirements: Instructors or administrators need a way to identify students' computer anxiety levels before LMS deployment
constraints: Findings map to the specific LMS and learning tools studied; caution is needed generalizing across other LMS technologies
target_learners: prospective LMS users in higher education
employees in corporate e-training
target_learning_goals: reducing computer anxiety to enhance e-learning experience and performance
examples: The study surveyed 649 students at semester end after a year of LMS use in undergraduate MIS and FIT courses

article_title: Digital Inclusion in Older Adults: A Comparison Between Face-to-Face and Blended Digital Literacy Workshops
citation: Martínez-Alcalá CI, Rosales-Lagarde A, Alonso-Lavernia MÁ, Ramírez-Salvador JÁ, Jiménez-Rodríguez B, Cepeda-Rebollar RM, López-Noguerola JS, Bautista-Díaz ML and Agis-Juárez RA (2018) Digital Inclusion in Older Adults: A Comparison Between Face-to-Face and Blended Digital Literacy Workshops. Front. ICT 5:21. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2018.00021
title: ASSURE instructional design model for face-to-face and blended older-adult instruction
description: The ASSURE model is the instructional design framework the authors used to structure both workshop modalities. It presents "6 phases: Analyze learners, State objectives, Select instructional methods and materials, Utilize materials, Require learner response, and Evaluation and revision." The authors chose it because it "has the necessary characteristics to implement face-to-face and blended instruction" and can adapt course or lesson design systematically. They credit it with producing adequate structure, attractive text colors and images, quality materials, and clear instructions attentive to older adults' visual, cognitive and emotional characteristics.
requirements: Instructors must analyze learner characteristics, including visual deficiencies, cognitive and emotional abilities, before designing materials
target_learners: older adults aged 60 and above with little or no ICT knowledge
target_learning_goals: digital literacy skills: use and knowledge of computers, the Internet, and daily life devices
examples: The blended workshop was developed under ASSURE guidelines, yielding a space with adequate structure and design, attractive text colors and images, quality teaching materials and clear instructions

Front. ICT 5:21. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2018.00021

article_title: Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: an event‐related brain potential study
citation: Stevens Courtney, Lauinger Brittni, Neville Helen. (2009). Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: An event-related brain potential study. Developmental Science, 12(4), 634-646. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00807.x
title: Because neural mechanisms underlying similar behavioral performance can differ by group, assessments should examine underlying processing mechanisms rather than relying on behavior alone
description: The article argues that examining the neural systems underlying a cognitive ability can reveal distinct mechanisms behind similar behavioral performance: "examining the neural systems underlying a particular cognitive ability can identify different mechanisms that give rise to similar impairments in behavioral performance." In the study, children with SLI showed a signal-enhancement deficit while children of lower maternal education showed a distractor-suppression deficit, though both involve impaired selective attention behaviorally. The authors also cite the D'Angiulli et al. study, in which lower-SES adolescents used different attentional mechanisms to achieve similar behavioral performance. This supports designing assessments and interventions informed by the specific processing stage at which difficulty arises.
requirements: Access to process-sensitive measures such as ERPs, which the article notes index attention online "without requiring overt behavioral responses"
constraints: ERP spatial resolution is poor, limiting inferences about specific neural networks; findings here concern early auditory selective attention specifically
target_learners: young children with attention or language difficulties, including children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds and children with specific language impairment
target_learning_goals: accurate identification of which attentional mechanism (signal enhancement vs. distractor suppression) underlies a learner's difficulty
examples: The article contrasts the distractor-suppression deficit it documents in children of lower maternal education with the signal-enhancement deficit previously reported in children with SLI using the same paradigm
key_sources: Stevens Courtney, Lauinger Brittni, Neville Helen. (2009). Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: An event-related brain potential study. Developmental Science, 12(4), 634-646. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00807.x

article_title: Associations between preschool language and first grade reading outcomes in bilingual children
citation: Davison, Megan Dunn; Hammer, Carol; Lawrence, Frank R. (2011). Associations between Preschool Language and First Grade Reading Outcomes in Bilingual Children. Journal of Communication Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3138808/
title: Assess bilingual children's language growth over time in both languages rather than performance at a single point
description: The article recommends that preschool programs target children's progress in acquiring language rather than their performance on a test at one time. It states that "language assessments that focus upon the growth of children's language development may provide a better understanding of the impact of children's language abilities upon reading development." Because bilingual children's proficiencies in each language are still changing, single-point assessments may miss their current underlying proficiencies; periodic assessment in both languages reveals whether growth is occurring and whether instructional modifications are needed.
requirements: Data on children's language abilities in both languages must be collected at entry to an educational setting and then assessed periodically to determine change in each language
constraints: The study's evidence base is limited to children in English-immersion Head Start classrooms; generalization to other instructional contexts is limited
target_learners: bilingual preschool children from low-socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: oral language development in both languages supporting later reading
examples: The study used growth curve modeling across four measurement occasions in Head Start rather than single-point scores, using raw scores to capture individual change patterns
key_sources: Davison, Megan Dunn; Hammer, Carol; Lawrence, Frank R. (2011). Associations between Preschool Language and First Grade Reading Outcomes in Bilingual Children. Journal of Communication Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3138808/

article_title: American Sign Language Syntax and Analogical Reasoning Skills Are Influenced by Early Acquisition and Age of Entry to Signing Schools for the Deaf
citation: Henner J, Caldwell-Harris CL, Novogrodsky R and Hoffmeister R (2016) American Sign Language Syntax and Analogical Reasoning Skills Are Influenced by Early Acquisition and Age of Entry to Signing Schools for the Deaf. Front. Psychol. 7:1982. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01982
title: American Sign Language Assessment Instrument (ASLAI)
description: The ASLAI is a computerized battery of receptive ASL assessments developed by the research team. As the article describes it, "The ASLAI is a comprehensive battery of 11 multiple choice receptive language tasks presented via computer." Stimuli and responses are presented via video; participants can pause or replay videos and select responses by clicking a button above a corresponding video. Two subtests were analyzed here: a 27-item syntactic judgment task tapping nine ASL syntactic structures, and a 24-item analogy task with six analogy types. Schools received detailed reports of students' ASL abilities for IEP planning.
requirements: Video presentation of stimuli in ASL; computer platform capable of displaying pictures and videos
constraints: The analyzed data came from students who scored above chance (25%) on the tasks; schools provided background records but no parental survey data on home signing amount or socio-economic status
target_learners: Deaf students ages 7;6–18;5 in schools for the Deaf
target_learning_goals: assessment of ASL syntactic knowledge
assessment of vocabulary and metalinguistic analogical reasoning skills
examples: Used with 688 students for the analogy task and 455 for the syntactic judgment task, administered in groups of 5–20 students

article_title: Intelligence quotient, short-term memory and study habits as academic achievement predictors of elementary school: A follow-up study
citation: Alberto Quilez-Robres, Alejandro González-Andrade, Zaira Ortega and Sandra Santiago-Ramajo. (2020). Intelligence Quotient, short-term memory and study habits as academic achievement predictors of elementary school: a follow-up study. https://www.frontiersin.org
title: Psychoeducational evaluation of low-achieving elementary pupils should assess study habits alongside IQ, and study-habit programs should start before age 8
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that evaluation of children with poor achievement must not rest on cognitive variables alone: "it is essential to measure  study habits also". Because study habits significantly predicted achievement in both years and are, per the authors, easy to learn, the article recommends programs "focused on improving the study  habits of children before 8 years". IQ and study habits should be evaluated preferentially, while short-term memory is apparently less important, though the authors call for more research on that point.
requirements: Evaluation of children with low academic performance should include both IQ and study-habit measures rather than cognitive variables alone.
constraints: The authors note more research is needed on the role of short-term memory, and results come from a small medium-high socioeconomic sample.
target_learners: Elementary school pupils aged 8-9 years
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement across curricular subjects
examples: The study measured study habits with the SHTQ questionnaire in 3rd grade and found study habits a significant predictor of grades in both 3rd and 4th grade.

article_title: Effects of problem size, operation, and working-memory span on simple-arithmetic strategies: differences between children and adults?
citation: Ineke Imbo · André Vandierendonck. (2008). Effects of problem size, operation, and working-memory span on simple-arithmetic strategies: differences between children and adults? Psychological Research (2008) 72:331–346. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-007-0112-8
title: Adaptive strategy choice model (ASCM) of simple-arithmetic strategy selection and efficiency
description: The adaptive strategy choice model (ASCM) of Siegler and Shipley (1995), as described in this article, holds that people have several strategies available and choose the fastest and most accurate one, governed by a confidence criterion determining how sure they must be to state a retrieved answer and a search length determining how many retrieval attempts are made before switching to a procedural strategy. Retrieval efficiency depends on the peakedness of problem–answer associations, whereas procedural efficiency depends on the difficulty of executing the particular procedure. The study used the model to derive the prediction that retrieval frequency correlates with retrieval efficiency but not with procedural efficiency.
requirements: Learners must have multiple strategies available (retrieval and procedural strategies) for the same problems
A confidence criterion and a search length criterion govern when retrieval is preferred over procedural strategies
constraints: The article tests the model's predictions only for simple addition and multiplication in primary-school children (second, fourth, and sixth grade)
target_learners: primary-school children learning simple arithmetic (second, fourth, and sixth graders)
target_learning_goals: simple-arithmetic fact retrieval and procedural strategy use in addition and multiplication
examples: The study regressed retrieval latencies and procedural latencies on percentage retrieval use per grade to test the model's prediction about which efficiencies correlate with retrieval frequency

article_title: The Same yet Different: Oral and Silent Reading in Children and Adolescents with Dyslexia
citation: Madelon van den Boer, Loes Bazen, Elise de Bree. (2022). The Same yet Different: Oral and Silent Reading in Children and Adolescents with Dyslexia. Journal of Psycholinguistic Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10936-022-09856-w
title: Include silent reading in dyslexia diagnosis and treatment, especially for adolescents, alongside oral reading assessment
description: The article recommends that diagnosis and intervention for dyslexia consider both reading modes, because diagnosis is usually based on oral reading while accommodations target silent reading. It states "It seems important to include silent reading in diagnosing reading disabilities and dyslexia especially for adolescents", and that specific treatment of silent reading, in addition to oral reading, should be considered, with continued monitoring of both modes for individuals with dyslexia.
requirements: Valid measures of silent reading fluency for education and diagnostic examinations, which the authors note still need development
constraints: For primary school children oral and silent fluency are still interchangeable, so the need is greatest from adolescence onwards; the silent task used included simple task performance, which may have underestimated silent reading ability
target_learners: children and adolescents with dyslexia
adolescents in secondary education
target_learning_goals: reading fluency assessment and diagnosis
reading fluency intervention and accommodations
examples: Study 2 used an ecologically valid silent reading task in which adolescents read a text including instructions for six simple tasks, following the procedure of Gagliano et al. (2015).

article_title: Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn
citation: Graesser, A. C. (2016). Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0086-4
title: AutoTutor Script Authoring Tool (ASAT) and generic AutoTutor Conversation Engine (ACE) licensed for new content and applications
description: The AutoTutor Script Authoring Tool (ASAT, Cai et al. 2015) lets researchers at other universities, businesses, and organizations develop their own content and integrate it with the generic AutoTutor Conversation Engine (ACE). The article reports that Wolfe et al. (2015) used the authoring tools to build a website on genetic risk factors for breast cancer (BRCA) and reported learning gains above the existing website on the same topic. Educational Testing Service is licensing ASAT for assessment in virtual worlds, and the Army Research Laboratory has incorporated AutoTutor in its open source Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT).
requirements: Authors supply their own content scripts via ASAT, which integrate with the generic ACE conversation engine
target_learners: middle school students (ALEKS mathematics integration)
adults reading about genetic risk (BRCA website)
assessment populations in English language learning, science, and mathematics (ETS)
target_learning_goals: domain learning across STEM topics, reading comprehension, writing, scientific reasoning, and competency assessment
examples: Wolfe et al. (2015) used the AutoTutor authoring tools to develop the BRCA website on genetic risk factors for breast cancer, reporting learning gains above the existing website on the same topic.

The article argues that a design combining social capital mechanisms with essential teacher learning and PD characteristics can support participation and collaborative knowledge building at a distance, and draws implications for asynchronous online PD approaches to reach more teachers.

constraints: Studied with a small number of teachers in the science domain

article_title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
citation: Shupin Li · Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen · Päivi Häkkinen (2022). Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:191–223 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09369-7
title: When assigning students to pairs for computer-based CPS tasks, attend to both their social and their cognitive CPS skill capacities
description: The article's pedagogical implication: because dyad composition in social and cognitive CPS skills relates to productive CPS, teachers should consider students' social and cognitive capacities when forming pairs for computer-based CPS tasks. The authors state that "our results offer empirical evidence recommending greater awareness of the students' social and cognitive capacities in CPS when assigning them into pairs for computer-based CPS tasks." The principle rests on the finding that pairs with at least one high-social/high-cognitive member conducted more actions and transitions. In authentic classrooms, groups are often formed voluntarily, which the article notes can lead to off-task behavior, so a retrospective look at skill composition matters.
requirements: Awareness of students' individual social and cognitive CPS skill levels (e.g., from assessment reports) before pair assignment; the ATC21S scoring engine produces reports for teacher and student use.
constraints: The pair composition–productivity relationship was examined retrospectively in one asymmetric task (Olive Oil) with randomly assigned pairs of sixth graders; no recommendation follows for optimal pair formations beyond awareness of capacities.
target_learners: sixth-grade students working in dyads in computer-based CPS assessment
target_learning_goals: productive collaboration and collaborative problem solving
examples: The study randomly assigned 166 sixth graders to 83 pairs (female, male, and mixed-gender pairs) and categorized them into five skill-based pair compositions before comparing their transition network measures.

citation: Carolyn Rosé · Sanna Järvelä. (2022). Supporting perspective taking across chasms of thinking: Do real-time analytics hold the key?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09378-6
title: Aim for assessment as both a measure of and catalyst for human growth beyond standardized achievement exams
description: In its wrapping-up section the editorial declares the articles "highlight the central importance of assessment as both a measure of and catalyst for human growth" and urge the field to aim for impact extending beyond standardized intellectual achievement exams, building technologies that enable and improve collaboration amid entrenched social conflict.

collaboration across perspectives
shared meaning making

article_title: Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process
citation: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328
title: Evaluate learners' Gf and Gc before designing comprehensive instructional interventions, relying on narrower CHC abilities for more focused areas
description: The article recommends that education planners assess broad fluid and crystallized abilities prior to intervention, stating that "the evaluation of these broad intelligence factors prior to any specific intervention may allow education planners to make more informed decisions." It advises educators and curriculum designers to bear both abilities in mind when designing comprehensive interventions and curricular materials, particularly for individuals with specific learning disabilities, while noting that interventions within more focused and limited areas should probably rely on narrower abilities within the CHC taxonomy.
requirements: Cognitive ability measures capable of indexing the broad Gf and Gc factors for the target population
constraints: The article limits the recommendation to comprehensive interventions; for focused, limited areas it recommends narrower CHC abilities instead
target_learners: Students in comprehensive instructional programs, including individuals with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Improved instructional design decisions and learning performance across intervention sequences
examples: The study modeled Gf and Gc as predictors of latent intercept and slope growth factors in a one-week instructional project

article_title: Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study
citation: Nederhand, M. L., Tabbers, H. K., Jongerling, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2020). Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09233-9
title: Ask students for grade estimates after each exam as an easy-to-implement way to improve calibration accuracy in secondary education
description: The article concludes that simply having students estimate their grade after each exam, before receiving the actual grade, improves their calibration accuracy over a school year without needing additional reflection support. As the authors state, "asking for grade estimates is an easy-to-implement way to improve calibration accuracy of students in secondary education." The practice fits existing classroom routines since grades are already collected.
requirements: Students must actually provide a grade estimate before receiving the actual grade, as part of regular exam administration.
constraints: Improvement was demonstrated in one subject (French) with objectively scored exams; calibration did not improve in non-intervention courses (German, Math).
target_learners: secondary school students, years 1–3 of Dutch pre-university education (ages 12–16)
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of exam performance; calibration accuracy; metacognitive monitoring
examples: Across a school year, students in all three conditions filled out an estimate form after each French exam, sealing it in an envelope before receiving the graded exam about a week later.
key_sources: Nederhand, M. L., Tabbers, H. K., Jongerling, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2020). Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09233-9

article_title: Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases
citation: van Gog, T., & Sweller, J. (2015). Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases. Educational Psychology Review, 27, 247–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9310-x
title: Association-building explanations for why the testing effect decreases with material complexity
description: The review advances an explanatory account built on two existing explanations for low element interactivity materials: free recall improves retention through organization of information during recall, and paired-associate testing strengthens memory traces via mediators. Both hinge on "elaborative processes that establish relations between information elements", which are less necessary when such relations are inherent to complex material, and restudy may instead afford relational processing of elements while maintaining student motivation.
requirements: The account assumes testing benefits arise mainly from establishing associations between elements during retrieval
constraints: The review notes "very few studies have systematically evaluated theoretical explanations for the memorial benefits of testing"
target_learners: school and university students learning curriculum content
target_learning_goals: explaining when and why retrieval practice benefits retention
key_sources: van Gog, T., & Sweller, J. (2015). Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases. Educational Psychology Review, 27, 247–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9310-x

article_title: Screening Smarter, Not Harder: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Screening Algorithms and Heuristic Stopping Criteria for Systematic Reviews in Educational Research
citation: Campos, D. G., Fütterer, T., Gfrörer, T., Lavelle-Hill, R., Murayama, K., König, L., Hecht, M., Zitzmann, S., & Scherer, R. (2024). Screening Smarter, Not Harder: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Screening Algorithms and Heuristic Stopping Criteria for Systematic Reviews in Educational Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09862-5
title: ASReview open-source machine-learning abstract screening software
description: ASReview is an open-source machine-learning tool for abstract screening in systematic reviews, used in this study's retrospective simulation. The article states that "the ASReview software, an open-source platform, provides multiple learning algorithms for both feature extraction and classification." Researchers install it, load a study database (titles and abstracts), classify a small initial subset, then choose a feature extraction method, classifier, balancing strategy (default dynamic resampling), and query strategy (default certainty-based sampling). The algorithm iteratively suggests the study predicted most relevant for the reviewer's include/exclude decision.
requirements: A study database including at least the titles and abstracts of the searched studies, in formats such as .csv, .txt, or .xlsx, plus initial classification of a small subset of relevant and irrelevant studies for training.
constraints: The article states that ASReview currently lacks clear guidelines for when to stop, and it continues to suggest studies until all records have been reviewed.
target_learners: Researchers conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses in education and educational psychology
target_learning_goals: Efficient and reliable identification of relevant studies during the abstract screening phase of systematic reviews
examples: The study ran 270 retrospective simulation runs (ten learning algorithms across 27 abstract collections) in ASReview's simulation mode, using dynamic resampling and certainty-based sampling.

Screening Smarter, Not Harder: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Screening Algorithms and Heuristic Stopping Criteria for Systematic Reviews in Educational Research. article_title: Active Student Participation in Whole-School Interventions in Secondary School. A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Sara Berti, Valentina Grazia, Luisa Molinari. (2023). Active Student Participation in Whole-School Interventions in Secondary School. A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09773-x
title: Five-level scale of Active Student Participation (ASP) in whole-school intervention activities
description: The review proposes an organizing structure that grades program activities on a 5-point scale of active student participation, partly following the school participation scale of the HBSC questionnaire (De Róiste et al., 2012). As the review states, "It ranged from Very high levels of ASP, attributed to activities in which students were given a fully decision-making role, to Very low levels of ASP, given to activities in which students were just the recipients of activities delivered by adults." Very high ASP covers decision-making processes and school action teams with students; high ASP covers student artifacts, student-led activities for peers and for adults; moderate ASP covers platforms, interactive assemblies and data collection; low ASP covers trainings, group and individual activities within adult-designed formats. Levels are not mutually exclusive, and coding was based on the qualitative analysis of students' role, not the number of students involved.
requirements: Activities must be coded by qualitative analysis of the role attributed to students, not by the number of students involved
Levels are not mutually exclusive, so each program may include different levels of ASP
constraints: In the reviewed sample, no program involved students solely as passive recipients (Very low ASP), since such studies were excluded by the inclusion criteria
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: student participation in school activities and decision-making
improving the school learning environment
examples: The review coded all 13 programs on this scale (Table 5): e.g., SEHER included activities at every level from decision-making committees to teacher-led workshops, while STAC's activities were limited to peer-leader trainings

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: Assessment Triangle Model: cognition, observation, and interpretation as interdependent elements of classroom assessment
description: The article adopts Pellegrino, Chudowsky, and Glaser's (2001) Assessment Triangle Model to structure how teachers engage in classroom assessment. The authors write: "According to this model, assessment involves the three core elements of cognition, observation, and interpretation, which Pellegrino and colleagues represented as three vertices of a triangle to highlight their interdependency." Cognition concerns models of student learning, observation concerns designing sensitive assessment events, and interpretation concerns making meaning from evidence to inform teaching.
requirements: Teachers must attend to all three interdependent components to create assessment events that measure learning, allow valid interpretation, and inform teaching decisions
constraints: Teachers often struggle to transform assessment information into instructional actions even with access to student responses
target_learners: teachers
teacher educators
target_learning_goals: designing and interpreting classroom assessment events
examples: Dr. Jones applies the three components when assessing students' understanding of Piaget, Vygotsky, and Information Processing Theory

article_title: Applying multilevel modelling to content analysis data: Methodological issues in the study of role assignment in asynchronous discussion groups
citation: De Wever, B., Van Keer, H., Schellens, T., & Valcke, M. (2007). Applying multilevel modelling to content analysis data: Methodological issues in the study of role assignment in asynchronous discussion groups. Learning and Instruction, 17, 436-447. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.04.001
title: ASIMeC — analysis scheme identifying message characteristics along five dimensions
description: ASIMeC is a content analysis scheme developed by the authors to identify message characteristics along five dimensions: moderating, summarising, adding new discussion points, adding theory, and adding external information. Unlike the Gunawardena et al. (1997) interaction analysis model, it "is specifically related to the different roles", and was developed "to provide more information about the actual role adoption in the discussion groups". Each unit of analysis (the complete message) receives a code along each dimension, with ordered categories such as mentioning versus actively discussing theory or sources. Krippendorff's alpha reliabilities ranged from 0.59 to 0.75 across dimensions.
requirements: Trained independent coders; the article reports approximately 3 hours of training plus 4 hours of joint coding before independent coding
Interrater reliability checked on a sample of transcripts using Krippendorff's alpha
constraints: Applied to transcripts of asynchronous discussion groups in an educational sciences course; approximately 2859 of 3345 messages were analysed along its five dimensions
target_learners: Freshmen students in asynchronous discussion groups
target_learning_goals: Identifying role adoption and message characteristics in collaborative discussion transcripts
examples: The dimension adding external information differentiates mentioning external sources without linking to the discussion from actively using and discussing new external sources

Applying multilevel modelling to content analysis data: Methodological issues in the study of role assignment in asynchronous discussion groups. article_title: Nonsymbolic and symbolic magnitude comparison skills as longitudinal predictors of mathematical achievement
citation: Xenidou-Dervou, I., Molenaar, D., Ansari, D., van der Schoot, M., & van Lieshout, E.C.D.M. (2017). Nonsymbolic and symbolic magnitude comparison skills as longitudinal predictors of mathematical achievement. Learning and Instruction, 50, 1-13. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.11.001
title: Assess both symbolic and nonsymbolic magnitude comparison when measuring children's early numerical cognition, because the two measures play different developmental and predictive roles
description: The article's design assessed children on "two well-known nonsymbolic and symbolic magnitude comparison measures" across three school years, together with IQ and working memory. Because the two skills showed different developmental trajectories and different predictive strengths for mathematics, studies of early numerical cognition should not rely on a single measure type. The article's own results motivate including both measure types in longitudinal designs.
requirements: Longitudinal assessment across at least kindergarten, grade 1 and grade 2 to capture the differing developmental trajectories and predictive windows
constraints: Nonsymbolic comparison was only moderately predictive in kindergarten, so its predictive value is limited to early stages
target_learners: children in kindergarten through grade 2
target_learning_goals: mathematical achievement
numerical magnitude comparison skills
examples: The study assessed a large sample in kindergarten, grade 1 and grade 2 on two well-known nonsymbolic and symbolic magnitude comparison measures, also assessing initial IQ and developing working memory capacities.

article_title: Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view
citation: Jessica Massonnié, Maryse Bianco, Laurent Lima, Pascal Bressoux. (2018). Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.005
title: Assess vocabulary, syntax and oral text comprehension separately when predicting early reading comprehension
description: The article recommends a fine-grained conceptualisation of oral comprehension in early reading instruction and assessment. Because a three-factor structure distinguishing "lower level language skills (vocabulary, syntax) and discourse skills (oral text comprehension)" fit better than a single oral language factor, aggregating these measures risks masking which component drives reading comprehension. In this study LLL skills, but not discourse skills, predicted end-of-first-grade reading comprehension, so aggregated measures would have obscured this differential contribution.
requirements: Measures of vocabulary breadth, syntactic skills and oral text comprehension must each be administered separately rather than combined into one oral comprehension score.
constraints: Evidence comes from French first-graders in a moderately transparent orthography; the two oral factors were highly correlated (.81 at T1, .73 at T2).
target_learners: First-grade pupils learning to read
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Oral language assessment
examples: The study assessed vocabulary breadth, syntactic skills and oral text comprehension as separate measures at T1 and T2 and entered them as distinct latent factors in SEMs.
key_sources: Jessica Massonnié, Maryse Bianco, Laurent Lima, Pascal Bressoux. (2018). Longitudinal predictors of reading comprehension in French at first grade: Unpacking the oral comprehension component of the simple view. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.01.005

description: The article's preregistration disclosure records the registration status of each study. It states: "Study 1 was not preregistered. Study 2 was preregistered at https://aspredicted.org/B4B_Z2Y; Study 3a at https://aspredicted.org/wdh4-776z.pdf and Study 3b at https://aspredicted.org/4g95-kcq3.pdf". The disclosure further answers that the analysis plan was registered prior to examining the data, that there were no additional registrations, no changes to the preregistered primary confirmatory analysis, and that all registered analyses are reported.
requirements: Preregistrations are hosted on AsPredicted at the printed links
constraints: Study 1 was not preregistered, per the disclosure

target_learning_goals: effects of adult ability attributions on children's test cheating

article_title: How you read affects what you gain: Individual differences in the functional organization of the reading system predict intervention gains in children with reading disabilities.
citation: Siegelman, N., Rueckl, J. G., van den Bunt, M., Frijters, J. C., Zevin, J. D., Lovett, M. W., Seidenberg, M. S., Pugh, K. R., & Morris, R. D. (2022). How you read affects what you gain: Individual differences in the functional organization of the reading system predict intervention gains in children with reading disabilities. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114(4). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000672
title: Evaluate reading intervention response separately for different reading outcomes rather than only composite gains
description: Because reliance on O-P and imageability differentially predicted gains across reading measures, the authors argue that "these results highlight the need to separately consider different intervention outcomes - as some individuals may show responses on some outcomes more than on others". Analyses of each of the five subtests separately revealed differential predictive effects that composite scores would have masked. Future studies should account for differential variability in gains across outcomes while recognizing that component skills ultimately impact one another.
requirements: Outcome measures covering distinct reading components (e.g., untimed and timed word and pseudoword reading, comprehension) administered at multiple time points
constraints: The reading system is dynamic and multidimensional; differential components should not be treated as fully orthogonal
target_learners: Children with reading disabilities receiving remediation
target_learning_goals: Word reading
Pseudoword decoding
Reading comprehension
examples: The study modeled gains separately for Word Attack, Phonemic Decoding Efficiency, Letter-Word Identification, Sight Word Efficiency, and Passage Comprehension
