article_title: Vocational interest profiles in secondary school: Accounting for multiplicity and exploring associations with future-oriented choices.
citation: Slot, E. M., Bronkhorst, L. H., Akkerman, S. F., & Wubbels, T. (2021). Vocational Interest Profiles in Secondary School: Accounting for Multiplicity and Exploring Associations With Future-Oriented Choices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(5), 1059–1071. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000475
title: Vocational interest assessment in secondary school should account for students holding interests in multiple vocational domains
description: Because many secondary students show similar levels of interest across different vocational activities, interest assessment should capture multiplicity rather than force a single dominant domain. The article notes that "vocational interest assessment tools generally do not account for the possibility that students are interested in multiple vocational domains, potentially challenging students' future-oriented decisionmaking processes". Profile-based assessment (e.g., latent profile analysis over RIASEC scales) is the article's approach to this.
requirements: Interest measures covering multiple vocational domains so combinations can be detected
constraints: The article does not claim nondifferentiated profiles indicate uncertainty; it finds the opposite pattern is not necessary
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: accurate vocational interest assessment
informed educational career decisions
examples: A latent profile analysis on six RIASEC interests in 358 Grade 9 students identified seven profiles, of which 40.8% were nondifferentiated

Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(5), 1059–1071. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000475

article_title: The function of selection of assessment leads evaluators to artificially create the social class achievement gap.
citation: Autin, Frédérique; Batruch, Anatolia; Butera, Fabrizio. (2019). The function of selection of assessment leads evaluators to artificially create the social class achievement gap. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000307
title: Use assessment for learning (formative comments) rather than selection (normative grading) to avoid evaluator bias against low-SES students
description: The article shows that the function assessment serves shapes evaluator behavior: when assessment is used to compare, rank and track students (normative grading), evaluators judge low-SES students' work more harshly; when used for learning (formative comments), this bias is reduced. The article reports the SES difference in mistakes was "reduced in the assessment for learning condition". This supports designing assessment to serve learning rather than selection where the goal is equitable evaluation.
requirements: Assessment tasks must be evaluated under a clearly learning-oriented framing (formative comments) rather than a selection framing (compare, rank and track students).
constraints: The bias-reduction effect did not reach significance in Experiment 4, though the internal meta-analysis confirmed the overall effect.
target_learners: lower and higher socio-economic status (SES) students in educational settings
target_learning_goals: equitable assessment of student performance
examples: Participants graded a test attributed to a high- or low-SES student using normative grading or formative comments; the low-SES penalty appeared under normative grading and was reduced under formative comments.
key_sources: Autin, Frédérique; Batruch, Anatolia; Butera, Fabrizio. (2019). The function of selection of assessment leads evaluators to artificially create the social class achievement gap. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000307

article_title: “So no one feels left out”: Latinx youths’ and parents’ reimagined school realities in the context of cultural stressors.
citation: Lorenzo-Blanco, Elma I., Henriquez, Kimberly L., Romero, Michelle Y. Martin, Stein, Gabriela Livas, & Isaza, Alejandra Garcia. (2025). “So no one feels left out:” Latinx youths’ and parents’ re-imagined school realities in the context of cultural stressors. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000956
title: Community cultural wealth, freedom dreaming, and desire-based frameworks positioning youths’ and parents’ reimagined realities as precursors for social change
description: The article draws on community cultural wealth (Yosso, 2005), freedom dreaming (Kelley, 2002), desire-based research (Tuck, 2009), and the integrative model of minority child development. These frameworks challenge deficit views and position hopes and dreams as “a precursor for social change.” The study focuses on aspirational capital, which “involves youths’ and families’ ability to maintain hopes and dreams in the face of structural inequality.” Participants’ magic-wand re-imaginations elicit this aspirational capital to identify school-level intervention targets.
requirements: Research must center youths’ and parents’ voices, positioning them as experts in naming their reality and desired changes.
constraints: The frameworks were applied to Latinx youth and parents in six high schools with high Latinx and economically disadvantaged enrollment in one Central Texas district.
target_learners: Latinx high school students and their parents
target_learning_goals: School belonging and engagement
Socio-emotional well-being
Healthy youth adjustment despite cultural stressors
examples: Youth and parents responded to the magic-wand prompt describing ideal school realities, which the authors read as expressions of aspirational capital in the context of cultural stressors.
key_sources: Lorenzo-Blanco, Elma I., Henriquez, Kimberly L., Romero, Michelle Y. Martin, Stein, Gabriela Livas, & Isaza, Alejandra Garcia. (2025). “So no one feels left out:” Latinx youths’ and parents’ re-imagined school realities in the context of cultural stressors. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000956

article_title: Students' motivational profiles and achievement outcomes in physical education: A self-determination perspective.
citation: Julie Boiché, Philippe Sarrazin, Frederick Grouzet, Luc Pelletier, Julien Chanal. (2008). Students’ Motivational Profiles and Achievement Outcomes in Physical Education. Journal of Educational Psychology, 100 (3), pp.688-701. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.100.3.688
title: Assess students' motivation as distinct profiles rather than a single global self-determination index
description: Because different types of motivation can combine into distinct profiles with different achievement consequences, educators and researchers should assess students' motivational profiles instead of relying only on a global indicator of self-determined motivation. The article states its purpose was to examine "whether the different types of motivation proposed by SDT can combine into distinct profiles" and discusses "the implications for the assessment of students' motivational profile." Identifying a student's profile allows targeting interventions at the dominant motivation types.
requirements: Measurement instruments capturing the separate intrinsic and extrinsic motivation types, plus a clustering procedure, to assign students to profiles.
constraints: Evidence comes from physical education settings with high school students over 10-week gymnastics cycles.
target_learners: high school students
target_learning_goals: achievement, effort, and performance in physical education
examples: Two studies assessed motivation at the start of gymnastics cycles and linked cluster-derived profiles to end-of-cycle performance, effort, and grades.

article_title: The method of educational assessment affects children’s neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence
citation: Howard, S. J., Burianová, H., Calleia, A., Fynes-Clinton, S., Kervin, L. and Bokosmaty, S. (2017). The method of educational assessment affects children's neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0010-9
title: For assessment to support tailored educational support, results must accurately reflect students' competency levels (assessment for learning)
description: The article argues that identifying student needs and providing tailored supports is a fundamental aim of assessment, necessitating that results "accurately reﬂect their levels of competency". It invokes the distinction between assessment of learning and assessment for learning, noting a student underperforming due to literacy or WM constraints rather than lacking numeracy knowledge may not benefit from mathematical remediation. Assessment methods should therefore be aligned with, and derived from, the intended learning outcomes.
requirements: Assessment must be clearly aligned with, and derived from, the intended learning outcomes
constraints: Even systematic bias preserves relative rankings across years, regions, schools and students, but undermines needs identification
target_learners: school students whose standardised assessment results inform educational support decisions
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of competency levels to guide bespoke educational support
examples: The article cites findings that WM training can improve numeracy among low-numeracy children, and that children not improving with remediation show immature WM-related strategies

article_title: Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning. npj Science of Learning 6:24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00103-w
title: Assess a learner's prior knowledge before teaching new content
description: Because prior knowledge steers learning in ways that depend on activation, relevance, and congruency, the article concludes that assessing what a learner already knows remains essential before instruction. The author writes "it remains of outmost importance to assess a learner ’s prior knowledge before teaching her some new content", while noting that how that knowledge steers learning is a matter for future research. Unraveling these systematics is explicitly flagged as unfinished work.
requirements: Determine not only the amount of prior knowledge but also whether it will be activated, is relevant, and is congruent with the to-be-learned content
constraints: The article offers no tested procedure for how assessment should capture activation, relevance, or congruency; the meta-analysis studies it reviews did not report correlations of misconceptions with learning gains
target_learners: students receiving domain-specific instruction at any level
target_learning_goals: improving learning gains from instruction by anticipating how existing knowledge will interact with new content
examples: The commentary recommends assessment in the context of the meta-analysis finding that pretest knowledge predicted outcomes but not gains, and notes the meta-analysis included misconception measures whose correlation with gains was not reported
key_sources: Garvin Brod. (2021). Toward an understanding of when prior knowledge helps or hinders learning. npj Science of Learning 6:24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00103-w

article_title: The Future of Adaptive Learning: Does the Crowd Hold the Key?
citation: Heffernan, N. T., Ostrow, K. S., Kelly, K., Selent, D., Van Inwegen, E. G., Xiong, X., & Williams, J. J. (2016). The Future of Adaptive Learning: Does the Crowd Hold the Key? Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:615–644. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0094-z
title: ASSISTments online learning platform and its experiment infrastructure
description: ASSISTments is a free online learning platform of Worcester Polytechnic Institute providing "students with assistance while offering teachers assessment", currently used by hundreds of teachers and over 50,000 students with over 10 million problems solved last year. It supports randomized controlled experiments with student-level randomization at low cost, has enabled over 18 peer-reviewed articles since 2002, and provides feedback types including correctness feedback, mistake messages, hints, and scaffolds, plus actionable item reports surfacing common wrong answers.

constraints: The framework set forth may or may not be generalizable to other platforms
target_learners: K-12 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics skill practice with elaborated feedback and teacher assessment
examples: Item reports show percent correct and common wrong answers (e.g., 27% correct on one problem, about half of wrong answers sharing the misconception 1/9^10) with a +feedback link for writing mistake messages

article_title: Intelligent Augmented Reality Training for Motherboard Assembly
citation: Giles Westerfield, Antonija Mitrovic & Mark Billinghurst. (2015). Intelligent Augmented Reality Training for Motherboard Assembly. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:157–172. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0032-x
title: ASPIRE constraint-based tutor authoring process applied to a procedural AR assembly task
description: ASPIRE is an authoring system and deployment environment for constraint-based tutors. For MAT the authors followed the standard ASPIRE procedure with no changes to the authoring system: describing task characteristics (an 18-step procedural assembly task), composing a domain ontology of 14 concepts with properties and relationships, specifying problem/solution structures (with multiple correct solutions accepted where several configurations are valid), and generating a domain model of 275 constraints. ASPIRE-Tutor then performs student modelling, feedback and problem selection, matching every student action to constraints and providing progressively more detailed feedback as the student struggles.
requirements: Feedback messages generated automatically from templates must be re-written by the author in some cases to be more understandable to students
constraints: ASPIRE generates text-based interfaces automatically, and supporting an external interface such as AR requires its remote procedure call protocol
target_learners: novice users learning procedural assembly skills
target_learning_goals: correctly performing multi-step procedural assembly with adaptive feedback
examples: The ITS used the Boolean isOpen property of the MemorySlot concept to determine whether a memory slot had been successfully opened, with the value set via the AR interface

article_title: Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs
citation: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:118–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0030-z
title: Astus's knowledge-based system: a knowledge representation approach in which each type of knowledge unit has a clearly defined semantic on which the MTT's pedagogical module can rely
description: Astus is a model-tracing tutor (MTT) framework whose knowledge-based system models the task as the teacher's instructions rather than as the procedural knowledge of an ideal learner. The article states this is "achieved by designing a knowledge representation approach in which each type of knowledge unit has a clearly defined semantic on which the MTT 's pedagogical module can rely on." Its procedural knowledge uses goals and procedures organized in a procedural graph comparable to hierarchical task networks; its declarative knowledge uses concepts, relations and functions accessed through a fixed task-independent query interface. This lets the pedagogical module "automatically generate interventions as well as the pedagogical content used to instantiate them."
requirements: The task model must be authored with goals, procedures, concepts, relations and functions whose semantics are known to the MTT, with task-specific manipulations done through Astus's fixed query interface
constraints: Astus does not have the capability to interpret how the requested information is produced, since instantiation through task-specific processes cannot be explained by the MTT
target_learners: computer science undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: well-defined procedural tasks such as AVL tree element insertion and subtraction
examples: The article illustrates hint generation using MTTs for the insertion of elements into an AVL tree and for subtraction, e.g. the totally ordered sequence procedure PInsert achieving the goal GInsert.
key_sources: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:118–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0030-z

article_title: Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs
citation: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:118–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0030-z
title: A taxonomy of error types an MTT can diagnose via impasse-and-repair interpolation, organized by knowledge unit, repair type and observed error
description: The article enumerates the error types Astus can diagnose in a table listing, for each error, "1) the knowledge unit that might have been incorrectly executed, 2) the possible sources of the error (repair types) and 3) a description of the observed error." The taxonomy includes path disruption, relation/function swap, relation/function place/parameter swap, incorrect condition, violated order constraint, incorrect object order, incomplete for-each procedure, loop early stop, continued loop and no loop. The article states "Table 1 contains a list of all the different types of error that Astus can diagnose."
requirements: Each error type is tied to a specific procedural knowledge unit type (query, conditional, sequence, for-each or loop procedure) whose semantics the MTT knows
constraints: Some error types can be associated with many repair types; when an error involves executing the wrong sub-goal, the article states it is not possible to accurately identify what caused the incorrect sub-goal to be executed
target_learners: computer science undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: negative feedback on errors in well-defined procedural tasks
examples: A violated order constraint error can be caused by an incorrect knowledge of the order constraint (barge-on), or by the learner avoiding the correct sub-goal via no-op or back-up.

article_title: The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading
citation: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8
title: Five-era historical taxonomy of ASAG systems: four methodology eras plus an evaluation era
description: The review organizes 35 identified ASAG systems into five thematically consistent time periods it calls eras. As the article states, "The five eras are concept mapping, information extraction, corpus-based methods, and machine learning, and evaluation"; the first four are method-based while the fifth is evaluation-based, reflecting a movement toward reproducibility, standardized corpora, and permanent evaluation. Each era is defined, then each system receives its own section with an ID cross-referenced to component tables.
requirements: Systems are assigned to their dominant era when they overlap multiple eras, keeping activities as disjoint as possible
constraints: Era time periods may overlap with others
The historical review covers 35 systems and 2 competitions as identified by the authors

target_learning_goals: automatic assessment of short natural-language responses to objective questions

article_title: The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading
citation: Steven Burrows, Iryna Gurevych, Benno Stein. (2015). The Eras and Trends of Automatic Short Answer Grading. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0026-8
title: ASAP '12 SAS Kaggle competition dataset for short answer scoring
description: The Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) short answer scoring competition was hosted on Kaggle in 2012, covering ten questions of varied high-school-level subject matter from arts to science. "The participants were given 1,800 student answers for training, which were randomly taken from a pool of 3,000." A further 6,000 student answers were used for testing, and agreement between predicted and human-judge-resolved scores was evaluated with quadratic weighted kappa. The review examines the top three systems from a modified ranking: Tandella '12, Zbontar '12, and Conort '12.
requirements: Each student answer is associated with the score to predict and a confidence score
constraints: A few participants kept their code and methodology private, forcing a modified top-5 ranking that excluded the original 1st, 5th, and 6th submissions
target_learners: high school students across arts and science subjects
target_learning_goals: predicting scores for short answers with agreement to human judges
examples: Zbontar '12 used stacking to combine ridge regression, support vector regression, gradient boosting, random forests, and k-nearest-neighbor base learners into a final ridge regression model

article_title: Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor
citation: Mehak Maniktala, Christa Cody, Tiffany Barnes, Min Chi. (2020). Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371
title: Assertions: unsolicited hint steps presented in the workspace as partially-worked example steps
description: Assertions are a hint delivery mechanism in the Deep Thought logic tutor: "Assertions are partially-worked example steps designed to appear within a student workspace, and in the same format as student-derived steps, to show students a possible subgoal leading to the solution." Each Assertion adds a cyan node with the hint content, labels it "Subgoal", marks it unjustified with a question mark, and asks the student to justify it before using it. They appear automatically after about 40% of steps, and their design draws on contiguity, attention, expectation, and persuasion principles to reduce help avoidance.
requirements: Requires data-driven hint content, generated in this tutor by the Hint Factory from prior students' transaction log data.
Assertions must be justified by the student before the hint content can be used in the solution.
constraints: Assertions were evaluated in a single domain (propositional logic proofs) with undergraduate engineering students.
Only one unsolicited hint may be present at a time and the hint content is not updated based on new student work.
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students learning propositional logic
target_learning_goals: multi-step problem-solving strategies
efficient proof construction
domain rule application
examples: In the Deep Thought tutor, students in the treatment condition received Assertions after about 40% of their steps, resulting in 3-4 hints per problem given the mean 9-step training solutions.
key_sources: Mehak Maniktala, Christa Cody, Tiffany Barnes, Min Chi. (2020). Avoiding Help Avoidance: Using Interface Design Changes to Promote Unsolicited Hint Usage in an Intelligent Tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.13371

article_title: Preface-Emerging Technologies and Landmark Systems for Learning Mathematics and Science: Dedicated to the Memory of Erica Melis-Part 2
citation: Sergey Sosnovsky & Bruce M. McLaren & Vincent Aleven. (2014). Preface-Emerging Technologies and Landmark Systems for Learning Mathematics and Science: Dedicated to the Memory of Erica Melis-Part 2. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0025-9
title: ASSISTments ecosystem: teacher-centric, minimalist-intelligence math homework platform enabling unobtrusive research at scale
description: ASSISTments is a mathematics learning system whose special-issue contribution focuses on its mission and lessons learned rather than a study summary. It outlines "the entire 'ASSISTments ecosystem' that enables collecting usage data and conducting research studies, while ensuring that the normal learning process is not compromised in any way." Its design is very teacher-centric, involving teachers from content authoring to planning experiments. Each year tens of thousands of school children use it to learn math. It deliberately follows a minimalist approach to intelligence and adaptivity, with no strong student model and no sophisticated adaptation procedure.
requirements: High level of teacher involvement in all aspects of the system's usage, from content authoring to planning experiments
constraints: Does not support a strong student model and does not implement a sophisticated adaptation procedure
target_learners: school children learning math
teachers
target_learning_goals: mathematics skills
examples: Used every year by tens of thousands of school children to learn math; research is conducted unobtrusively within normal classroom use.

article_title: Short-Answer Grading for German: Addressing the Challenges
citation: Ulrike Padó, Yunus Eryilmaz, Larissa Kirschner. (2024). Short-Answer Grading for German: Addressing the Challenges. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00383-w
title: ASYST: an easy-to-use automated grading system with local processing and Excel-based workflow
description: ASYST (Automated Grading System) is a graphical user interface wrapping the German Transformer SAG model (and an English model) so that teachers without programming skills can generate automated grade suggestions. It "takes as input an Excel sheet containing student answers and correct reference answers", optionally accepts existing manual grades for reliability analysis, and runs grading locally: "Automated grading is fully local, which precludes data protection issues because the student answers never leave the teacher's computer." Results are saved as an Excel sheet for teacher review. It is released as a compiled Windows 11 executable with open-source Python code.
requirements: An Excel sheet containing student answers and correct reference answers as input
constraints: The tool covers only the languages supported by its wrapped SBERT models; an evaluation mode for model performance on one's own data is a future development goal
target_learners: teachers grading short-answer tests in German universities and schools
target_learning_goals: efficient and trustworthy automated short-answer grading support
examples: Six experienced teachers generated grade suggestions with ASYST in individual test runs and saved results in a new Excel sheet, with 100% task completion and SUS 88.8

article_title: Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback
citation: Gerdes, A., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & van Binsbergen, L. T. (2016). Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0080-x
title: Ask-Elle: a strategy-based model tracing and property-based testing tutor for Haskell
description: Ask-Elle is a web-based intelligent tutoring system for the functional programming language Haskell that supports the stepwise development of programs by verifying the correctness of incomplete programs and providing hints. Its main functionality is obtained by means of "strategy-based model tracing and property-based testing": a programming strategy derived from teacher-specified model solutions is used to trace a student's refinement steps, and QuickCheck properties are tested when no model solution can be recognised. Teachers add exercises by providing a task description, model solutions, and properties, and can annotate these with feedback messages and adjust the flexibility allowed in student solutions.
requirements: Teachers must provide a task description, one or more model solutions, and a configuration file with QuickCheck properties for each exercise
constraints: The tutor cannot give feedback on student programs that deviate from a path towards one of the model solutions
target_learners: first-year computer science students learning Haskell
target_learning_goals: incremental development of correct, well-designed functional programs
key_sources: Gerdes, A., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & van Binsbergen, L. T. (2016). Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0080-x

article_title: Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback
citation: Gerdes, A., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & van Binsbergen, L. T. (2016). Ask-Elle: an Adaptable Programming Tutor for Haskell Giving Automated Feedback. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0080-x
title: Class 3 programming exercises with teacher-configurable feedback and flexibility
description: Ask-Elle offers class 3 programming exercises, which can be solved by applying alternative solution strategies, in contrast to class 1 exercises with a single correct solution and class 2 exercises with different implementation variants of a fixed strategy. Teachers add exercises by providing model solutions and a configuration file, and can use annotations (DESC, FB, MUSTUSE, ALT) to adapt feedback and control which implementations are accepted. This design allows teachers to accept or reject solutions based on different model solutions, such as an inefficient but simple recursive solution.
requirements: Teachers must specify model solutions and a configuration file with properties for each exercise
constraints: The tutor cannot give feedback on programs that deviate from a path towards a model solution
target_learners: first-year computer science students
target_learning_goals: independent program design using alternative solution strategies

title: Design online coursework through an asset lens that considers students' cultural and racialized experiences
description: The principle holds that instructors designing online coursework should treat students' cultural and racialized experiences as assets rather than deficits. The article states that instructors "might consider the cultural and racialized experiences of their students through an asset lens as they design online coursework." It frames this as a design orientation for equitable online instruction.

constraints: Offered as a commentary recommendation during COVID-19 emergency online teaching, not a tested design

article_title: An exploratory case study of the use of a digital self-assessment tool of 21st-century skills in makerspace contexts
citation: Ourania Miliou, Maria Adamou, Aekaterini Mavri, Andri Ioannou. (2024). An exploratory case study of the use of a digital self-assessment tool of 21st-century skills in makerspace contexts. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10314-0
title: Assessmake21 digital self-assessment tool for 21st-century skills in makerspaces
description: Assessmake21 is a web-based digital self-assessment tool, developed as an expansion of SkillsTrack, that supports self-assessment of 21st-century skills in makerspace contexts. Students tag a skill they are using during making, which triggers reflection challenges such as building a visual portfolio with uploaded photos; completing challenges progresses them through levels, and educators award badges. It offers a Definitions feature with conceptual and operational definitions drawn from frameworks such as P21, and an educator's dashboard showing individual and classroom progress. The article reports it offers tagging of five skills: Collaboration, Creativity, Problem-solving, Life/Social Skills, and Communication.
requirements: A teacher sets up and manages a virtual classroom on the educator's dashboard, registering students with a unique login code and choosing one of three self-assessment approaches (parallel, parallel tapping with challenges at the end, or at-the-end).
constraints: The tool offered limited options for skills that could be tagged, and teachers recommended expansion to a broader skills repertoire; tablet use posed typing and multi-tab difficulties.
The vocabulary of the skill conceptualisations was difficult for some 12-year-old students.
target_learners: K-12 students aged 12-18 in makerspace contexts
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment and reflection on 21st-century skills (collaboration, creativity, problem-solving, life/social skills, communication) during making activities
examples: Six teachers used the tool across formal and non-formal makerspaces for 6-7 months, with activities including programming, digital fabrication, robotics, circuitry, and arts and crafts.

strategic problem solving

article_title: Socioeconomic and economic factors affecting access and progression in medical schools: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Arianpoor Arash, Pena Alexia, Mercer Annette, Cox Jennifer, Lekkas Dimitra, Geronimo Francis Ruel, Waldron Heidi, Randal John, Dabner Marcus, Lynagh Marita, Pather Nalini, Shepherd Nicole, Robb Nigel, Berdin Rose, Wilkinson Tim, Hu Wendy, Shulruf Boaz, Huang Pin-Hsiang. (2026). Socioeconomic and economic factors affecting access and progression in medical schools: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.6
title: ASReview Lab with the SAFE procedure for machine-learning-assisted systematic review screening
description: The review used ASReview Lab (version 2.1.1) to prioritize records for title-abstract screening via active learning, following the five-step SAFE stopping procedure: random training-set screening, model-prioritized review with the ELAS-u4 model, stopping after at least 50 consecutive irrelevant records, a second pass with ELAS-h3, and quality assurance of the 10 highest- and lowest-ranked unscreened records. The authors state that "ASReview was used to prioritize records for screening, and screening continued until the predefined stopping rules (SAFE…) were met." Of 2,822 deduplicated records, 477 were manually reviewed and 32 studies included.
requirements: A manually screened random training subset containing at least 1 relevant and 1 irrelevant record is required to train the active learning model.
constraints: Records ranked below the SAFE stopping point were not manually screened and were assumed irrelevant based on model predictions; the authors note potential model-related omissions as a technical challenge.
target_learners: researchers conducting systematic reviews in education and health professions education
target_learning_goals: efficient and transparent study screening in systematic reviews
examples: The review screened 2,822 records, manually reviewed 477 titles and abstracts, and included 32 studies; a second round with an independent training set identified no new relevant studies.

article_title: Annual Research Review: Associations of socioeconomic status with cognitive function, language ability, and academic achievement in youth: a systematic review of mechanisms and protective factors.
citation: Rakesh, D., Lee, P. A., Gaikwad, A., & McLaughlin, K. A. (2025). Annual Research Review: Associations of socioeconomic status with cognitive function, language ability, and academic achievement in youth: a systematic review of mechanisms and protective factors. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 66(4), 417–439. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.14082
title: ASReview: machine-learning-based tool for systematic review screening
description: The review used ASReview (Active learning for Systematic Reviews), a machine-learning-based tool to conduct systematic reviews. ASReview uses a combination of human input and machine learning to iteratively select and classify relevant research papers for inclusion. Starting from a randomly presented list of records, the researcher labels records as relevant or not relevant, and ASReview learns from this input and progressively reorders records from most to least relevant. Simulations indicate that screening a range of 8%–33% of records can identify at least 95% of the relevant records.
requirements: Selection criteria and stopping rule must be pre-established for ASReview to be effective.
constraints: ASReview is not entirely bias-free.

article_title: The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review.

title: Arthroscopic Surgical Skill Evaluation Tool (ASSET) global rating scale
description: ASSET is a global rating scale for arthroscopic surgical skills. The review describes that the "ASSET global rating scale consists of nine domains, including a weighted descriptor, 'additional complexity of procedure', as a control measure for special skills", with each domain discriminating novice, competent and expert levels on a 5-point Likert-type scale. It was the most frequently used GRS in the reviewed studies (10 studies) and, per the review, the only GRS demonstrating reliability in both simulated and clinical environments.

surgeons

title: ASAP-SAS corpus of short-answer scoring prompts and rubrics
description: The ASAP-SAS corpus "comprises diverse prompts and scoring rubrics for short answer scoring" and was the subject of a Kaggle competition from over a decade ago. It contains 10 rubric-scored items used across the meta-analyzed studies, with human-rater QWK benchmarks available for each item (Shermis, 2015). Despite sophisticated prompt engineering and fine-tuning, state-of-the-art models including frontier decoders fall short of human-level agreement on this corpus. The dataset is publicly available at https://www.kaggle.com/c/asap-sas.

article_title: Asymdystopia: The Threat of Small Biases in Evaluations of Education Interventions That Need to Be Powered to Detect Small Impacts
citation: John Deke, Thomas Wei, and Tim Kautz. (2018). Asymdystopia: The threat of small biases in evaluations of education interventions that need to be powered to detect small impacts. SREE Spring 2018 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Asymdystopia: larger samples are not necessarily better for Type 1 error control when bias persists
description: Asymdystopia is the authors' named concept for a context in which increasing sample size does not improve, and can worsen, inference. They define it as "a context in which a larger sample size is not necessarily better and could even be worse from the perspective of controlling the Type 1 error rate." The mechanism is that the standard error in the t-statistic denominator shrinks faster than a biased numerator, so a fixed bias can turn a non-significant estimate significant as samples grow.
requirements: Applies when bias stays the same or shrinks less slowly than the standard error as sample size grows
constraints: Illustrated with a hypothetical example in which bias of 0.05 with standard error 0.20 gives a non-significant t-statistic, but bias 0.025 with standard error 0.01 gives t = 2.5
target_learners: education researchers and evaluators designing impact studies
target_learning_goals: understanding how study design choices affect the validity of impact estimates
key_sources: John Deke, Thomas Wei, and Tim Kautz. (2018). Asymdystopia: The threat of small biases in evaluations of education interventions that need to be powered to detect small impacts. SREE Spring 2018 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED591611

Two hint types (video versus text) were randomly assigned when students answered incorrectly, with video content designed to mirror the text hint. The dataset includes problem-level log data prior to condition assignment.

Learner analysis should decide "the most suitable method and material selection"

title: “Ask, write, throw” (AWT) peer question-exchange writing technique
description: AWT is a classroom writing activity for foreign-language learners in which students write questions on paper, fold it "like a snowball and throwing it to a random student in the class," answer the question received, and write a new one to throw onward. The teacher collects the papers at the end, lists errors, and students correct them on the board in the next lesson. It was designed to create a communicational environment, lower the affective filter, and engage cognitive, sensual and psychomotor skills.

A teacher in a facilitating role who does not interfere too much
End-of-lesson collection of papers and board-based error correction

No similar technique existed in the field, preventing comparison with another method

vocabulary
communication in daily interactions
examples: In the study, the experimental group performed the 20-minute activity at the end of each 6-hour weekly lesson across 8 weeks

citation: Silverthorn, N., DuBois, D. L., Lewis, K. M., Reed, A., Bavarian, N., Day, J., Ji, P., Acock, A. C., Vuchinich, S., & Flay, B. R. (2017). description: The article argues that important areas of impact on self-esteem-related outcomes may be overlooked without differentiated assessments of both self-esteem levels and processes. Prior studies focused nearly exclusively on levels of self-esteem, while the processes involved in forming and maintaining self-esteem can have implications for adjustment independent of resulting levels. The trial measured global and domain-specific self-esteem alongside adaptive and maladaptive processes, revealing effects on adaptive processes that a levels-only design would have missed.

article_title: Asymdystopia: The Threat of Small Biases in Evaluations of Education Interventions That Need to Be Powered to Detect Small Impacts. NCEE 2018-4002
citation: Deke, J., Wei, T., Kautz, T. (2017). Asymdystopia: The threat of small biases in evaluations of education interventions that need to be powered to detect small impacts. (NCEE 2018–4002). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Asymdystopia: larger finite samples are not necessarily better for Type 1 error control
description: Asymdystopia is the article's name for a context in which "a larger (but finite) sample size is not necessarily better and could even be worse from the perspective of controlling the Type 1 error rate". It arises because as sample size grows the standard error of the impact estimate shrinks while bias stays the same or shrinks more slowly, so the t-statistic's denominator shrinks faster than its numerator and biased estimates become statistically significant. The article examines this for attrition bias in RCTs and functional form misspecification in RDDs, the two most rigorous designs commonly used in education research.
requirements: Studies must be designed to have just enough statistical power to detect the smallest substantively important impact, rather than being overpowered
constraints: The paper does not focus on overpowered studies, particularly retrospective nonexperimental studies using administrative data
target_learners: students in education interventions evaluated via RCTs and RDDs
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of education intervention impacts
examples: The article illustrates the mechanism with bias of 0.05 and a standard error shrinking from 0.20 to 0.01, turning a non-significant t-statistic of 0.25 into a significant 2.5

citation: Koedinger, K. R., McLaughlin, E. A., & Heffernan, N. T. (2010). A quasi-experimental evaluation of an on-line formative assessment and tutoring system. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 43(4), 489-510. https://doi.org/10.2190/EC.43.4.d

citation: Goksu, I. and Gulcu, A. (2016). The Evaluation of the Cognitive Learning Process of the Renewed Bloom Taxonomy Using a Web Based Expert System. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(4). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Academic Success Test (AST) aligned to RBT cognitive process levels
description: The AST is a mathematics achievement test developed for this study to measure academic success across the RBT cognitive process dimension. It was built from four basic algebraic expressions gains expanded into 16 sub-gains, with at least two questions per gain, reviewed by four expert educators, one research associate and three mathematics teachers, piloted with 171 high-school first-grade students, and refined to 42 items. "At the end of the analysis, it's been seen that a reliability coefficient is .86."
requirements: Questions selected to include at least two questions for each gain and to comply with the RBT cognitive process dimension
constraints: Developed specifically for eighth-grade mathematics algebraic expressions gains
target_learners: eighth-grade middle school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: algebraic expressions gains across remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating and creating
examples: The same 42-item AST was used as both pre-test and post-test for experimental and control groups

article_title: Differences in Classroom versus Online Exam Performance Due to Asynchronous Discussion
citation: Robert L. Jorczak, Danielle N. Dupuis. (2011). Differences in Classroom Versus Online Exam Performance Due to Asynchronous Discussion. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Differences+in+Classroom+Versus+Online+Exam+Performance+Due+to+Asynchronous+Discussion
title: Use and refine asynchronous peer discussion in online courses, and add asynchronous discussion to classroom courses via hybrid designs
description: Based on the observed exam advantage for asynchronous peer text discussion, the article recommends that online courses continue to use and refine asynchronous discussion in support of learning, and that classroom courses adopt hybrid designs incorporating asynchronous discussion activities through an online forum. The recommendation rests on the finding that the online sections' "asynchronous small group text discussion" was the key differing instructional activity and on the cognitive advantages the authors attribute to slowed processing, review ability, and equal access.
requirements: Discussion design must meet at least minimum quality standards typical of current online classes using peer discussion
constraints: The study did not manipulate discussion synchronicity within a single environment, so the recommendation depends on the causal interpretation of a quasi-experimental comparison
The grading incentive difference (online students earned participation points) should be controlled in future studies
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: exam performance reflecting knowledge acquisition and concept formation
examples: The online sections used asynchronous peer discussion graded for participation, while the classroom section used synchronous instructor-led and small-group oral discussion.
key_sources: Robert L. Jorczak, Danielle N. Dupuis. (2011). Differences in Classroom Versus Online Exam Performance Due to Asynchronous Discussion. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Differences+in+Classroom+Versus+Online+Exam+Performance+Due+to+Asynchronous+Discussion

article_title: 'Asegúrate' Program: Effects on Cyber-Aggression and Its Risk Factors
citation: Del Rey, R., Mora-Merchán, J.A., Casas, J.A., Ortega-Ruiz, R., & Elipe, P. (2018). 'Asegúrate' Program: Effects on cyber-aggression and its risk factors. Comunicar, 56, XXVI. https://doi.org/10.3916/C56-2018-04
title: The 'Asegúrate' program is structured around three main pillars: normative social behavior, self-regulation skills, and adolescent ideas/beliefs
description: The 'Asegúrate' program is a teacher-implemented intervention against cyberbullying and its associated risks. It is "structured around three main pillars": the theory of normative social behavior, self-regulation skills, and the ideas/beliefs held by adolescents. The normative pillar presents positive identification models and examines students' expectations; the self-regulation pillar includes reflective practice to enhance metacognitive skills; and the beliefs pillar uses a constructivist sequence of activities to identify, analyze, and reshape pre-existing ideas about virtual environments.
requirements: Teachers are responsible for implementing the program, and quasi-experimental schools had to commit to implementing at least four of the program's teaching modules.
constraints: The program primarily works in virtual environments, though results demonstrate transfer of control to physical environments.
target_learners: Compulsory Secondary Education students aged 12 to 18 years
target_learning_goals: Reduce involvement in cyber-aggression, bullying aggression, sexting, and abusive use of the Internet and social networks
examples: The program's activity sequence identifies pre-existing ideas about virtual environments, analyzes behavior, reflects on reasons and consequences, and generalizes achievements to other relationship contexts.
key_sources: Del Rey, R., Mora-Merchán, J.A., Casas, J.A., Ortega-Ruiz, R., & Elipe, P. (2018). 'Asegúrate' Program: Effects on cyber-aggression and its risk factors. Comunicar, 56, XXVI. https://doi.org/10.3916/C56-2018-04

article_title: Improving Outcomes for Refugee Children: A Case Study on the Impact of Montessori Education along the Thai-Burma Border
citation: Tobin, T., Boulmier, P., Zhu, W., Hancock, P., & Muennig, P. (2015). Improving outcomes for refugee children: A case study on the impact of Montessori education along the Thai-Burma border. The International Education Journal: Comparative Perspectives, 14(3). http://openjournals.library.usyd.edu.au/index.php/IEJ/index
title: Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ) as a cross-cultural developmental assessment tool
description: The ASQ is a developmental screening instrument used here as the primary outcome measure for displaced children. It "generally consists of tasks rather than test questions, rendering it easy to administer in cross-cultural settings." It is divided into five categories: gross motor, fine motor, communication, problem solving and personal-social, with children scored on a scale from 0 to 60. The authors selected it over NIH toolbox alternatives because it does not require a computer, measures a broad range of developmental outcomes, and is relatively brief and simple to execute.
requirements: Multi-lingual interviewers fluent in the languages spoken by parents and children; identical sets of materials used to assess all children
constraints: The article notes the ASQ's cognitive measures are much more rudimentary than comprehensive cognitive and spatial test batteries, and it does not test for regaining a sense of normalcy
target_learners: Children aged 3 to 6 in cross-cultural, low-resource settings
target_learning_goals: Screening developmental outcomes across gross motor, fine motor, communication, problem solving, and personal-social domains
examples: The 54-month ASQ was administered irrespective of students' ages because students and parents often did not know their correct age

article_title: Beyond AI Detection: A Decision-Making Guide for Strategic Assessment Design in Nursing Education.
citation: McCusker KA, Kennedy BB, Parish A. (2026). Beyond AI Detection: A Decision-Making Guide for Strategic Assessment Design in Nursing Education. Nurse Educator. https://doi.org/10.1097/NNE.0000000000002281
title: Assessment and AI Vulnerability Decision-Making Guide for Nursing
description: A downloadable decision-making guide that produces a total AI vulnerability score (0-15) from two domains: assessment setting (Part A, scored 0-6, with 6 being the lowest AI vulnerability) and assessment method (Part B, scored 0-3). The article states it "can be downloaded and used by nurse educators for evaluating existing assessments or guiding the creation of new assessments" and pairs scores with a targeted improvement guide for faculty.
requirements: Developed through collaborative expert review by 3 graduate nursing faculty from 2 institutions using a backward design approach anchored on a known low-vulnerability assessment
constraints: Developed based on current AI capabilities (as of 2026); criteria may require reevaluation as generative AI evolves
Developed specifically for nursing education; discipline-specific validation may be necessary before adoption in other fields
target_learners: pre- and postlicensure nursing students
target_learning_goals: valid competency-based evaluation of clinical judgment and practice readiness
examples: Applied across multiple assessment types: a proctored multiple-choice exam, an asynchronous at-home multiple-choice exam, a case-based at-home written exam, a simulation, and process-based clinical note writing

article_title: Mental Imagery to Enhance Procedural Skills in Peripheral Venous Catheterization: A Randomized Simulation Study in Medical Students.
citation: Boulet N, Nairv H, Mezzarobba M, Saadi L, Morin D, Roger C. (2026). Mental Imagery to Enhance Procedural Skills in Peripheral Venous Catheterization: A Randomized Simulation Study in Medical Students. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2069
title: Assess procedural-training interventions with clinically meaningful performance and safety outcomes, not only learning progression
description: The article argues procedural-skill research should target higher-level Kirkpatrick outcomes. The authors state that by "selecting uncomplicated first-puncture success rate and complication incidence as primary and secondary outcomes, we deliberately emphasized performance quality rather than learning progression alone", addressing a gap where prior studies rarely measured actual performance improvement or patient benefit.
requirements: Outcome measures must be objective and clinically meaningful (e.g., success with functional perfusion and no complications)
constraints: The authors note most previous studies focused on early skill-acquisition phases; shifting to performance outcomes requires designs able to capture them
target_learners: health professions education researchers
simulation course designers
target_learning_goals: procedural competence and patient-safety-relevant performance
examples: The article cites the Snelgrove et al. umbrella review's finding that prior motor-learning studies rarely addressed higher-level outcomes, and aligns its design with Kirkpatrick Levels 3 and 4.

article_title: Mental health and depression as mediators between social media use screen time and academic integrity among tertiary students in Ghana.
citation: Ntumi Simon, Nimo Daniel Gyapong, Ammah Christina, Donkor Betty, Agbenyo Sheilla, Deku Harriet Delali, Sunu Seth. (2026). Mental health and depression as mediators between social media use screen time and academic integrity among tertiary students in Ghana. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-40285-0
title: Assessment Integrity Scale (researcher-developed, 10-item)
description: A researcher-developed instrument adapted from an Academic Dishonesty Inventory, measuring "behavioral engagement in dishonest practices (e.g., copying during tests, unauthorized collaboration, plagiarism) and attitudinal tolerance toward such practices." It comprises 10 items on a 5-point Likert scale, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.76 and McDonald's omega of 0.78. CFA supported a unidimensional structure with good fit (CFI = 0.95; RMSEA = 0.056).
requirements: Reverse-coding of the item on reporting a peer who cheats; administration in English
constraints: Developed and validated specifically for Ghanaian tertiary student populations
target_learners: Tertiary students in Ghanaian Colleges of Education
target_learning_goals: Measuring assessment integrity and tolerance for academic dishonesty

article_title: Does working memory moderate the effect of fading on math performance?
citation: Miller‐Cotto, D., & Medrano, J. (2026). Does working memory moderate the effect of fading on math performance? British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 108–126. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12781
title: ASSISTments-delivered faded worked example homework unit on surface area and volume
description: An instructional element consisting of 18 geometry problems assigned as homework through the ASSISTments online tutoring platform across a five-day procedure: "Participants were presented with 18 problems across three sessions in this study, with six problems presented per session." Day 1 covered surface area, day 2 volume, day 3 a mix; problems came from curricula such as EngageNY. Conditions varied only in the presence of faded steps or self-explanation prompts, with a pretest, WOMBAT working memory task, per-problem-set cognitive load ratings, and a parallel posttest.
requirements: Unique participant links to ensure correct condition assignment; parental consent via teachers
constraints: All data were anonymized, so no school-level information was available or controlled for; the study lacked worked-examples-only and self-explanation-only conditions
target_learners: 6th-grade middle school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: calculating surface area and volume of three-dimensional shapes
examples: Self-explanation prompts included one question per problem, such as asking why the total volume was divided by 3

article_title: Academic Self-Efficacy as a Mediator Between Risk for Social Media Addiction, Nomophobia, and Clinical Performance Among Nursing Internship Students: A Structural Equation Model.
citation: Berdida, Daniel Joseph E., Jacinto‐Caspillo, Ingrid, Conde, Maurine T., Bharathi, Bindu, Daoala, Annabel Lee C., Lopez, Leticia, Lopez, Hilda T., Aldughmi, Ohoud Naif, Gutiérrez-Puertas, Lorena. (2026). Academic Self‐Efficacy as a Mediator Between Risk for Social Media Addiction, Nomophobia, and Clinical Performance Among Nursing Internship Students: A Structural Equation Model. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/2184983
title: Bandura's self-efficacy theory framing academic self-efficacy as a protective intrinsic asset for nursing interns
description: The study is framed by Bandura's self-efficacy theory, distinguishing academic self-efficacy (ASE)—the student's belief that talents and past experiences contribute to excellent academic results—from performance self-efficacy derived from prior experience. ASE is described as "a vital catalyst for learning novel skills", crucial when interns confront unfamiliar clinical tasks. The authors extend the concept empirically, positioning ASE as "a protective intrinsic asset against unfavorable conditions" that buffers the adverse effects of SMA and nomophobia on clinical performance, supported by the mediation findings.
requirements: Requires measurement of ASE (e.g., the GASE scale) alongside the risk factors whose effects it buffers
constraints: ASE functioned as a partial mediator only; direct pathways from SMA and nomophobia remained significant, so it does not fully explain the relationships
target_learners: nursing internship students in their final clinical internship year
target_learning_goals: clinical performance competencies
academic self-efficacy and self-regulated engagement in clinical learning
examples: The emerging SEM model positioned ASE as a mediator between SMA/nomophobia and clinical internship grades among 585 Saudi nursing interns

article_title: Lived experiences of peer learning to improve the professional capabilities of hospital managers: a phenomenological study.
citation: Tabatabaei Far SS, Ahmadi Marzaleh M, Moradi Farahani M, Jafari F, Sarooeyeh F. (2025). Lived experiences of peer learning to improve the professional capabilities of hospital managers: a phenomenological study. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07616-2
title: Embedding peer learning within existing monthly managers' assembly meetings as a structured platform for guided collaborative reflection
description: The study used monthly managers' assembly meetings as the platform for a structured peer learning process, embedding peer learning within existing administrative routine. The premise is that these administrative structures "often lack a deliberate focus on knowledge sharing." The meetings created a formal space for managers to learn from each other's experiences and problem-solving approaches, with the guided, collaborative reflection on shared challenges treated as the core learning intervention distinct from the formal agenda.
requirements: Existing regular managerial meetings that can be repurposed with a deliberate knowledge-sharing focus
constraints: Barriers include meetings not held for remote hospitals due to geographical location and undermining of the assembly by higher organizations
target_learners: Current and former hospital managers
target_learning_goals: Sharing experiences and problem-solving approaches to improve managerial capability
examples: Interviews asked managers whether attendance at joint meetings of managers helped them learn and how.

article_title: Competencies and Needs of Older Volunteers: A Comparative Survey.
citation: Yang, L.-C., LAI, C.-Y., Chen, K.-M., Chen, M.-C., Chang, C.-C., Lin, T.-Y., & Kuo, C.-F. (2025). Competencies and needs of older volunteers: A comparative survey. The Journal of Nursing Research. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000712
title: Assess volunteer competencies and needs before training and task assignment
description: The article argues that assessing competencies and needs is the critical first step in organizing effective training: "training programs for older volunteers must be planned in accordance with their competencies and needs." Its survey demonstrates that needs vary systematically by age, experience, and education, so a single undifferentiated program will mismatch many volunteers. The conclusion recommends that community care centers "conduct pre-employment assessments to optimally allocate tasks as well as provide opportunities for on-the-job training."
requirements: A validated multi-dimensional needs-assessment instrument (the authors use the OVCS) and routine reassessment to support task assignment
constraints: The study's cross-sectional, self-report design limits causal and in-depth interpretation, and results may not generalize beyond southern Taiwan community care centers
target_learners: older adult volunteers in community-based care services
target_learning_goals: aligning volunteer training content and task allocation with assessed competency needs
examples: The study surveyed 1,000 older volunteers with the OVCS and found the oldest age group, least-experienced, and lowest-educated participants reported the highest overall needs

article_title: How differentiated can a new tablet-based reading screening measure the reading proficiency of students with intellectual disabilities? Comparing the impact of disability, disability type and grade level on reading skills.
citation: Ebenbeck Nikola, Zentel Peter, Gebhardt Markus. (2024). How differentiated can a new tablet-based reading screening measure the reading proficiency of students with intellectual disabilities? Comparing the impact of disability, disability type and grade level on reading skills. Journal of Intellectual Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/17446295241282750
title: Base reading instruction decisions on standardized individual assessment rather than disability labels, grade level, or disability severity
description: The article argues that indicators such as age, grade level, or grade of disability are insufficient for deciding reading instruction, because students show wide and overlapping reading abilities regardless of label. "It is crucial to consider the unique learning needs of each student based on standardized assessments, like the screening in this study, and prioritize personalized approaches rather than relying solely on diagnostic labels." Screening results support data-based decision making for assigning suitable reading instruction.
requirements: Standardized screening measures that can differentiate low performance levels and align with instructional support areas
constraints: Teacher judgment accuracy is lower for low-performing students than for high-performing students
target_learners: students with intellectual disabilities
students with special educational needs in inclusive classes
target_learning_goals: reading proficiency across phonological awareness, vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension
examples: The screening was used at the start of the school year to identify reading skills and areas where instruction needs to focus

description: Because producing a health education video demands clinical knowledge plus communication, teamwork, problem-solving, critical thinking, and technical skills, the authors argue teachers "should assess students’ competence levels and provide necessary support to prevent failure." They further state it is critical that teachers plan tasks so that learning of cross-curricular content is progressive or taught through specific courses, rather than assuming students arrive with the needed digital and collaborative competencies.
requirements: Prior assessment of students' competence levels

Progressive or course-specific teaching of cross-curricular skills

communication and teamwork skills
effective health information communication
examples: In the study, facilitators were available for individual or group tutorials upon request and a rubric was provided from the course start

article_title: Characteristic competencies for effective teachers in healthcare education.
citation: Iahn-Aun Marina; Aun Marcelo Vivolo; Pereira Welbert Oliveira. (2025). Characteristic competencies for effective teachers in healthcare education. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12539862/
title: Align assessment with learning objectives so assessment functions as a learning tool rather than prompting exam-focused study
description: The review argues that assessing student learning and progress in knowledge, skills and attitudes, based on learning objectives, lets professors, students and institutions correct or enhance adopted strategies. Well-designed assessment becomes "a learning tool" and engages and reassures students. If teachers do not verify outcomes against objectives, students may focus on passing exams rather than integrating and applying knowledge, and perceived disconnect between teaching and assessment requirements produces a sense of injustice that hinders learning.
requirements: Correctly constructed and applied assessments; increasing numbers of assessment tools make specialist assessment expertise in faculties necessary, per the review
target_learners: healthcare higher education teachers
students in healthcare programs
target_learning_goals: learning for integration and application rather than test performance

article_title: Comparison of A Mini-Clinical evaluation exercise with the routine logbook in assessing clinical competence of operating room trainees: A parallel randomized controlled trial.
citation: Bagheri Sara, Sedigh Amin, Zarei Zahra, Kazemzadeh Mozhgan, Sharifi Nader. (2025). Comparison of A Mini-Clinical evaluation exercise with the routine logbook in assessing clinical competence of operating room trainees: A parallel randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07560-6
title: Shift clinical assessment from assessment of learning to assessment for learning using multidomain feedback
description: The article argues successful evaluation encourages students to seek more information, and that the focus of assessment should move from judging learning to enhancing it. It states: "It is therefore suggested that the focus of assessment should be shifted from “assessment of learning” to “assessment for learning”". For assessment for learning, tools like multidomain feedback identify the strengths and weaknesses of an individual student, and this information is then used to enhance learning and maximize competency. The trial's Mini-CEX condition, with immediate written and oral feedback after each observation, exemplifies this approach.
requirements: Assessors need training in offering feedback and assigning scores, and feedback must be delivered promptly after observation.
constraints: The effectiveness of Mini-CEX implementation remains uncertain in some settings: prior studies found feedback often generic, scheduling difficult in busy workplaces, and misalignment with learning objectives.
target_learners: undergraduate operating room students
trainees in clinical clerkships
target_learning_goals: clinical competence and skill improvement through formative feedback
examples: In the trial, Mini-CEX trainees promptly received verbal and written feedback after each of three observed surgical procedures, enabling them to gain insights into their clinical performance.

citation: Bond, Carmel, Painter, Joanna M., Barnett, Donna. (2025). Exploring the Skills Prioritised in the Assessment of Students Pursuing Adult Nursing, Post‐COVID: A Qualitative Analysis. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70236
title: Two-theme taxonomy of adult nursing practice assessment priorities: task-focused competencies and relational/transformative aspects of care
description: The article organises practice assessors' comments into two core themes derived inductively through qualitative content analysis. Task-focused competencies cover practical and technical nursing skills, subdivided into skills relevant to all nursing fields (e.g. aseptic technique, venepuncture, NEWS observations) and skills specific to adult/general nursing (e.g. bladder scanning, fracture assessments). Relational/transformative aspects of care cover values-based attributes, subdivided into personal attributes and characteristics, values, and work ethic. The article states: "The analysis identified two core themes: task‐focused competencies and relational/transformative aspects of care."
requirements: Inductive open coding by two researchers with category checking against the study aims, as the article describes
constraints: Derived from comments of 27 assessors at one NHS organisation within a single UK university's assessment documentation

target_learning_goals: clinical skill proficiency
values-based and compassionate care
professional communication
examples: Tables 1 and 2 list theme elements, from ECGs, catheterisation and CPR to communication, compassion, dignity/respect, and work ethic items such as punctuality and keenness to learn

article_title: Higher level domain specific skills in mathematics; The relationship between algebra, geometry, executive function skills and mathematics achievement.
citation: Spiller J, Clayton S, Cragg L, Johnson S, Simms V, Gilmore C. (2023). Higher level domain specific skills in mathematics; The relationship between algebra, geometry, executive function skills and mathematics achievement. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0291796
title: Use specific measures of mathematical processes alongside context-rich achievement assessments to understand mechanisms linking cognitive skills to mathematics outcomes
description: The article concludes that "using specific measures of mathematical processes as well as context-rich assessments of mathematical achievement is important to understand these mechanisms". Because executive function skills relate to achievement partly through specific components (number facts, calculation, algebra, geometry) and partly through direct pathways, assessments capturing only one level obscure the mechanisms. The study demonstrated this by showing algebra and geometry added 15% of explained variance beyond arithmetic-based measures.
requirements: Battery must include measures of specific mathematical components (e.g. number fact knowledge, calculation, algebra, geometry) as well as a broad context-rich achievement test
constraints: Findings derive from a correlational cross-sectional design with 95 adolescents; single measures per construct limit construct separation
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
mathematical component skills
examples: The study used the WIAT-II mathematical reasoning subtest (context-based word problems) alongside targeted tasks for number facts, calculation, concepts, algebra and geometry in 95 adolescents

article_title: Assignment strategies modulate students' academic performance in an online learning environment during the first and second COVID-19 related school closures.
citation: Spitzer Markus Wolfgang Hermann, Moeller Korbinian, Musslick Sebastian. (2023). Assignment strategies modulate students’ academic performance in an online learning environment during the first and second COVID-19 related school closures. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0284868
title: Assign mathematics problem sets in small single sets one by one rather than as entire books or self-selected work in online learning environments
description: The article recommends that teachers present learning content in small chunks: assigning "smaller bits of learning content in terms of smaller sets of problem sets as compared to entire books as well as compared to letting students self-select problem sets was most beneficial for students’ mathematical learning". The authors align this with spaced learning, noting "spacing out learning content over time, provided to students in small chunks, leads to enhanced learning outcomes". The recommendation rests on large-scale observational log data, not an experiment.
requirements: Teachers must have an online environment that supports both single problem set and entire book assignment modes, as Bettermarks does.
constraints: Results stem from students aged 10–16 in grades 4–10 and are limited to that age range; the data do not include information on why some teachers assigned single problem sets versus bundles.
target_learners: Students in grades 4–10 (age range 10–16) learning mathematics online
target_learning_goals: Mathematics performance on fractions, percentages, and linear equations problem sets

article_title: From summative MAAS Global to formative MAAS 2.0 - a workshop report.
citation: Stamer Tjorven, Essers Geurt, Steinhäuser Jost, Flägel Kristina. (2023). From summative MAAS Global to formative MAAS 2.0 – a workshop report. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2023-40/zma001591.shtml
title: Focus communication assessment on the patient's frame of reference rather than the physician's words
description: The MAAS 2.0 revision systematically shifts item wording toward the patient's perspective: summarizing should use "the patient's words" rather than the physician's own words, and information transfer should occur "within the patient's reference framework". The rationale printed is that focusing on the physician's words "would draw the patient's narrative into the direct frame of reference of the practitioner", whereas the patient-oriented focus means "the patient would also feel better heard and understood".
requirements: Assessors must evaluate whether information transfer takes place within the patient's reference framework and whether summaries use the patient's words
constraints: Grounded in the context of GP consultations as described in this report; the authors note the formative implementation in postgraduate feedback remains to be examined

physicians with a license for post-graduate training

summarizing and imparting information in consultations
examples: The sub-item "in own words" under item 12 was changed to "uses the patient's words"; "ask what the patient understood" was replaced by the broader "checking comprehension".

article_title: Integrating Point of Care Ultrasound Education into Clinical Practice at the Emergency Department.
citation: Ienghong Kamonwon, Cheung Lap Woon, Tiamkao Somsak, Bhudhisawasdi Vajarabhongsa, Apiratwarakul Korakot. (2022). Integrating Point of Care Ultrasound Education into Clinical Practice at the Emergency Department. Tomography. https://doi.org/10.3390/tomography8020085
title: Assess POCUS trainees in the workplace on real patients in real time, because simulated assessments miss real clinical contexts
description: The article argues that OSCE-style assessments using simulated pathology videos or mannequins are limited compared with real cases, and that a year of real-practice assessments showed "the measurable benefits of a POCUS course being integrated into real clinical practice". It emphasizes "evaluating trainees in the workplace in real time as the 'core of medical competence'", alongside formal training, a formal competency assessment tool, and integration of POCUS education into real clinical practice as future priorities.
requirements: Recorded ultrasound images and video clips from real examinations, blinded expert raters with ultrasound credentials, and a grading rubric mapped to performance grades
constraints: The study was not designed to demonstrate limitations of individual learners; findings come from one residency program in a resource-limited setting
target_learners: Emergency medicine residents
target_learning_goals: POCUS competency assessment across image acquisition, interpretation, and clinical integration
examples: Researchers staff rated 3014 real-patient ultrasound clips and images recorded by residents during one year of on-shift clinical practice at Srinagarind Hospital

description: ASPIRE (Aim, Storyboarding, Populating, Implementing, Release, Evaluation) is the co-creation methodology the ACoRD project used to transfer eLearning object development knowledge from UK/EU to Malaysian universities. It sequences stakeholder and train-the-trainer workshops, internal storyboard workshops with educators and students, specification writing and review, technical creation of RLOs, release into curricula with an open access repository, and evaluation of quality, effectiveness and usage. The article states each knowledge component "would have gone through the same knowledge transfer process along the project time frame".

constraints: Its development process in receiver institutions was described as challenged by limited time frames, technical resources and institutional support

University educators and learning technologists

examples: Used in the ACoRD project, where UK/EU partners cascaded pedagogical, technical and design skills in building RLOs to three Malaysian universities
