article_title: The role of virtual reality simulation in surgical training in the light of COVID-19 pandemic: Visual spatial ability as a predictor for improved surgical performance: a randomized trial.
citation: Sommer GM, Broschewitz J, Huppert S, Sommer CG, Jahn N, Jansen-Winkeln B, Gockel I, Hau HM. (2021). The role of virtual reality simulation in surgical training in the light of COVID-19 pandemic: Visual spatial ability as a predictor for improved surgical performance: a randomized trial. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000027844
title: Assess visual spatial ability with a simple test to identify training needs in surgical novices
description: The article concludes that VSA assessment is practical and informative for surgical education: "Assessing VSA with a simple test is feasible and high VSA scores indicate superior surgical spatial performance in VR simulator tasks." Because VSA correlates with performance mainly at the start of training, identifying VSA levels allows training needs analysis at the individual level, while low-VSA trainees can be expected to catch up with structured practice.

constraints: The article cautions that whether future residency performance can be predicted from VSA remains unclear, and that pre-existing advantages can be outweighed by training and experience.

medical students entering surgical training
target_learning_goals: prediction of initial laparoscopic performance
individualized training needs analysis
examples: In the trial, all 60 participants passed the tube figure test on day 1 and again on day 9, and the training group was median-split into high- and low-VSA subgroups for learning-curve analysis.

article_title: Flipped learning enhances non-technical skill performance in simulation-based education: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Moll-Khosrawi Parisa, Zöllner Christian, Cencin Nadine, Schulte-Uentrop Leonie. (2021). Flipped learning enhances non-technical skill performance in simulation-based education: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02766-w
title: AS-NTS behavioural marker system for rating students' non-technical skills
description: The German version of "Anaesthesiology students´ Non-Technical skills" (AS-NTS) is a validated behavioural marker system used by instructors to rate non-technical skills. It is composed of three dimensions — planning tasks, prioritising and problem-solving; teamwork and leadership; team orientation — rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = very good; 5 = very poor) with behaviourally anchored rating examples clarifying what good or poor performance looks like on each dimension. In this trial it served both as the primary outcome measure and as the content students learned to apply for debriefing.
requirements: An underlying skill structure with behaviourally anchored rating examples to clarify performance levels; instructors trained in rating NTS during simulation trainings
constraints: Validity, feasibility and sufficient coverage of relevant NTS were previously reported by the developers, not established in this trial
target_learners: Anaesthesiology and medical students in simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: Assessment of non-technical skills: planning and problem-solving, teamwork and leadership, team orientation
examples: Instructors rated NTS with AS-NTS in both trainings, and observing students in the intervention group filled out AS-NTS scores and used them to conduct peer debriefings

article_title: A quasi-experimental study of ethnic and gender bias in university grading.
citation: Bischoff Carina Saxlund, Ejrnæs Anders, Rubin Olivier. (2021). A quasi-experimental study of ethnic and gender bias in university grading. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0254422
title: Asymmetric information and decision stakes explain weaker discrimination in grading than in employment, housing, and financial markets
description: The article proposes that name-based discrimination varies across decision domains because of two factors: information asymmetry and the stakes of wrong decisions. In grading, "examiners have all the relevant information in the form of the actual assignment to make a grading decision," whereas employment, financial, and housing decision-makers face asymmetric information that invites statistical discrimination as a screening mechanism. Grading also carries low stakes, with no immediate repercussions beyond occasional student complaints, so risk-averse decision-makers in high-stakes markets discriminate more. The article uses this account to interpret its null grading results against stronger bias findings in other markets.
requirements: Decision domains must differ in the information available to decision-makers and in the consequences of wrong decisions for the account to predict differential discrimination
constraints: The authors present this as a tentative explanation inviting further qualitative studies; it is an interpretation of their null result, not a tested mechanism
target_learners: university students in graded assessment
target_learning_goals: fair and unbiased assessment of student performance
examples: The article contrasts its null grading results with cited experimental evidence of name-based discrimination in job applications, rental housing, credit provision, and Danish primary school access inquiries
key_sources: Bischoff Carina Saxlund, Ejrnæs Anders, Rubin Olivier. (2021). A quasi-experimental study of ethnic and gender bias in university grading. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0254422

citation: Carenzo L, Cena T, Carfagna F, Rondi V, Ingrassia PL, Cecconi M, Violato C, Della Corte F, Vaschetto R. (2021). Assessing anaesthesiology and intensive care specialty physicians: An Italian language multisource feedback system. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0250404
title: When implementing MSF, assess the capability of each assessor group to evaluate the targeted professional and humanistic skills, especially non-clinical ones
description: The article proposes that MSF implementation should match items to what each rater group can legitimately assess, because different respondents focus on characteristics they can observe. It states that "When implementing a feedback system, it is important to assess the capability of the assessor group to evaluate different aspects of humanistic and professional skills, especially the non-clinical ones", grounded in the high unable-to-assess rates on coworker items.
requirements: Rater groups must have opportunity to observe the behaviors being assessed
constraints: In this study some non-medical coworkers appeared unable or untrained to assess specific non-clinical characteristics of doctors

target_learning_goals: professionalism
leadership
communication

article_title: Are we generating more assessments without added value? Surgical trainees' perceptions of and receptiveness to cross-specialty assessment.
citation: Burm Sarah, Sebok-Syer Stefanie S., Van Koughnett Julie Ann, Watling Christopher J. (2020). Are we generating more assessments without added value? Surgical trainees’ perceptions of and receptiveness to cross-specialty assessment. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-020-00594-0
title: Separating the assessor role from the coach role undermines trainees' receptivity to assessment
description: The article develops the argument that assessment and coaching roles are difficult to separate in formative contexts. Trainees sought "a coach—someone who could break their performance into its critical individual components—as opposed to an assessor whose role was limited to scoring their performance". The authors conclude the findings complicate advocacy for separating coach and assessor roles and suggest developing clinicians to concurrently take on both roles without diminishing effectiveness.
requirements: Assessors who provide credible, constructive feedback that trainees perceive as useful and trustworthy
constraints: The authors do not claim to have figured out the optimum balance between assessment and coaching
Findings are drawn from a single program's trainees in a formative, simulated context
target_learners: Postgraduate surgical trainees
Faculty assessors in competency-based medical education
target_learning_goals: Meaningful engagement with assessment and feedback to support trainee learning and development
examples: In the study, trained non-surgeon faculty could record procedural errors on a checklist, but trainees still sought staff surgeons who could physically guide their hands through the motion

title: Assess EBM ability at program entry and provide time and resources to advance trainees to a standard level
description: The article recommends that because trainees in Qatar come from diverse educational backgrounds, programs should identify gaps in individual learners' EBM knowledge through assessments at initiation and then provide protected time and resources. The authors state there "should be more emphasis on identifying gaps in individual learner's knowledge through assessments at initiation". This responds to their finding that trainee aptitude was suboptimal despite favorable attitudes.

constraints: The article notes instructional methods for increasing EBM knowledge and application require further study of what works best

target_learning_goals: evidence-based medicine knowledge and application skills
examples: The study used the validated ACE tool to measure actual EBM aptitude among 80 trainees at an ACGME-I accredited program in Qatar.

article_title: The status of training in new technologies in advanced endoscopy: from defining competence to credentialing and privileging.
citation: Yang D., Wagh M.S., Draganov P.V. (2020). The status of training in new technologies in advanced endoscopy: from defining competence to credentialing and privileging. Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gie.2020.05.047
title: ASGE major/minor skill framework for classifying and training in new endoscopic technologies
description: The ASGE framework distinguishes a "major skill", described as "a new technique or procedure that involves a high level of complexity, interpretative ability, and/or new type of technology" requiring formal supervised training, from minor extensions of established procedures acquirable through limited education such as didactic videos and short courses. Competence in a major skill comprises six components, from understanding indications and risks to providing a comprehensive pre- and postprocedural plan. The review applies the framework to classify procedures such as EUS, ERCP, ESD, and POEM as major skills. It stresses the classification is background-dependent: radiofrequency ablation may be minor for an experienced endoscopist but major for a novice.
requirements: Formal training under the supervision of a preceptor(s) for major skills
Competence includes both technical and cognitive components, ending in independent performance
constraints: The ASGE definitions should only be used as a framework, since required training fluctuates with the endoscopist's background
target_learners: advanced endoscopy fellows
practicing endoscopists seeking training in new technologies
target_learning_goals: safe and proficient performance of new endoscopic procedures
recognizing and managing adverse events
interpreting endoscopic findings for patient management
examples: Table 1 classifies EUS, ERCP, ESD, and POEM as major skills and radiofrequency ablation of Barrett's esophagus, intragastric balloon placement, and over-the-scope clip as minor skills

article_title: Clinical reasoning for acute dyspnoea: comparison between final-year medical students from discipline- and competency-based undergraduate programmes.
citation: Czeskleba A., Holzhausen Y., Peters H. (2020). Clinical reasoning for acute dyspnoea: comparison between final-year medical students from discipline- and competency-based undergraduate programmes. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02055-y
title: ASCLIRE computer-based test of clinical reasoning for acute dyspnoea
description: The ASCLIRE test is a computer-based instrument for assessing clinical reasoning using six digitally presented video cases of patients with acute dyspnoea and different underlying diagnoses. It "allows the evaluation of three partly correlated but distinct aspects of the clinical decision process: choice of relevant diagnostic information, time to a diagnostic decision and accuracy of the diagnostic decision." Participants choose type, order and number of diagnostic tests from a graphical interface and select from 20 diagnoses; the test takes about 60 minutes. Validation studies report good psychometric properties and differentiation between trainees and experts.
requirements: Requires digitally presented video-based patient cases with a standardized actor presentation and a graphical interface for selecting diagnostic tests
Requires an expert standard of diagnostic test selections from medical specialists for scoring relevance
constraints: Available only for the acute dyspnoea content domain, not for other content domains
target_learners: final-year medical students in clerkships
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning in acute dyspnoea: diagnostic test selection, decision time, and diagnostic accuracy
examples: In this study, 60 final-year clerkship students completed the ASCLIRE test with six randomly ordered cases after a training case, with all selected diagnostic measures and timing recorded.

article_title: Anaesthesiology students' Non-Technical skills: development and evaluation of a behavioural marker system for students (AS-NTS).
citation: Moll-Khosrawi P, Kamphausen A, Hampe W, Schulte-Uentrop L, Zimmermann S, Kubitz JC. (2019). Anaesthesiology students’ Non-Technical skills: development and evaluation of a behavioural marker system for students (AS-NTS). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1609-8
title: AS-NTS: a three-dimension behavioural marker system for rating undergraduates' non-technical skills in anaesthesiology simulation
description: AS-NTS is a rating tool developed to assess non-technical skills in undergraduate emergency medicine and anaesthesiology education. It rates performance on three dimensions — "Planning tasks, prioritizing and problem solving", "Teamwork and leadership", and "Team orientation" — each on a five-point Likert scale, with behaviourally anchored rating examples clarifying what "good" or "poor" performance looks like. It was designed to be usable without video recording or extended rater training.
requirements: Requires only a five-minute introduction for raters, and no video recording, per the study design
constraints: The AS-NTS has only been tested in German language at one institution with a limited number of teachers; validity, reliability and feasibility of the English version are not established
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in anaesthesiology and emergency medicine training
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills: planning, teamwork, leadership, team orientation in emergency care
examples: Used by two or three supervising anaesthesiologists to rate the student leading the team in each of 98 standardized simulation scenarios across four training sessions

citation: Moll-Khosrawi P, Kamphausen A, Hampe W, Schulte-Uentrop L, Zimmermann S, Kubitz JC. (2019). Anaesthesiology students’ Non-Technical skills: development and evaluation of a behavioural marker system for students (AS-NTS). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1609-8

article_title: Cognitive and noncognitive predictors of success.
citation: Duckworth, A. L., Quirk, A., Gallop, R., Hoyle, R. H., Kelly, D. R., & Matthews, M. D. (2019). Cognitive and noncognitive predictors of success. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1910510116
title: Assess a broader array of domain-relevant abilities when predicting success
description: The article recommends that research and practice measure a wider set of abilities than is typical, because the largest effect sizes came from domain-matched prediction: cognitive ability for academic performance and physical ability for physical performance. It suggests assessing "a more expansive array of domain-relevant abilities (e.g., military acumen, artistic talent, emotional intelligence) than is typical in research and practice." This follows from the finding that each ability best predicted its own domain's outcome.

constraints: Findings are from a highly selective military setting; the authors state generalizability cannot be assumed and the longitudinal data are correlational, limiting inferences to prediction rather than causes

students in selective performance-oriented programs
target_learning_goals: predicting academic, physical, and military performance
predicting retention and long-term completion
examples: In the West Point megaanalysis, cognitive ability was the strongest predictor of academic GPA while physical ability was the best predictor of physical GPA

article_title: Simulation-based ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia curriculum for anesthesiology residents.

Assessment tools include a validated multiple-choice sonoanatomy exam, UGRA-specific checklists and global rating scales, and the ACGME/American Board of Anesthesiology Milestone Project with five proficiency levels measured primarily by the level of supervision required.

article_title: Uncovering the relation between clinical reasoning and diagnostic accuracy - An analysis of learner's clinical reasoning processes in virtual patients.
citation: Hege I, Kononowicz AA, Kiesewetter J, Foster-Johnson L. (2018). Uncovering the relation between clinical reasoning and diagnostic accuracy – An analysis of learner's clinical reasoning processes in virtual patients. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0204900
title: Assess clinical reasoning by the details of the process of reaching a correct diagnosis rather than by first-attempt diagnostic accuracy
description: The article argues that diagnostic accuracy defined as reaching the correct final diagnosis on the first attempt should not stand alone as an indicator of clinical reasoning competence. Because the reasoning processes of learners who succeed on the first attempt and those who revise over several attempts are largely indistinguishable, while those who give up differ sharply, assessment should "focus[] more on the details of the process to reach a correct diagnosis, rather than whether it was made in the first attempt". Virtual patient designs should therefore allow retries or requesting the solution, distinctions that one-shot scenarios cannot capture.
requirements: A VP or assessment environment in which learners can submit multiple diagnoses, request the correct solution, and have their reasoning process captured and scored, such as via the concept mapping tool
constraints: One-shot VP designs in which learners cannot retry or request the solution make the distinction between giving up and revising impossible; the authors note the approach has not yet been formally integrated into a curriculum
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
healthcare students in clinical reasoning training
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning competency assessment
diagnostic accuracy
examples: The study compared use patterns and scores of maps solved on the first attempt, solved after multiple attempts, and maps in which learners requested the system's solution, finding the largest differences between self-solved and system-solution maps
key_sources: Hege I, Kononowicz AA, Kiesewetter J, Foster-Johnson L. (2018). Uncovering the relation between clinical reasoning and diagnostic accuracy – An analysis of learner's clinical reasoning processes in virtual patients. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0204900

article_title: The role of the assessment policy in the relation between learning and performance.
citation: Kickert R, Stegers‐Jager KM, Meeuwisse M, Prinzie P, Arends LR. (2018). The role of the assessment policy in the relation between learning and performance. Medical Education 52(3):324–335. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13487
title: Design assessment policies with awareness that stakes and performance standards shape student learning, motivation and performance
description: The article's central practical implication is that medical schools should recognise that assessment policy characteristics influence student learning and academic performance. It reports that "Developing an assessment policy that boosts motivation might be an efficient way to challenge students to perform better", and that external triggers may have a powerful additional effect on academic motivation alongside intrinsic motivation. The recommendation rests on the observed higher performance, SRL and participation under the higher-stakes policy.
requirements: Assessment content and pass/fail standard setting should be kept stable across policies, as the article notes both were held constant while stakes and standards changed
constraints: The article states correlational data preclude firm causal conclusions, and that long-term consequences of higher stakes and standards, including possible negative effects on motivation to learn, need investigation
target_learners: Year-1 medical students
target_learning_goals: academic performance
self-regulated learning
participation in scheduled learning activities
examples: The Erasmus MC medical school replaced a conjunctive lower-stakes policy with a compensatory higher-stakes, higher-standard policy requiring all 60 Year-1 credits within one year, one resit per examination and an average grade of at least 6.0
key_sources: Kickert R, Stegers‐Jager KM, Meeuwisse M, Prinzie P, Arends LR. (2018). The role of the assessment policy in the relation between learning and performance. Medical Education 52(3):324–335. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13487

article_title: Approaches to studying predict academic performance in undergraduate occupational therapy students: a cross-cultural study.
citation: Bonsaksen T, Brown T, Lim HB, Fong K. (2017). Approaches to studying predict academic performance in undergraduate occupational therapy students: a cross-cultural study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0914-3
title: ASSIST (Approaches and Study Skills Inventory for Students), 52-item section B
description: The ASSIST is a self-report inventory of students' approaches to studying used in this study to measure study approaches among occupational therapy students. "The ASSIST has three sections, including a 6-item questionnaire of students' conceptions of studying (section A), a 52-item questionnaire of students' approaches to studying (section B), and an 8-item questionnaire of student preferences for teaching." Following Entwistle and McCune's recommendation, the study used only the 52-item section B. Factor analysis organises items into three main factors — deep, strategic, and surface — comprising 13 subscales; internal consistency is reported as Cronbach's α 0.61–0.88 (English version) and 0.70–0.81 (Norwegian version).
requirements: Administration requires a validated language version (English or Norwegian here) and informed student consent
constraints: The study notes prior criticisms of the theoretical model underpinning the ASSIST, suggesting the deep versus surface dichotomy is overly simplistic
target_learners: undergraduate higher education students, here occupational therapy students in four countries
target_learning_goals: measuring students' deep, strategic and surface approaches to studying
examples: Data collected in 2015 via questionnaires distributed to students during classroom breaks across Australia, Hong Kong, Norway and Singapore
key_sources: Bonsaksen T, Brown T, Lim HB, Fong K. (2017). Approaches to studying predict academic performance in undergraduate occupational therapy students: a cross-cultural study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0914-3

article_title: English Language Proficiency and Early School Attainment Among Children Learning English as an Additional Language.
citation: Whiteside, Katie E.; Gooch, Debbie; Norbury, Courtenay F. (2017). English Language Proficiency and Early School Attainment Among Children Learning English as an Additional Language. Child Development, 88(3), 812-827. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12615
title: Assess individual English language proficiency rather than relying on EAL status when determining support for children with EAL
description: The article argues that the EAL label, based on home language exposure, masks the full continuum of English proficiency and that group-level attainment gaps are misleading. It endorses the recommendation that, to determine required support for individual children with EAL, "it is important to consider their English language proficiency rather than just their EAL status." All EAL advantages in the study emerged only when monolingual peers were matched on proficiency.
requirements: A valid, continuous measure of English language proficiency (the study used the teacher-rated CCC-S) collected at school entry
constraints: The study used indirect, teacher-rated measures of language and behavior with a single informant; executive functioning and proficiency in the home language were not measured
target_learners: Children learning English as an additional language in the first years of school (ages 4–7)
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency
Early academic attainment (literacy, mathematics)
Social, emotional, and behavioral functioning
examples: Teachers rated 7,267 reception-year children on the CCC-S, and children with EAL were compared to monolingual peers across the continuum of proficiency rather than as a group
key_sources: Whiteside, Katie E.; Gooch, Debbie; Norbury, Courtenay F. (2017). English Language Proficiency and Early School Attainment Among Children Learning English as an Additional Language. Child Development, 88(3), 812-827. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12615

article_title: ASPECT: A Survey to Assess Student Perspective of Engagement in an Active-Learning Classroom.
citation: Wiggins Benjamin L., Eddy Sarah L., Wener-Fligner Leah, Freisem Karen, Grunspan Daniel Z., Theobald Elli J., Timbrook Jerry, Crowe Alison J. (2017). ASPECT: A Survey to Assess Student Perspective of Engagement in an Active-Learning Classroom. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-08-0244
title: ASPECT: a 16-item survey measuring student self-reported engagement in active-learning classrooms
description: ASPECT (Assessing Student Perspective of Engagement in Class Tool) is a 16-item, six-point Likert survey measuring three constructs: value of group activity (9 items), personal effort (3 items), and instructor contribution (4 items). It was developed through a mixed-methods process of student interviews, focus groups, think-alouds, and factor analysis, and "takes students on average 6–7 minutes to complete," providing a rapid tool for assessing engagement in large active-learning classrooms.
requirements: Administered after an in-class activity; best use requires validation in new classroom environments to ensure question language and interpretation are meaningful for the new population
constraints: Developed and validated in a single introductory biology course at one university and may not apply to other course levels, STEM majors, or populations
Self-report measure with inherent biases; not intended as a psychometric analysis of the mental construct of student engagement
target_learners: undergraduate introductory biology students in large-enrollment courses
target_learning_goals: student self-reported cognitive and affective engagement during in-class active-learning exercises
examples: Administered to a large introductory biology class after short clicker-activity days and long worksheet activity days; responses analyzed with exploratory factor analysis and linear mixed-effects models
key_sources: Wiggins Benjamin L., Eddy Sarah L., Wener-Fligner Leah, Freisem Karen, Grunspan Daniel Z., Theobald Elli J., Timbrook Jerry, Crowe Alison J. (2017). ASPECT: A Survey to Assess Student Perspective of Engagement in an Active-Learning Classroom. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-08-0244

article_title: A survey of the current utilization of asynchronous education among emergency medicine residents in the United States.
citation: Mallin Mike MD, Schlein Sarah MD, Doctor Shaneen MD, Stroud Susan MD, Dawson Matthew MD, Fix Megan MD. (2014). A Survey of the Current Utilization of Asynchronous Education Among Emergency Medicine Residents in the United States. Academic Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/ACM.0000000000000170
title: Asynchronous education as a student-centered online modality for residency learning
description: The article defines asynchronous education as "a student-centered modality of teaching which involves sharing online learning resources and promotes peer-to-peer interactions." It situates this within Free Open Access Medical Education (#FOAMed) — blogs, podcasts, Twitter, iTunes U, Vimeo, and YouTube — and cites the 2008 CORD Academic Assembly Conference Alternatives Workgroup recommendation that "a deliberate mixture of synchronous learning activities and asynchronous learning activities is ideal." The survey operationalizes this framework by measuring residents' use of and preferences for asynchronous resources.
requirements: A deliberate mixture of synchronous and asynchronous learning activities, per the CORD Workgroup recommendation the article cites
constraints: The article states more research is needed to identify the optimal balance between just-in-time learning and traditional methods of education
target_learners: Emergency medicine residents
Medical residents at all levels of training
target_learning_goals: Extracurricular medical knowledge acquisition through online multimedia resources
examples: The survey of 226 residents measured use of podcasts, blogs, UpToDate, and other asynchronous resources

A Survey of the Current Utilization of Asynchronous Education Among Emergency Medicine Residents in the United States. Academic Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/ACM.0000000000000170

article_title: The feasibility of a train-the-trainer approach to end of life care training in care homes: an evaluation.
citation: Mayrhofer A, Goodman C, Smeeton N, Handley M, Amador S, Davies S. (2016). The feasibility of a train-the-trainer approach to end of life care training in care homes: an evaluation. BMC Palliative Care 15:11. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12904-016-0081-z
title: Assess organisational readiness before implementing peer-to-peer end of life care training in care homes
description: The article argues that a structured pre-intervention assessment of a care home's readiness should precede end of life care training programmes. It states "What is needed is a structured approach that can be used to highlight which organisational factors need to be addressed", involving discussion and review between care home and palliative support staff to identify facilitators, barriers, learning styles and required facilitation. Readiness assessment itself can build commitment, particularly if prospective trainers and learners join the pre-assessment process.
requirements: A pre-intervention phase of discussion and review between care home and palliative support staff to identify facilitators and barriers, favoured learning styles, and the level of facilitation required
constraints: Findings come from pre-selected homes in one geographical region, without pre-post measures, and may have been influenced by existing initiatives in some homes
target_learners: care home staff, from senior managers to support workers, being trained in end of life care
target_learning_goals: end of life and palliative care knowledge and skills for long-term care settings
examples: The TTT pilot recruited homes based on prior ABC engagement without assessing capacity to participate; in hindsight a facilitator noted successful homes had strong managers, strong leaders and stability
key_sources: Mayrhofer A, Goodman C, Smeeton N, Handley M, Amador S, Davies S. (2016). The feasibility of a train-the-trainer approach to end of life care training in care homes: an evaluation. BMC Palliative Care 15:11. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12904-016-0081-z

article_title: E-assessment and an e-training program among elderly care staff lacking formal competence: results of a mixed-methods intervention study.
citation: Nilsson Annika, Engström Maria. (2015). E-assessment and an e-training program among elderly care staff lacking formal competence: results of a mixed-methods intervention study. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-015-0843-y
title: Base competence development for staff without formal education on individually assessed needs and tailor training to assessment outcomes and learning styles
description: The article recommends assessing staff members' established knowledge, skills and abilities first, then building training on the identified deficiencies. The e-training program was "individualized and based on each staff member's practical and theoretical assessment outcomes as well as tailored to suite their learning styles", and the authors align this with a review concluding that education programs "should be based on staff needs, as identified by staff members themselves". Assessment of learning style is described as central to any training program.
requirements: Voluntary participation and manager encouragement, since staff motivation depended on organizational support and manager willingness
constraints: Some staff felt too old or uninterested and declined the training; time pressure and self-imposed demands made completion difficult for some
target_learners: elderly care staff with no formal education, employed often on temporary basis
target_learning_goals: lifelong learning
competence development outside formal education institutions
examples: Competence needs identified at the individual level in the e-assessments were the basis for implementation of a professional e-training program tailored to every individual's needs

article_title: Active learning not associated with student learning in a random sample of college biology courses.
citation: Andrews T. M., Leonard M. J., Colgrove C. A., Kalinowski S. T. (2011). Active Learning Not Associated with Student Learning in a Random Sample of College Biology Courses. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.11-07-0061
title: Instructors should assess the effectiveness of their active-learning instruction with pre/post concept tests rather than assume active learning is working
description: Because active learning as typically implemented may not produce gains, the article recommends that "no one can assume that they are teaching effectively just because they are using active learning." It recommends using reliable and valid tests "in a pre/posttest design to assess the effectiveness of instruction, as well as using formative assessments to monitor learning throughout instruction." This makes instructors responsible for verifying that their active-learning exercises actually improve learning.
requirements: Access to reliable and valid concept tests suitable for pre/post administration
constraints: The recommendation arises from a study of introductory biology courses teaching natural selection
target_learners: college science instructors
target_learning_goals: evaluating and improving the effectiveness of one's own instruction
examples: The study itself used pre/post administration of the CINS-abbr and an open-ended application question across 33 courses to measure learning gains
key_sources: Andrews T. M., Leonard M. J., Colgrove C. A., Kalinowski S. T. (2011). Active Learning Not Associated with Student Learning in a Random Sample of College Biology Courses. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.11-07-0061

article_title: Asynchronous vs didactic education: it's too early to throw in the towel on tradition.
citation: Jordan Jaime, Jalali Azadeh, Clarke Samuel, Dyne Pamela, Spector Tahlia, Coates Wendy. (2013). Asynchronous vs didactic education: it's too early to throw in the towel on tradition. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-13-105
title: Use asynchronous computer-based instruction as a complement to, not a replacement for, traditional didactics for novice learners
description: The article recommends blending interactive didactics with asynchronous modules rather than substituting one for the other, "capitalizing on the strengths of both techniques and minimizing the weaknesses". It reports that asynchronous modules alone were not equivalent to lectures for novice learners of acute care topics, while retention was similar, so each method has distinct strengths.
requirements: At least equivalency with current teaching methods should be demonstrated before investing in an asynchronous program
constraints: The study urges caution specifically for novice learners in emergency medicine and acute care; results may not generalize to all formats of asynchronous instruction or to experienced learners
target_learners: fourth-year medical students (novice learners in acute care)
target_learning_goals: acute care medical knowledge (shock, acute abdomen, dyspnea, trauma, chest pain, EKG interpretation, pain management)
examples: The course delivered half its core content via lectures and half via asynchronous modules, then held a one-hour interactive review covering both before the post-test
key_sources: Jordan Jaime, Jalali Azadeh, Clarke Samuel, Dyne Pamela, Spector Tahlia, Coates Wendy. (2013). Asynchronous vs didactic education: it's too early to throw in the towel on tradition. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-13-105

article_title: Effect of Night Laboratories on Learning Objectives for a Non-Major Astronomy Class
citation: Ian C. Jacobi, Heidi Jo Newberg, Darren Broder, Rose A. Finn, Anthony J. Milano, Lee A. Newberg, Allan T. Weatherwax, and Douglas C. B. Whittet. (2008). Effect of Night Laboratories on Learning Objectives for a Non-Major Astronomy Class. https://www.rpi.edu/dept/phys/observatory/labs.html
title: 25-question astronomy assessment test aligned to course learning objectives
description: A purpose-built assessment examination created for this study and printed in Appendix A, consisting of 25 multiple-choice questions aligned to the introductory astronomy courses at Siena College and Rensselaer. The authors chose it over the standard Astronomy Diagnostic Test because the ADT "did not align well enough to the course content to be a reliable indicator of student performance." It was reviewed through several iterations by three Siena and two Rensselaer faculty members and administered as pretest and posttest in both study years.
requirements: Faculty review iterations to ensure clarity of each question and relevance to the classes
Administration as both pretest and posttest to the same students
constraints: It was written a year before the night laboratories, so it was not designed specifically for the laboratories
Question 4 is flagged by the authors as generating ambiguous results that are hard to interpret
target_learners: Undergraduate non-science majors in introductory astronomy
target_learning_goals: General astronomical concepts addressed in the Earth and Sky course, including moon phases, telescope resolving power, seasons, and scales of the Solar System
examples: Administered to 82 students (pre and post) in Fall 2006 and 68 students in Fall 2007, with results tabulated per question

article_title: Some remarks on a current study involving preservice elementary teachers and some basic astronomical phenomena
citation: Alejandro Gangui, María Iglesias & Cynthia Quinteros. (2010). Some remarks on a current study involving preservice elementary teachers and some basic astronomical phenomena. Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 260. https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.0179
title: Twelve-question diagnostic questionnaire on basic astronomical notions for preservice elementary teachers
description: A questionnaire of twelve questions covering eight topics in basic astronomy, designed using prior studies of preservice teachers' most frequent answers. Q1 and Q2 ask about verticality and gravitation; Q3–Q5 about simple astronomical concepts; Q6–Q8 about the Moon's movement and the three-body system; Q9 about Earth's real movements; Q10 about Moon phases; and Q11–Q12 test cultural aspects of basic astronomy. The authors "have designed some tools (and show here results with a questionnaire) that proved helpful in putting in evidence some of the most frequently used alternative models".
requirements: Questions were refined through pilot testing; some questions were modified after the first tests while others were kept unchanged
constraints: The percent results presented are descriptive and, per the authors, do not have statistical value
target_learners: preservice elementary teachers
target_learning_goals: basic astronomical notions such as gravitation, seasons, Earth and Moon movements, Moon phases, and astronomical elements of everyday language
examples: Tested with preservice elementary teachers from various normal schools in Buenos Aires; total n of 51 with the final questionnaire, and 65 or 81 for unmodified questions

article_title: Do Prescribed Prompts Prime Sensemaking During Group Problem Solving?
citation: Martinuk, M. and Ives, J. (2010). Do Prescribed Prompts Prime Sensemaking During Group Problem Solving? Physics Education Research conference proceedings style manuscript, University of British Columbia.
title: Require students to state modeling assumptions to induce conceptual discussion, because reconciliation between formal physics and everyday intuition is required
description: The article's most successful prompt was the explicit requirement to state modeling assumptions, which prompted Conceptual Discussion from every group studied and had the highest overall percentage of Conceptual Discussion. The authors believe this prompt succeeds "only because reconciliation between formal physics and everyday intuition is required to complete this task, and so a certain amount of Conceptual Discussion is necessary." It is the one prescribed prompt that reliably induced sensemaking in this setting.
requirements: The task must be one where reconciliation between formal physics and everyday intuition is required to complete it.
constraints: Other prescribed prompts, including those explicitly intended to promote sensemaking, did not reliably induce Conceptual Discussion in this course's context-rich problems.
target_learners: novice introductory physics students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: sensemaking of physics situations
connecting formal physics to everyday intuition
examples: In Physics 100 worksheets, step 3 (Model: Identify Assumptions and Relationships) required groups to state assumptions, and all six studied groups engaged in Conceptual Discussion during that segment.
key_sources: Martinuk, M. and Ives, J. (2010). Do Prescribed Prompts Prime Sensemaking During Group Problem Solving? Physics Education Research conference proceedings style manuscript, University of British Columbia. https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.5400

article_title: Preparing Undergraduates for Research Careers: Using Astrobites in the Classroom
citation: Sanders, N. E., Kohler, S., Newton, E., & the Astrobites collaboration. (2012). Preparing Undergraduates for Research Careers: Using Astrobites in the Classroom. http://astrobites.com
title: Astrobites: a graduate-student-authored website publishing daily accessible summaries of new astrophysics research
description: Astrobites, founded in December 2010, is an online reader's digest for the astrophysics preprint server astro-ph, written and maintained by graduate students in astrophysical sciences from the United States and Europe. It "publishes succinct (~4–7 paragraph) summaries of the methods, results, conclusions, and context of new research papers in astrophysics posted to astro-ph," designed for undergraduates with physical-science coursework, with terminology defined, links to references, and figures from the original papers. About 30 rotating authors each write one post per month, supported by about 10 additional contributors, and the site also publishes career advice and notices of opportunities such as REU programs twice per week.
requirements: Content is prepared by graduate-student authors who are expert enough to summarize research papers yet aware of the undergraduate target audience's level of familiarity
constraints: Knowledge of basic physical concepts such as energy conservation or blackbody radiation is assumed in readers
All authors contribute on an unpaid basis and the website is presented without advertising and entirely as a not-for-profit enterprise
target_learners: undergraduates in physics and astronomy who have taken coursework in the physical sciences
target_learning_goals: comprehension of specialized jargon and idioms of the field
understanding of research practices and technical methods
familiarity with the technical literature
examples: Summaries are published at a current rate of one per day, with about 400 posted to date; the site received about 300 regular readers per day as tracked by Google Analytics in 2012.
key_sources: Sanders, N. E., Kohler, S., Newton, E., & the Astrobites collaboration. (2012). Preparing Undergraduates for Research Careers: Using Astrobites in the Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4791

article_title: Preparing Undergraduates for Research Careers: Using Astrobites in the Classroom
citation: Sanders, N. E., Kohler, S., Newton, E., & the Astrobites collaboration. (2012). Preparing Undergraduates for Research Careers: Using Astrobites in the Classroom. http://astrobites.com
title: Two documented course designs using Astrobites: student blogging modeled on the site, and journal-club paper selection with Astrobites as context source
description: Two prior university courses illustrate reusable designs for incorporating Astrobites. In a Caltech inquiry-based introductory astronomy course, students maintained their own blogs to record problem-solving techniques and produce original content such as interviews with astronomers and research-topic summaries, with Astrobites presented as a model blog. In a Swarthmore journal-club-style discussion course for advanced undergraduates, students selected and summarized papers on a rotating basis, using Astrobites "as a resource for selecting interesting papers and as a source for background information and context."
requirements: In the journal-club design, students must be responsible for selecting and summarizing research papers for the week's seminar on a rotating basis
The blog-based design requires students to record problem-solving techniques and produce original content including interviews and research summaries
constraints: These designs were reported as anecdotes from a small educator/student survey, described by the authors as illustrating only a subset of the possibilities
target_learners: introductory undergraduate astronomy students
advanced undergraduate astronomy students
target_learning_goals: engagement with modern research topics
selecting and summarizing research papers
increasing student engagement outside the classroom
examples: The article cites the Caltech Astronomy 20 course (Fall 2012, Prof. John Johnson) and the Swarthmore Astronomy 61 course (Spring 2012, Prof. Eric Jensen) as its two anecdotes.

article_title: A collaboration to support novice instructors in research-based astronomy teaching
citation: Sissi L. Li, Gabriela Serna, Jocelyn S. Read, Joshua R. Smith, Heather Chilton, Michael E. Loverude. (2015). A collaboration to support novice instructors in research-based astronomy teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.5738
title: A three-part reform-implementation model: workshops, peer-instructor teams, and researcher collaboration
description: The article presents a model of reform implementation for introductory astronomy built on three key features. The authors state: "First, our astronomy instructors learned to use research-based curricular materials by attending workshops before and after first implementation." Second, instructors collaborated with student Peer Instructors to document and reflect on implementation; third, the team worked with science education researchers to collect information on common student conceptual difficulties and develop strategies from the research literature. The model targets novice university instructors adopting research-based instructional strategies.
requirements: Requires departmental support and close collaboration with science education researchers, as at the authors' institution
constraints: Implemented at one institution with junior faculty teaching introductory astronomy for the first time; the authors note implementation of course reforms can be highly sensitive to local context
target_learners: University non-science majors in introductory astronomy
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of big ideas in astronomy
Understanding the nature of science
examples: Seven sections of reformed introductory astronomy taught from Fall 2011 to Spring 2013 with peer-instructor support and reflective journaling

article_title: Peer-review Platform for Astronomy Education Activities
citation: Russo, P., Heenatigala, T., Gomez, E., & Strubbe, L. (2015). Peer-review Platform for Astronomy Education Activities. eLearning Papers, n.º 40. https://www.openeducationeuropa.eu/en/elearning_papers
title: astroEDU: an open-access peer-review platform for astronomy education activities
description: astroEDU is a web platform for sharing astronomy education activities such as activity guides and tutorials, where each submission is peer-reviewed by an educator and an astronomer before publication. The article states that "Each of the astroEDU activities is peer-reviewed by an educator as well as an astronomer to ensure a high standard in terms of scientific content and educational value." Reviewed materials are stored in a free open online database, licensed Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported, and distributed in PDF, .doc, HTML and epub formats including source files for translation and remixing.
requirements: Activities must be submitted through the astroEDU activity template and pass double-blind review by an educator and an astronomy researcher
constraints: Platform content is astronomy education activities only; at the time of writing it was available in English, though submissions in any language were welcomed
target_learners: school and informal-education learners of all ages reached through educators using the activities
target_learning_goals: astronomy and science education content delivered through reviewed activity guides
examples: Activities are labeled with a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) for persistent identification, and successful activities are syndicated through repositories such as Scientix and TES
key_sources: Russo, P., Heenatigala, T., Gomez, E., & Strubbe, L. (2015). Peer-review Platform for Astronomy Education Activities. eLearning Papers, n.º 40. https://www.openeducationeuropa.eu/en/elearning_papers

article_title: Peer-review Platform for Astronomy Education Activities
citation: Russo, P., Heenatigala, T., Gomez, E., & Strubbe, L. (2015). Peer-review Platform for Astronomy Education Activities. eLearning Papers, n.º 40. https://www.openeducationeuropa.eu/en/elearning_papers
title: astroEDU activity template: a structured taxonomy for peer-reviewable activity guides
description: The astroEDU editorial board established an activity template so that learning outcomes are identified and can be evaluated during review. The article states that "The components can be broken in four main areas: Objectives (What will your students learn?), Materials (What are the teaching instruments?), Processes (How will you teach your students?) and assessment (How will you assess your students' learning?)." Table 2 details sections including keywords, age range, education level, time, group size, cost, location, overall goals, learning objectives, evaluation, background information, core skills, type of learning activity, and curriculum connection.
requirements: Submissions must identify specific learning outcomes that enable the logic of the activity and the evaluation structure
constraints: The template was designed by the astroEDU editorial board for astronomy education activities specifically
target_learners: teachers and educators preparing astronomy activities for school-age and other learners
target_learning_goals: clearly specified learning objectives tied to evaluation in activity design
examples: The template's core-skills field uses science-practice categories such as asking questions, developing and using models, and analysing and interpreting data

article_title: High energy astroparticle physics for high school students
citation: Maria Krause, Hans-Peter Bretz, Lew Classen, Markus Holler, Moritz Hütten, Susanne Raab, Julian Rautenberg, Anneli Schulz. (2015). High energy astroparticle physics for high school students. The 34th International Cosmic Ray Conference. https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.03968
title: Three-part authentic data-analysis masterclass structure: shower core, arrival direction, lateral distribution
description: The masterclass activity is structured so each student reconstructs an event measured by the Pierre Auger Observatory. "The project is divided into three main parts": first reconstructing the impact point of the shower core via a signal-weighted center-of-mass calculation, then evaluating the arrival direction, and lastly analyzing the lateral distribution of the air shower. The activity "has been designed to be inexpensive and easy reproducible with little prior knowledge", using a common spreadsheet program.
requirements: A common spreadsheet program such as Microsoft Excel or LibreOffice Calc
Public event data from the Pierre Auger Observatory webpages
constraints: Designed for students with little prior knowledge
Uses only surface detector station data
target_learners: High school students aged 15 to 19
target_learning_goals: Reconstructing basic properties of air showers using classical physics and high school mathematics
Training the center-of-mass problem and spreadsheet use
examples: For the example event, the center-of-mass calculation yields Xcenter-of-mass ≈ 468848 m and Ycenter-of-mass ≈ 6087798 m, marked as the shower core position
key_sources: Maria Krause, Hans-Peter Bretz, Lew Classen, Markus Holler, Moritz Hütten, Susanne Raab, Julian Rautenberg, Anneli Schulz. (2015). High energy astroparticle physics for high school students. The 34th International Cosmic Ray Conference. https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.03968

article_title: Astronom\'ia al Aire: Media Convergence in Astronomy & Astrophysics
citation: L. A. N´ u˜ nez and H. Rago (2015). Astronom´ıa al Aire: Media Convergence in Astronomy & Astrophysics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.07147
title: Astronomía al Aire: a converged-media astronomy outreach initiative
description: An outreach initiative of the Relativity and Gravitation Research Group and the School of Physics at Universidad Industrial de Santander that "mixes traditional media like radio broadcast with blog and microblogging, discussing science topics related to Astronomy and Astrophysics". Its components are 4–5 minute audio clips, a 30-minute weekly radio program, daily AM broadcasts retransmitted through the RRULAC university radio network, a project blog and the @AstroAlAire Twitter identity.
requirements: Access to a university radio station and broadcast schedule, web 2.0 tools (blog, microblogging), and scientist authors willing to serve as storyteller narrators
constraints: The authors note the initiative was in its first year and that "more time is needed to fully evaluate its impact"
target_learners: Spanish-speaking general public in Latin America
laypeople with limited or no access to the internet
target_learning_goals: interest in Astronomy and Astrophysics
appreciation of the values of science: its structure, beauty and creative freedom
examples: Clips are "regularly broadcast three times (7:30am, 12:30pm and 5:30pm) per day by 670Khertz AM UIS University radio in Bucaramanga" and retransmitted by RRULAC members in Mexico, Colombia and Venezuela
A "30m weekly radio program complements audio clips presenting and discussing recent advances in Physics and Astrophysics"
key_sources: L. A. N´ u˜ nez and H. Rago (2015). Astronom´ıa al Aire: Media Convergence in Astronomy & Astrophysics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.07147

article_title: Astronom\'ia al Aire: Media Convergence in Astronomy & Astrophysics
citation: L. A. N´ u˜ nez and H. Rago (2015). Astronom´ıa al Aire: Media Convergence in Astronomy & Astrophysics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.07147
title: Astronomía al Aire audio clips: short scientist-narrated weekly podcasts
description: Audio clips of about four to five minutes "are the central part of Astronom´ ıa al Aire project and currently 35 of them have been produced and disseminated weekly" through the project website. Topics include scientists who built theories, supernovae, stars, black holes, exoplanets, neutrinos, antimatter and the large structure of the universe, emphasising the relation between theory and observations. Background music deliberately avoids science clichés, using tango, salsa, Beatles, Stravinsky or Xenakis themes.
requirements: The clip author is the storyteller narrator: "The voice of a scientist that knows and understands the emphasis on content, is preferable and more credible than the neutral, trained voice of a professional broadcaster"
constraints: "There are necessary overlapping of themes and subjects": clips on the evolution of stars share concepts with those on neutron stars, pulsars and black holes
target_learners: general radio audiences in Spanish-speaking Latin America
target_learning_goals: interest in scientific inquiry about astronomical objects and events
appreciation of the intimate relation between theory and observations
examples: Clips are worked out about scientists who have built theories and made discoveries, and about objects and events such as supernovae, black holes and exoplanets
key_sources: L. A. N´ u˜ nez and H. Rago (2015). Astronom´ıa al Aire: Media Convergence in Astronomy & Astrophysics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.07147

article_title: When physical intuition fails
citation: Chandralekha Singh, University of Pittsburgh. (2016). When physical intuition fails. https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.06637
title: Instructors should assess the difficulty of a problem from the perspective of beginning students, since perceived complexity depends on experience and familiarity as well as inherent complexity
description: Because perceived problem complexity depends not only on inherent complexity but also on the experience, familiarity, and intuition a solver has built about a class of problems, instructors should evaluate problems as beginning students would. The article states "There are likely to be less surprises if we put ourselves in students' shoes and analyze the diﬃculty of a problem from their p erspective", using the ballistic pendulum as an example of a problem easy for professors but hard for students.
requirements: Instructors must consider the experience, familiarity, and intuition students lack relative to their own
constraints: Applies to introductory-level problems; the article notes few introductory problems show such universally lacking expert intuition as the one studied
target_learners: beginning introductory physics students
target_learning_goals: accurate instructor calibration of problem difficulty
physics problem solving
examples: Professors found the ballistic pendulum problem easy because they had built intuition about that class of problems, while students struggle to focus on several aspects simultaneously
key_sources: Chandralekha Singh, University of Pittsburgh. (2016). When physical intuition fails. https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.06637

article_title: Teaching Data Science
citation: Robert J. Brunner and Edward J. Kim. (2016). Teaching Data Science. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.07397
title: ASA Data Expo 2009 airline on-time performance dataset as the recurring data backbone for programming assignments
description: Many programming assignments used "the airline on-time performance data set from the American Statistical Association (ASA) Data Expo 2009," originally from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics, tracking all commercial U.S. flights between 1987 and 2012. The full data set has "more than 120 million records in total and taking up twelve Gigabytes," so the course instead used the 2001 CSV file with around six million rows, twenty-nine columns, and 573 Megabytes. Assignments built on it included aggregating flight counts and temperatures for the top twenty airports and PCA-plus-k-means clustering of aircraft.
requirements: Out-of-memory data size motivates using the single-year 2001 CSV extract rather than the full twelve-Gigabyte set
An SVG template with city-named circle elements and access to the FAA web service for the airport visualization task
constraints: The full dataset "precludes traditional, in-memory processing," so only the 2001 subset was used
target_learners: Undergraduate and graduate students learning data processing, aggregation, visualization and machine learning on realistic data
target_learning_goals: Grouping and aggregation of large tabular data; web data retrieval and XML/SVG processing; PCA and k-means clustering
examples: One assignment visualized total flights and current temperature of the top twenty U.S. airports (Figure 3); another clustered Delta Airlines aircraft from a CSV with thirty-four features from forty-four aircraft (Figure 4)
key_sources: Robert J. Brunner and Edward J. Kim. (2016). Teaching Data Science. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.07397

article_title: Incorporating Current Research into Formal Higher Education Settings using Astrobites
citation: Nathan E. Sanders, Susanna Kohler, Chris Faesi, Ashley Villar, Michael Zevin, and the Astrobites Collaboration. (2017). Incorporating Current Research into Formal Higher Education Settings using Astrobites. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.01165
title: Astrobites: a free online resource of graduate-student-written summaries of astrophysical research papers
description: Astrobites is a free online resource, authored by volunteer graduate students, that publishes "brief and accessible summaries of recent research papers targeted at an undergraduate-level audience." Summaries translate jargon, add context on essential past work and current motivations, and link back to the original technical publications. The article positions Astrobites as a scaffold for students reading journal papers in astrophysics for the first time, and as a resource instructors can integrate into formal courses.
requirements: Readers are assumed to have "a working knowledge of the basic principles of mechanics, electromagnetism, optics" and other undergraduate-level physics subjects
constraints: Content addresses the astrophysical literature; the model has been extended to other fields and languages only through separately operated sister sites such as particle physics and oceanography
target_learners: undergraduate physics or astronomy majors
graduate students in the physical sciences
target_learning_goals: comprehension of primary research literature
context for modern research results and motivations
examples: Each day one graduate student member drafts an original summary of a recent peer-reviewed or astro-ph preprint publication while another member edits it
key_sources: Nathan E. Sanders, Susanna Kohler, Chris Faesi, Ashley Villar, Michael Zevin, and the Astrobites Collaboration. (2017). Incorporating Current Research into Formal Higher Education Settings using Astrobites. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.01165

article_title: Navigation in the Ancient Mediterranean and Beyond
citation: M. Nielbock. (2017). Navigation in the Ancient Mediterranean and Beyond. AstroEDU manuscript no. astroedu1645. https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.07700
title: AstroEDU lesson unit on ancient Mediterranean celestial navigation with two hands-on activities
description: A 90-minute lesson unit for ages 14–19 developed within the EU Space Awareness project that "provides an insight into the history and navigational methods of the Bronze Age Mediterranean peoples." It combines background reading on ancient seafaring with two hands-on activities: drawing circumpolar ranges on star charts for six cities, and producing a stellar compass from a spreadsheet of bright stars. Materials include worksheets, compasses, protractors, and an Excel file of bright stars.
requirements: Worksheet, pair of compasses, pencil, ruler, calculator, protractor, computer with MS Excel, and the supplied Excel spreadsheet
constraints: Suggested age range 14–19 years; duration 90 minutes; third activity is supplemental and requires a clear evening sky
target_learners: Middle School and Secondary School students, ages 14–19
target_learning_goals: describe methods to determine cardinal directions from observing the sky
explain the nature of circumpolar stars and constellations
use an Excel spreadsheet for calculations
examples: Students calculate angular radii from the celestial pole for cities such as Tunis, Cape Town, Plymouth, Wellington, Mumbai and Grytviken, then draw circles on star maps to find circumpolar constellations
key_sources: M. Nielbock. (2017). Navigation in the Ancient Mediterranean and Beyond. AstroEDU manuscript no. astroedu1645. https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.07700

article_title: Indy: a virtual reality multi-player game for navigation skills training
citation: Arnaud Mas, Idriss Ismaël, Nicolas Filliard. (2018). Indy: a virtual reality multi-player game for navigation skills training. EDF R&D. none in text
title: Asymmetric collaboration roles (immersed hunters vs desktop radios) to make team communication necessary
description: Indy relies on an asymmetric collaboration method in which some learners, wearing a head-mounted display, play the "hunters" who find their way, while others use floor maps and 360° photographs on a desktop computer as the "radios" who guide them. Because learners have access to complementary information according to their role, each one holds a key capability to achieve the scenario objective, which makes communication within the team necessary to navigate the virtual building. Visibility rules keep hunters from simply following the radio: hunters cannot see the radio's avatar or pointing ray.
requirements: Complementary information distribution across roles so each member has a key capability
oral communication and pointing as communication channels
constraints: Designed to be run within a training sequence where participants are physically co-located, to preserve social interaction
target_learners: adult professional trainees in industrial settings
target_learning_goals: collaborative route communication
survey knowledge and map reading
examples: Before starting the hunt, each team gathers around the radio's computer to prepare its itinerary and select alternative paths
key_sources: Arnaud Mas, Idriss Ismaël, Nicolas Filliard. (2018). Indy: a virtual reality multi-player game for navigation skills training. EDF R&D. none in text. https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.04184

article_title: Un enfoque de ense\~nanza de la Astronom\'ia: Algunas consideraciones epistemol\'ogicas y did\'acticas
citation: Gangui, A. y Adúriz-Bravo, A. (2016). Un enfoque de enseñanza de la Astronomía: Algunas consideraciones epistemológicas y didácticas. http://www.ceip.edu.uy/documentos/normativa/programaescolar/ProgramaEscolar_14-6.pdf
title: Enseñar la Astronomía a partir de las vivencias astronómicas del observador terrestre, tratando la rotación y la traslación como hipótesis explicativas
description: El artículo recomienda que la enseñanza de la Astronomía escolar en Inicial y Primaria trabaje desde las experiencias del observador en la Tierra (sombras, salidas y puestas del Sol, cielo diurno y nocturno) en lugar de limitarse a declarar los movimientos reales del planeta. Los autores sostienen que "la propuesta de trabajar a partir de las vivencias astronómicas del observador terrestre resulta mucho más rica que el mero hecho de declarar cuáles son los movimientos reales que tiene nuestro planeta". Siguiendo a Martínez Sebastià (2004), el objetivo es que los estudiantes expliquen hechos y fenómenos astronómicos del entorno mediante esas dos nociones entendidas como genuinas hipótesis, y no como ideas adquiridas.
requirements: Comenzar con actividades para conocer y hacer explícitos los saberes previos sobre el tema, como se hizo en el caso narrado
constraints: Los autores reconocen que los contenidos prescritos sobre el sistema Sol-Tierra apuntan a un nivel de abstracción difícil de lograr con niños de hasta 12 años
target_learners: estudiantes de educación inicial y primaria (hasta 12 años)
target_learning_goals: explicar hechos y fenómenos astronómicos del entorno mediante la rotación y la traslación de la Tierra
examples: En el caso narrado, el docente propuso actividades para hacer explícitos los saberes previos y centró la enseñanza en los aspectos vivenciales y descriptivos de los fenómenos astronómicos, con un intercambio de cierre entre sexto y tercer grado sobre sombras y el recorrido aparente del Sol
key_sources: Gangui, A. y Adúriz-Bravo, A. (2016). Un enfoque de enseñanza de la Astronomía: Algunas consideraciones epistemológicas y didácticas. http://www.ceip.edu.uy/documentos/normativa/programaescolar/ProgramaEscolar_14-6.pdf

article_title: Un enfoque de ense\~nanza de la Astronom\'ia: Algunas consideraciones epistemol\'ogicas y did\'acticas
citation: Gangui, A. y Adúriz-Bravo, A. (2016). Un enfoque de enseñanza de la Astronomía: Algunas consideraciones epistemológicas y didácticas. http://www.ceip.edu.uy/documentos/normativa/programaescolar/ProgramaEscolar_14-6.pdf
title: La Astronomía escolar como entretejido de tradiciones disciplinares organizadas en hilos conductores a lo largo de los grados
description: El artículo propone un marco de análisis curricular según el cual el programa uruguayo de Astronomía "trenza" contenidos de diferentes tradiciones disciplinares que han estado históricamente más cerca o más lejos unas de otras. Estas tradiciones se reconocen como "hilos conductores" del programa: cada hilo arranca en un grado determinado, más o menos tempranamente, y luego se sostiene a lo largo de los demás grados ampliándose y profundizándose. Los ejes identificados incluyen la Astronomía descriptiva y matemática tradicional (rotación, traslación, sistema Tierra-Sol), su interfaz con la física y otras ciencias (mecánica, óptica, astrofísica, cosmología), contenidos procedimentales de orientación y representación, y contenidos de historia y naturaleza de la ciencia (modelos geocéntrico y heliocéntrico, teorías sobre el origen del Universo).
requirements: Leer cuidadosamente los contenidos prescritos para indagar en el proceso de producción curricular y fundamentar mejor la enseñanza
constraints: El marco describe el Programa de Educación Inicial y Primaria de Uruguay (Año 2008, tercera edición 2013); los autores señalan que algunas formulaciones del programa son poco claras
target_learners: maestras y maestros de educación inicial y primaria
target_learning_goals: comprender los fundamentos epistemológicos de los contenidos de Astronomía del currículo y fundamentar el diseño de secuencias de enseñanza
examples: El artículo caracteriza la Astronomía escolar mediante cinco preguntas sobre ubicación y constitución de los sistemas, su origen y evolución, interacciones entre sus partes, su descripción y representación, y las visiones históricas que la humanidad ha generado sobre ellos
key_sources: Gangui, A. y Adúriz-Bravo, A. (2016). Un enfoque de enseñanza de la Astronomía: Algunas consideraciones epistemológicas y didácticas. http://www.ceip.edu.uy/documentos/normativa/programaescolar/ProgramaEscolar_14-6.pdf

article_title: Secret objectives: promoting inquiry and tackling preconceptions in teaching laboratories
citation: Paul A. Bartlett, K. Dunnett. (2019). Secret objectives: promoting inquiry and tackling preconceptions in teaching laboratories. https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.07267
title: Align laboratory assessment with inquiry behaviours and skill acquisition rather than task completion
description: The article states that 'the course assessment should not be on experiment completion or similar, but focus on skill acquisition', because an observed limitation on the success of such experiments is assessment that emphasises task completion or record keeping rather than recognising and rewarding inquiry behaviours. Students should be given permission to fail, with assessment based on what they have done rather than completion of predefined tasks.
requirements: Assessment instruments that reward critical examination and exploration, such as laboratory notebooks
constraints: Stated as an observed limitation: misaligned assessment limits the success of secret-objectives experiments
target_learners: first-year undergraduate physics students
target_learning_goals: inquiry behaviours
critical examination of experiments
examples: In the first-year undergraduate laboratories at UCL, assessment focuses on keeping a laboratory notebook and critical examination and exploration of the experiment
key_sources: Paul A. Bartlett, K. Dunnett. (2019). Secret objectives: promoting inquiry and tackling preconceptions in teaching laboratories. https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.07267

article_title: The African School of Fundamental Physics and Applications (ASP)
citation: Kétévi Adiklè Assamagan, Mounia Laassiri. (2019). The African School of Fundamental Physics and Applications (ASP). https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.06309
title: African School of Fundamental Physics and Applications (ASP): biennial three-week physics capacity-building school
description: The ASP is a biennial school held in a different African country each edition, aiming to "build capacity to harvest, interpret, and exploit the results of current and future physics experiments and to increase proficiency in related applications." It runs for three weeks and covers particle physics, detectors, astroparticle physics and cosmology, computing, accelerator technologies, medical physics, condensed matter, and light sources. International lecturers deliver courses adapted to diverse student levels, and full bursaries are provided to selected students.
requirements: Host country selected two and a half years in advance through a competitive bidding process considering participant safety and host-government support
Funding from institutes in Africa, Asia, Europe and the USA
target_learners: African MSc-level and other university physics students selected from across Africa
target_learning_goals: Fundamental physics knowledge and research capacity
Applications including Grid computing and medical physics
examples: Five editions held 2010–2018 in Stellenbosch, Kumasi, Dakar, Kigali and Windhoek, with a 2020 edition planned in Morocco
key_sources: Kétévi Adiklè Assamagan, Mounia Laassiri. (2019). The African School of Fundamental Physics and Applications (ASP). https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.06309

title: ASP continuous mentorship program pairing students with international lecturers beyond the school
description: The ASP mentorship program is "a dedicated effort to mentor ASP students in collaboration with their academic advisors" and "runs continuously even when there is no formal school." International lecturers help select and mentor students, and the mentorship helps the organizers track alumni academic development. The conclusion notes it allows African students to stay connected to lecturers from abroad and benefit from active mentorship supplementing academic advisors' efforts.
