article_title: Student Epistemological Framing on Paper-Based Assessments
citation: Kelli Shar, Rosemary S. Russ, James T. Laverty. (2021). Student Epistemological Framing on Paper-Based Assessments. https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.07442
title: Assessment design should account for the epistemological messages assessments send to students, not only the evidence they collect
description: Existing assessment design theories such as the Assessment Triangle, Evidence-Centered Design, and the BEAR Assessment System focus on obtaining evidence about student knowledge while paying little attention to the messages assessments send students. This article argues assessments communicate what faculty and researchers think it means to know and do physics, and that these messages shape how students frame and engage with assessment tasks. Designers should therefore consider how features like the presence or absence of numbers cue particular epistemological framings.
requirements: Assessment designers must anticipate which epistemological resources and frames assessment features may activate in students
constraints: The article studied paper-based summative assessments in introductory undergraduate physics; the authors note future work is needed to create assessment questions that deliberately prompt resource shifts
target_learners: undergraduate introductory physics students
target_learning_goals: appropriate engagement with assessment tasks
epistemological framing of physics problem solving
examples: The Ferris Wheel problem's lack of numbers shifted two students' epistemic form from Number to Reasoning and their frame from Algorithmic to Conceptual Physics, while the Gravitron problem's explicit request for reasoning through words failed to shift students' frames
key_sources: Kelli Shar, Rosemary S. Russ, James T. Laverty. (2021). Student Epistemological Framing on Paper-Based Assessments. https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.07442

article_title: Beyond teaching methods: highlighting physics faculty's strengths and agency
citation: Strubbe, L. E., Madsen, A. M., McKagan, S. B., & Sayre, E. C. (2024). Beyond teaching methods: highlighting physics faculty's strengths and agency. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07502
title: Asset-based agentic paradigm for modeling faculty teaching
description: The article's proposed alternative to the teaching-method-centered paradigm for modeling faculty teaching. Its focus is "not whether and how faculty use teaching methods defined and valued by others, but rather how faculty's own productive ideas and values shape their teaching". The authors combine a framework of teaching and learning principles (How Learning Works) with a framework of faculty agency (Self-Determination Theory) and illustrate the paradigm through three case studies of physics faculty talking about their teaching.
requirements: Combines a framework of principles of teaching and learning (the article uses How Learning Works) with a framework of faculty agency and motivation (the article uses Self-Determination Theory)
constraints: Intended primarily for PER researchers who study faculty change, professional development providers, and curriculum developers; faculty who teach physics are not among the primary intended audiences
target_learners: physics faculty developing their teaching practice
target_learning_goals: making thoughtful teaching decisions aligned with one's own values and goals
developing as a teacher
examples: Three case study faculty (Profs. Sigma, Zeta, and Delta) whose teaching ideas and motivations were analyzed through the HLW and SDT frameworks
key_sources: Strubbe, L. E., Madsen, A. M., McKagan, S. B., & Sayre, E. C. (2024). Beyond teaching methods: highlighting physics faculty's strengths and agency. https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07502

article_title: The Inspiring Universe
citation: George Miley, Carolina Ödman and Pedro Russo. (2015). The Inspiring Universe. http://www.unawe.org/resources/spacescoop/
title: Use astronomy as a holistic gateway to science, technology and culture

UNAWE applies this by encapsulating space-based themes in stories to develop language skills and in problems that develop numerical skills.

target_learners: young children aged 4 to 10
target_learning_goals: language skills
numerical skills
introduction to science and technology

article_title: Continuing education: a solution proposal for problems in the teaching of Astronomy

title: Six-module astronomy course structure grounded in project pedagogy and active methodologies
description: The course was divided into six modules — Tópicos de Astronomia, Observações do Céu, Práticas astronômicas (building a simple telescope), História Oral, Tópicos em Matemática and Metodologias Ativas — 'a partir de uma proposta fundamentada na pedagogia de projetos e nas metodologias ativas', all structured from the guiding question of what one sees when looking at the sky. target_learning_goals: Updated astronomical knowledge to reduce conceptual errors
Connection with nature and recognition of star groupings
Application of project methodology to astronomy teaching
examples: In the Observações do Céu module, night-sky observation was encouraged as a contemplative act so participants could draw their own conclusions about the movement of the stars.

article_title: Continuing education: a solution proposal for problems in the teaching of Astronomy
citation: Adriano Mesquita Oliveira, Cibele kemeicik da silva machado, Augusto Cézar Tiradentes Monteiro, Rafael Cerqueira do Nascimento, Pollyana dos Santos. (2020). Formação continuada: uma proposta de solução para problemas no ensino de Astronomia. ISSN 2359-4799. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2359-4799
title: Use astronomy teaching as a vehicle for scientific literacy and interdisciplinary work in elementary teachers' continuing education
description: The article positions astronomy teaching as a resource for basic formation, valuing 'seu potencial de letramento científico e seu caráter multidisciplinar', and argues that continuing education lets municipal-network teachers contact specialists and researchers in astronomy. It follows Candau's orientation of valuing teachers' professional knowledge and Harres's call for gradual change in professional knowledge, so the course targets critical reflection on pedagogical practice and the insertion of new practices and knowledge in the classroom.
requirements: Contact with specialists and researchers in astronomy, since textbook-only practice keeps professionals 'alheios ao pensar científico' and distant from the current state of the art.
constraints: A large share of professionals use only the textbook as source of knowledge and teaching instrument, which limits the investigative goals of the national curriculum's scientific-literacy proposal.
target_learners: Elementary-school teachers in municipal education networks
target_learning_goals: Scientific literacy instruction
Interdisciplinary connections with mathematics, history, literature and the arts
Change in teaching and learning conceptions through participatory dialogue
examples: The course was designed around the Terra e Universo thematic unit of the 2018 BNCC, through which astronomy runs across all years of elementary education and dialogues with other areas.
key_sources: Adriano Mesquita Oliveira, Cibele kemeicik da silva machado, Augusto Cézar Tiradentes Monteiro, Rafael Cerqueira do Nascimento, Pollyana dos Santos. (2020). Formação continuada: uma proposta de solução para problemas no ensino de Astronomia. ISSN 2359-4799. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/2359-4799

article_title: AstroDance: Engaging Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Students in Astrophysics via Multimedia Performances
citation: Nordhaus, J., Campanelli, M., Bochner, J., Warfield, T., Bischof, H.-P., & Noel-Storr, J. (2020). AstroDance: Engaging Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Students in Astrophysics via Multimedia Performances. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10543
title: AstroDance multimedia dance-theater performance on gravitational-wave astrophysics
description: AstroDance is an original dance and theatrical multimedia performance communicating gravitational-wave astrophysics, created by a collaboration of astrophysicists, theater artists, educators, and scientists at RIT for "diverse audiences such as deaf and hard-of-hearing students". It paired scientific visualizations drawn from the RIT group's numerical modeling of gravitational-wave sources with dance, music, and narration in spoken English and American Sign Language, and was performed primarily for secondary and post-secondary audiences.
requirements: Collaboration among researchers, scientists, artists, and educators; visual imagery obtained from the research group's modeling and simulation of gravitational-wave sources was a cornerstone of the project
constraints: The project website evaluation was planned but not completed due to unforeseen delays in the website's development
Because the performance was consistent across venues, the individual effects of dance, signed narration, or scientific visualizations cannot be isolated
target_learners: secondary and post-secondary students
deaf and hard-of-hearing audiences
members of the general public
target_learning_goals: gravitational-wave astronomy and gravitational physics concepts, including black holes, neutron stars, and supernovae
examples: Premiered at the Little Theatre in Rochester NY on Sept. 22, 2012, followed by a year-long tour of ~20 venues in the northeastern US, all at least three years before the announced direct detection of gravitational waves
key_sources: Nordhaus, J., Campanelli, M., Bochner, J., Warfield, T., Bischof, H.-P., & Noel-Storr, J. (2020). AstroDance: Engaging Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Students in Astrophysics via Multimedia Performances. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10543

article_title: AstroDance: Engaging Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Students in Astrophysics via Multimedia Performances
citation: Nordhaus, J., Campanelli, M., Bochner, J., Warfield, T., Bischof, H.-P., & Noel-Storr, J. (2020). AstroDance: Engaging Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Students in Astrophysics via Multimedia Performances. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10543
title: AstroDance vignette structure: narrated story in spoken English and ASL followed by interpretative dance with music and scientific visualizations
description: Each AstroDance vignette teaches one scientific concept through complementary components: "a short story was ﬁrst narrated on-stage in both spoken English and American Sign Language", followed by "an interpretative dance accompanied by music and accurate scientiﬁc visualizations (projected in the background)". Each component of the vignette was designed to be complementary and to reinforce the scientific concept, with visualizations referenced from the RIT group's published simulations.
requirements: Each scientific concept requires a narrated story in both spoken English and American Sign Language plus a complementary interpretative dance with music and accurate scientific visualizations
target_learners: secondary and post-secondary students
deaf and hard-of-hearing audiences
target_learning_goals: gravitational science concepts such as black hole mergers, core-collapse supernovae, and galactic mergers
examples: Performers interpreted the movement of a black hole triple system as the black holes orbit and coalesce, the implosion and explosion of a massive star as a core-collapse supernova, and the collision of two galaxies
key_sources: Nordhaus, J., Campanelli, M., Bochner, J., Warfield, T., Bischof, H.-P., & Noel-Storr, J. (2020). AstroDance: Engaging Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Students in Astrophysics via Multimedia Performances. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10543
grain_size: performance segment (one scientific concept per vignette)

article_title: Astronomy Paper Seminar Participation Guide & Reading Walkthrough
citation: Cooke, K. C., Connelly, J. L., Jones, K. M., Kirkpatrick, A., Mills, E. A. C., & Crossfield, I. J. M. (2020). Astronomy Paper Seminar: Participation Guide & Reading Walkthrough. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.12566
title: Astrobites and AAS Nova paper-summary websites as entry points to the literature
description: Astrobites is a daily-updated website hosting graduate-student-written summaries of astronomy papers and their results, offering short, focused reviews from a student perspective; AAS Nova is a similar site hosted by the American Astronomical Society that often reposts Astrobites articles of noteworthy papers. The guide positions both as starting locations for undergraduates and graduates who lack the time or comfort to read papers in full, and notes Astrobites accepts guest authors seeking writing experience.
requirements: Internet access; for writing experience, acceptance as a guest author
constraints: Summaries abbreviate detail, so full understanding still requires the primary paper
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate astronomy students
target_learning_goals: keeping up with scientific literature
learning to digest paper results efficiently
examples: The guide suggests these sites for readers who 'don't have the time or don't feel comfortable reading a paper in full'

article_title: Video Killed the Writing Assignment
citation: Nicolle Zellner. (2018). Video Killed the Writing Assignment. Journal of Astronomy and Earth Sciences Education, 5. https://campus.albion.edu/nzellner
title: Astronomy video assignment with rubric, peer and instructor grading, and class viewing
description: A course activity in which pairs of students create a 5:30 ± 30-second video on an astronomy topic of their choice, combining photographs, video, animation, sound, music, and text — what the author calls "digital storytelling." Videos require a title, at least three credible references (not Wikipedia as primary source), and posting online; grading averages classmates' evaluations (33%) with the instructor's (67%) and counts 10% of the course grade, using criteria of content, science, delivery, scientific accuracy, and adherence to requirements.
requirements: A title and a reference list with at least three credible sources, also submitted as a hard or electronic copy
Videos posted on youtube.com, the college public drive, or a shared Google drive and tested on classroom equipment
Attendance at all class viewing days and participation in evaluating classmates' videos
constraints: Videos over 6 minutes are turned off and not considered in viewing or grading
A 10% grade deduction applies for not adhering to requirements, including non-participation in evaluation or absence from viewing
target_learners: undergraduate non-science majors in an introductory Astronomy survey course
target_learning_goals: in-depth investigation of a self-chosen astronomy topic
scientific accuracy and synthesis in a creative product
constructive peer critique and collaboration
examples: Topics ranged from women in astronomy (10 videos) to dark matter (2 videos); styles included documentary (45 videos), voice over (22), TV-show spoofs (20), and reenactment (17) across 140 videos in 18 semesters.
key_sources: Nicolle Zellner. (2018). Video Killed the Writing Assignment. Journal of Astronomy and Earth Sciences Education, 5. https://campus.albion.edu/nzellner

article_title: Educational and Outreach Resource for Astroparticle Physics
citation: Y. Kazarina, V. Khristyuk, A. Kruykov, E. Postnikov, V. Samoliga, A. Shigarov, V. Tokareva, and D. Zhurov. (2020). Educational and Outreach Resource for Astroparticle Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.10920
title: astroparticle.online educational and outreach web resource
description: An educational and outreach web resource for astroparticle physics deployed since 2018 within the German-Russian Astroparticle Data Life Cycle Initiative (GRADLCI), built on WordPress and hosted at the Matrosov Institute for System Dynamics and Control Theory. Its main target audience is "students, who are interested in astroparticle physics and would like to collaborate with the Baikal region astroparticle physics experiments". It offers News, Science, Experiments and Projects sections plus a large Online School section, and serves the Baikal Multimessenger Lab as an education and outreach instrument.
requirements: Built on the free and open-source content management system WordPress, with servers located at the Matrosov Institute for System Dynamics and Control Theory
Content of materials and tasks in astroparticle physics is regularly updated
constraints: Video materials are borrowed from other sources and must refer to the source
target_learners: students interested in astroparticle physics
schoolchildren and younger students
target_learning_goals: understanding astroparticle physics and multi-messenger astronomy
collaborating with Baikal region astroparticle physics experiments

article_title: Educational and Outreach Resource for Astroparticle Physics
citation: Y. Kazarina, V. Khristyuk, A. Kruykov, E. Postnikov, V. Samoliga, A. Shigarov, V. Tokareva, and D. Zhurov. (2020). Educational and Outreach Resource for Astroparticle Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.10920
title: Astroparticle CNN client prototype for gamma/hadron separation
description: A prototype interactive service in the Online School's Data Analysis subsection giving students hands-on access to gamma/hadron separation with convolutional neural networks developed in the GRADLCI project. "The Monte Carlo events of the TAIGA-IACT telescope are used as input for this prototype", and the network outputs a gamma-reconstruction probability per event. The back end is a Docker microservice written in Python on the Django framework with SQLite, with dataset and event tables populated from HDF5 files at deployment.
requirements: Monte Carlo events of the TAIGA-IACT telescope as input
Back end deployed as a Docker microservice written in Python based on the Django framework, with SQLite populated from HDF5 files during deployment
constraints: The SQLite database contains only information about preloaded datasets
target_learners: students in the Online School Data Analysis subsection
target_learning_goals: understanding gamma/hadron separation in gamma-ray astronomy
checking skills in gamma-event identification from telescope images
examples: Students can check their skills in gamma/hadron separation using the telescope image, whose elliptical parameters (length, width, distance, angular miss-alignment) the network takes into account

article_title: The AstroCamp Project
citation: C. J. A. P. Martins. (2021). The AstroCamp Project. Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 367. https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03587
title: AstroCamp: a two-week residential academic excellence program in astronomy and physics
description: AstroCamp is an international academic excellence program in astronomy and physics created in 2012 and organized by CAUP with the Paredes de Coura municipality and partners including ESO. Its core is "a two-week residential camp, held in mid-August" at the Centre for Environmental Education of the Corno de Bico protected landscape. It targets students in the last 3 years of pre-university education and, since 2017, includes the European Southern Observatory as a partner.

constraints: Due to COVID-19 the 2020 edition was a hybrid one, with students living in Portugal in residence as usual and students living in other countries joining through a set on online collaboration tools

target_learning_goals: scientific knowledge in astronomy and physics
critical thinking
team work and group responsibility

citation: C. J. A. P. Martins. (2021). The AstroCamp Project. Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 367. https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03587
title: Residential immersion with deliberately restricted internet and phone access to maximize peer interaction and learning pace

constraints: the no-internet rule was adopted by the organizers' choice for this camp; the 2020 hybrid edition required online collaboration tools for remote students
target_learners: pre-university students in the last 3 years of secondary education
target_learning_goals: peer interaction across backgrounds
focused learning at an accelerated pace
examples: The 2020 edition was hybrid due to COVID-19, with foreign students joining through online collaboration tools while Portuguese students remained in residence

article_title: Astro-animation - A Case Study of Art and Science Education
citation: Arcadias, L., Corbet, R.H.D., McKenna, D., & Potenziani, I. (2021). Astro-animation - A case study of art and science education. https://astroanimation.org
title: Astro-animation course: a 15-week, jointly-taught art-science collaboration between MICA animation students and NASA Goddard scientist mentors
description: An undergraduate elective at the Maryland Institute College of Art, jointly taught by an astrophysicist and an animator, in which student groups of two or three are randomly assigned a research topic and a mentor scientist and produce animations presented at a NASA GSFC screening. The course "takes place for 15 weeks with three credits awarded for science and three credits for animation", beginning with astronomy and transitioning to an animation studio. Scientists present topics such as black holes, supernovae, dark matter, and gravitational waves; students visit NASA GSFC to present storyboards, and finished films are posted on AstroAnimation.org.
requirements: Access to collaborating scientists who volunteer as mentors and present their research topics to the class
A venue and scientist audience for a final screening of the student animations
constraints: Student films are free-form artistic responses constrained by scientific rigor, deliberately different from NASA's accurate graphic visualizations
target_learners: undergraduate animation students at an art and design college
target_learning_goals: understand basic concepts of astrophysics and the possibilities and limitations of scientific research
learn that science is a way of thinking as much as a body of knowledge
translate scientific concepts into animation reaching a broader public
examples: Students produced approximately six to eight group projects per year, communicated with mentors via email and Tumblr, and screened films at the NASA GSFC Visitor Center on Take Our Daughters and Sons to Work Day
key_sources: Arcadias, L., Corbet, R.H.D., McKenna, D., & Potenziani, I. (2021). Astro-animation - A case study of art and science education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.06215

description: The AstroBVI educational kit is a set of 3D-printed tactile relief images of galaxies used as the main workshop element. school students
adults

galaxy types and the electromagnetic spectrum
the Moon and the Solar System
examples: Used as the main element in seven Lima workshops in 2019, alongside a 3D printed Moon, cold-ceramic Solar System models, and NASA spatial sound files

article_title: CosmoAmautas: Astrophysics in the high school classroom (2nd edition)
citation: El Equipo CosmoAmautas. (2022). Al científico que todo niño lleva dentro. Segunda edición, Publicado por CosmoAmautas. https://www.cosmoamautas.org/
title: Use analogies to familiar domains when introducing abstract astronomical quantities
description: Section and figure titles in the book systematically introduce abstract stellar quantities by analogy with familiar reference frames: "La magnitud aparente de una estrella es análoga al ﬂujo" and "La magnitud absoluta de una estrella es análoga a la luminosidad"; stellar spectral classes are presented as "La tabla periódica de las estrellas"; and cosmological model-building is framed as "Receta para cocinar un universo: Lambda CDM" with its ingredients (barionic matter, dark matter, dark energy) treated as recipe components. These framings scaffold unfamiliar astronomy onto chemistry, cooking and measurement ideas students already hold.
requirements: A familiar anchor domain whose structure genuinely parallels the target concept
constraints: Analogies are labeled as analogies ('es análoga a'); they are scaffolds, not identities
target_learners: school students new to stellar magnitude and cosmology
target_learning_goals: apparent versus absolute magnitude
spectral classification
composition of the Lambda CDM model
examples: The chapter on cosmology introduces Lambda CDM under the heading 'Receta para cocinar un universo' with subsections for each ingredient

article_title: How to write and develop your astronomy research paper
citation: Knapen, J. H., Chamba, N., & Black, D. (2023). How to write and develop your astronomy research paper. https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.05503
title: Astronomy research papers follow an IMRaD section structure with an overall hourglass shape
description: The guide prescribes a canonical section organisation for astronomy research papers: 'Introduction, Methods/Sample/Data, Results, Discussion, Conclusion (IMRaD)', kept as separate, short, logical sections broken into 'bite-sized chunks' by sub-sections and paragraphs. It adds an hourglass shape: the paper 'starts broadly, with the 'big picture' in the introduction, then narrows down into the details of methods and results, before broadening again at the end'. Sections should not be mixed, and the narrative defined in the outline is delivered through them.
requirements: Sections kept logical and as short as possible, with sub-sections and paragraphs separating text into bite-sized chunks
The narrative defined in the writer's outline organises the sections
constraints: Described for professional refereed papers in astronomy; other fields may differ
target_learners: master's and PhD level students writing their first scientific paper
target_learning_goals: structure a scientific research paper so its message comes across clearly
examples: The guide advises against mixing IMRaD sections and against letting new background appear in the discussion or conclusions

article_title: Development and validation of an astronomy self-efficacy instrument for understanding and doing
citation: Rachel Freed, David McKinnon, Michael Fitzgerald, and Christina M. Norris. (2022). Development and validation of an astronomy self-efficacy instrument for understanding and doing. Physical Review Physics Education Research 18, 010117. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevPhysEducRes.18.010117
title: Astronomy self-efficacy instrument: 13-item two-scale survey (8 APSE items, 5 ISE items) on an 11-point Likert scale
description: A domain-specific self-efficacy instrument for students, developed following Bandura's guide and modeled on the constructs of the STEBI, probing two aspects: Astronomy Personal Self-Efficacy (content understanding, 8 items) and Instrumental Self-Efficacy (using remote robotic telescopes, 5 items). Unlike the original STEBI instruments, it "employed an 11-point Likert scale of 0 ¼ Strongly Disagree to 10 ¼ Strongly Agree". Scale scores are formed by summing item scores, ranging 0 to 80 for APSE and 0 to 50 for ISE. It is intended as a precursor to investigating science identity in astronomy.
requirements: Developed following Bandura's Guide to Constructing Self-Efficacy Scales; responses collected via SurveyGizmo in undergraduate astronomy classes
constraints: Does not explicitly address all four components of self-efficacy as laid out by Bandura; vicarious experiences, social persuasion, and physiological state are only implicitly embedded
The ISE scale was highly skewed for students who had already used robotic telescopes, and confirmatory factor analysis remains future work
target_learners: undergraduate astronomy students
high school and teacher research-experience participants (intended wider use)
target_learning_goals: astronomy content understanding
self-efficacy for using remote robotic telescopes and astronomical imagery
examples: Administered to 252 students one month into a semester-long astronomy course using robotic telescopes and to 72 students in a regular astronomy course without robotic telescopes at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill

article_title: The ASIMOV Prize for scientific publishing -- HEP researchers trigger young people toward science
citation: W.M. Alberico et al. (2022). The ASIMOV Prize for scientific publishing: HEP researchers trigger young people toward science. 41st International Conference on High Energy physics - ICHEP2022. https://www.premio-asimov.it/
title: The ASIMOV Prize: a national book prize in which high-school students read, review and vote for popular science books
description: The ASIMOV Prize is a non-profit Italian initiative, founded in 2016, "aiming to bring the young generations closer to scientific culture, through the critical reading of popular science books." A National Committee of scientists, professors, writers, journalists and about 800 school teachers selects a shortlist; the national jury is composed of participating high-school students, each of whom registers on the website, chooses, reads, reviews and votes (rating from 1 to 10) on finalist books. Student reviews are anonymously judged for originality and content validity with anti-plagiarism checks, and the winning author is proclaimed at a final ceremony.
requirements: Books must be suitable for non-expert audiences and published in Italian (or in translation) for the first time in the two years prior to the current edition
A National Committee including a large number of school teachers selects the finalist shortlist
Students register on the official website to read, review and vote
constraints: Coverage limited to books published in Italian (or translation) in the two years before each edition
The 2020 and 2021 final ceremonies were held online only due to Covid-19 restrictions
target_learners: Italian high-school students, most frequently in the 3rd and 4th classes (aged 17-18)
target_learning_goals: Critical reading of popular science literature
Engagement with scientific culture across chemistry, medicine, physics, mathematics, astronomy and other subjects
Developing critical and conscious judgment through book reviewing
examples: In 2022 the prize was awarded ex aequo to Licia Troisi for "La sfrontata bellezza del cosmo" and Agnese Collino for "La malattia da 10 centesimi"
A selection of the best student review videos is published on the official YouTube channel http://youtube.com/PremioAsimov

description: ASP2022 was the seventh edition of the African School of Physics, organized at Nelson Mandela University in Gqeberha, South Africa, from November 28 to December 9, 2022. The scientific program was arranged in three distinct components: a full-duration program for university students, a parallel program for high school teachers (November 28 to December 2), and an outreach event for high school pupils (December 5–9). The event combined plenary and parallel lectures, hands-on tutorials and experiments, and computing tutorials in fundamental and applied physics.

Developing and maintaining interest in physics among pupils

title: Assess only the basics of computational thinking needed to assess introductory physics knowledge
description: The article's interviews indicate that a CT assessment for introductory physics should stay minimal: the authors conclude that "the importance really comes from using computational thinking to learn and understand physics better," so the assessment should target reading code, identifying core physics, and modifying programs rather than production programming. Developed in partnership with the American Physical Society Bridge Program, it aligns with recommendations covering social integration, academic success, mentorship, research experiences, professional skills, and financial well-being. article_title: The International Space Station (ISS) Contest as STEM Educational Project
citation: Bonacci, E. (2023). The International Space Station (ISS) Contest as STEM Educational Project. Athens Journal of Sciences, 10(3), 153-180. https://doi.org/10.30958/ajs.10-3-3
title: Astronomy as a gateway science for STEM education
description: The article confirms Astronomy as a gateway science that should be inserted in any school curriculum (Percy, 2005). The ISS contest demonstrated that astronomy-themed projects serve as an entry point for engaging secondary students across the full spectrum of STEM disciplines, including chemistry, physics, biology, and mathematics. The competition's seven thematic areas connected astronomical and space-science contexts to practical experimentation, engineering design, and digital technology. The authors argue that emerging as pivotal of superb STEM pedagogy, astronomy should be included in every school's curriculum as a single subject or interdisciplinary course, supported by permanent partnerships with national or international space agencies.

School infrastructure supporting interdisciplinary STEM projects
constraints: The evidence comes from a single national contest in Italy and is not a controlled study

Scientific literacy
Interdisciplinary understanding

article_title: Learners Teaching Novices: An Uplifting Alternative Assessment
citation: Ali Malik, Juliette Woodrow, and Chris Piech. 2024. Learners Teaching Novices: An Uplifting Alternative Assessment. In Proceedings of the 55th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V. 1 (SIGCSE 2024). https://doi.org/10.1145/3626252.3630887
title: Assessment via Teaching (AVT): a formative assessment in which learners tutor more novice students in 1:1 help sessions
description: AVT is a formative assessment method in which course learners (Learners) demonstrate and refine their understanding by tutoring novice students (Novices) who are several weeks behind, typically from a lagged online version of the same course. Each assignment requires the learner to hold a 1-hour tutoring help session, preparing for a subset of topics and being paired 1:1 with novices stuck on related problems. The key idea is that "in order to support novices effectively, learners have to develop a strong understanding of the course material", and in helping novices the learners deepen their understanding and identify what they still need to study. The authors characterise it as authentic, service-oriented, repeatable, impactful for novices, and hard to cheat.
requirements: Access to a population of novices who are reliably available, appropriately levelled, and verified so interactions are safe
Recorded sessions and monitoring for safety, with a reporting feature for both novices and learners
constraints: Finding a novice population has no existing out-of-the-box solution
Sessions may be uncomfortable for introverted learners or those reluctant to take a position of authority, which can be damaging early in a new subject
target_learners: CS1 university students (learners who teach)
Novice students taking a lagged online version of the course
target_learning_goals: CS1 programming fundamentals such as control flow, function decomposition, graphics and animation
Leadership and communication skills through explaining concepts
examples: In the CS1 case study, learners prepared for topics such as control flow, function decomposition, and pre/post conditions (midterm) or graphics, animation, and keyboard interactions (final), then hosted video-conferencing help sessions with novices from an online course of about 10,000 students
key_sources: Ali Malik, Juliette Woodrow, and Chris Piech. 2024. Learners Teaching Novices: An Uplifting Alternative Assessment. In Proceedings of the 55th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V. 1 (SIGCSE 2024). https://doi.org/10.1145/3626252.3630887

article_title: Learners Teaching Novices: An Uplifting Alternative Assessment
citation: Ali Malik, Juliette Woodrow, and Chris Piech. 2024. Learners Teaching Novices: An Uplifting Alternative Assessment. In Proceedings of the 55th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V. 1 (SIGCSE 2024). https://doi.org/10.1145/3626252.3630887
title: Design assessments that are hard to over-optimise or cheat by making the assessment itself an act of teaching
description: The article argues that assessment suffers from Goodhart's law—"when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"—as students study for the test rather than for understanding. AVT counters this because there is no clear way to study for the assessment itself; the best way to perform well at AVT is to actually improve understanding. It also resists cheating because a live help session acts as biometric verification and resembles an adaptive oral interview in which understanding must be drawn on dynamically as novice issues arise.
requirements: A live, interactive session format so the learner must respond dynamically to authentic novice questions
constraints: Oral-interview-style probing is effective but, the article notes, impossible to scale on its own; AVT integrates these dynamics into its design
target_learners: CS1 university students
target_learning_goals: Authentic demonstration of conceptual understanding resistant to test-directed study and LLM-assisted cheating
examples: The article's RCT used live recorded video-conferencing sessions in which learners could see the novice's source code but could not directly make edits
key_sources: Ali Malik, Juliette Woodrow, and Chris Piech. 2024. Learners Teaching Novices: An Uplifting Alternative Assessment. In Proceedings of the 55th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V. 1 (SIGCSE 2024). https://doi.org/10.1145/3626252.3630887

title: Use an aspirational Likert scale point to separate desired-but-unused goals and activities from actual course practice
description: When surveying instructors about course goals and activities, the article recommends including an aspirational response option alongside actual-use options. Interviewees repeatedly selected Minor Goal for items they said were not goals of their course but wished to implement, distorting data. article_title: Ask-Before-Detection: Identifying and Mitigating Conformity Bias in LLM-Powered Error Detector for Math Word Problem Solutions
citation: Hang Li, Tianlong Xu, Kaiqi Yang, Yucheng Chu, Yanling Chen, Yichi Song, Qingsong Wen, Hui Liu. (2024). Ask-Before-Detection: Identifying and Mitigating Conformity Bias in LLM-Powered Error Detector for Math Word Problem Solutions. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16838
title: Ask-Before-Detection (AskBD) framework for adaptive reference-solution generation
description: AskBD is a four-stage LLM pipeline that generates an adaptive reference solution tailored to each input solution before grading, addressing conformity bias without fine-tuning. As the article describes it, "AskBD consists of four components, executed sequentially to generate an adaptive reference answer tailored to the input solution": a Condition and Question Extractor (CQE), a Solution Step Inquirer (SSI) that converts the solution into step-wise questions, a Step Question Responder (SQR) that answers them using the extracted conditions, and a Reference-Enhanced Grader (REG) that grades using the generated reference. Because references are generated to match the given solution, mismatch risk is reduced and the approach extends to novel solutions without task-specific training.
requirements: An LLM with sufficient problem-solving capability to generate accurate step-wise reference answers; the article notes base models with weaker reasoning fail to fully leverage the generated references
constraints: Benefits are less evident for base LLMs under naive prompting; the article attributes this to relatively weaker reasoning capabilities of base models
target_learners: Students whose math word problem solutions are graded by LLM-powered error detectors
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of erroneous steps and error categories in student math word problem solutions
examples: The framework was implemented with 10 LLMs (five base, five advanced) and evaluated on 200 GSM8K examples with four injected error types per solution
key_sources: Hang Li, Tianlong Xu, Kaiqi Yang, Yucheng Chu, Yanling Chen, Yichi Song, Qingsong Wen, Hui Liu. (2024). Ask-Before-Detection: Identifying and Mitigating Conformity Bias in LLM-Powered Error Detector for Math Word Problem Solutions. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16838

article_title: Ask-Before-Detection: Identifying and Mitigating Conformity Bias in LLM-Powered Error Detector for Math Word Problem Solutions
citation: Hang Li, Tianlong Xu, Kaiqi Yang, Yucheng Chu, Yanling Chen, Yichi Song, Qingsong Wen, Hui Liu. (2024). Ask-Before-Detection: Identifying and Mitigating Conformity Bias in LLM-Powered Error Detector for Math Word Problem Solutions. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16838
title: Automatic Solution Permutation (ASP) pipeline for generating alternative solutions
description: ASP is the article's three-stage method for building high-quality alternative solution datasets. As printed, "The ASP method operates in three stages: Extract, Permute, and Explain": it encapsulates a conventional solution's steps into a single mathematical expression, applies operations such as factorization, distribution, and order rearrangement that preserve mathematical equivalence, and then prompts LLMs to explain the permuted expression as step-by-step alternative solutions. Expressions failing to produce correct answer values are discarded at each filtering step. The article used GPT-4o as the backbone LLM for each stage and a graduate student from the education department to review and select the highest-quality alternative for each of 200 GSM8K samples.
requirements: Detailed and specific instructions about the solving strategy (the permuted expressions), since simple prompts yield mere paraphrases of conventional solutions
constraints: Built and evaluated only on 200 randomly sampled GSM8K question-and-answer pairs
target_learners: Researchers and educators building error-detection datasets for math word problem solutions
target_learning_goals: Exposing conformity bias in LLM-powered error detectors by supplying genuinely different, valid solution paths
examples: For each of 200 GSM8K samples, ASP was applied three times to generate three candidate permuted solutions, from which the highest-quality one was selected

article_title: Online Advanced Labs in Physics
citation: Peter A. Bennett. (2025). Online “Advanced Labs” in Physics. https://asuonline.wistia.com/medias/dxmzjxu13t
title: Custom-built simulator modules replicating real-world data imperfections for online Advanced Lab experiments
description: The core instructional component of the online courses: custom-built simulator modules that "produce signals with the full scope of “imperfections” inherent in real measurements including noise (Poisson, 1/f), background, backlash, resolution and bandwidth limitations, aberrations, non-linearity". Noise sources are determined from real measurements and incorporated via semi-empirical functions. Data are delivered as synchronized videos or still images; students choose scan parameters and wait real collection times. Most modules are Excel VBA macros for Windows, some ported to HTML5 for browser use.
requirements: VBA modules run only on Windows machines; HTML5 ports run via browser on any platform and suit server deployment with large classes
constraints: Alignment errors do not propagate in the simulators, so students can always obtain good data, unlike in-person labs
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate physics majors in fully online degree programs
target_learning_goals: data collection parameter choice
apparatus alignment
fitting data to model functions with uncertainties
exploration of systematic uncertainties
examples: The interferometry simulator uses spot-triplet alignment, micrometer vernier reading with backlash, and Fabry-Perot ring-pattern linescan fitting yielding r = 0.90±.05; the X-ray simulator adds Poisson noise with √N standard deviation and matches the physical lab spectrum for intensity, position and width of features.

title: AstroTutor: a domain-specific multi-agent RAG Socratic tutoring system for astronomy
description: AstroTutor is a domain-specific tutoring chatbot built on Gemini-2.0-Flash (later 2.5-Flash) using a multi-agent RAG architecture: a course-material agent over the lecturer's notes, a reference textbook agent, a paper-recommendation agent over a curated arXiv astro-ph database, and a Moderator Agent enforcing pedagogical guidelines. title: Assess instructional impact of visual representations with process measures (task time, efficiency), not only outcome measures
description: The article argues that the instructional impact of visual representations "should not only be assessed by learning outcomes, but also by their role in supporting cognitive processing and structuring task performance". In the study, outcome measures showed no representation differences, yet process data revealed large efficiency differences between the representations. Designers and researchers comparing representations should therefore record processing time and efficiency alongside pre-post tests and cognitive load ratings.
requirements: Application-oriented tasks whose completion time and accuracy per time can be logged, in addition to outcome tests.
constraints: Processing time should be interpreted with caution and always in relation to task performance and cognitive load, as the article states longer times may reflect deeper engagement or difficulty.
target_learners: Secondary and post-secondary learners working with visual-graphical representations of abstract science concepts
target_learning_goals: Efficient application of represented concepts during task solving
examples: The study measured task accuracy, task time, and efficiency (correct solutions divided by time) for five application-oriented tasks, and found representation effects only in the process measures.
key_sources: Linda Qerimi, Sarah Malone, Eva Rexigel, Jochen Kuhn and Stefan Küchemann. (2025). Comparing Visual Qubit Representations in Quantum Education: The Bloch sphere Enhances Task Efficiency. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21721

article_title: Challenging Data Aggregation Practices: A MAIHDA Study of Asian Student Outcomes in Introductory Physics
citation: Vy Le, Grace Angell, Jayson Nissen, Ben Van Dusen. (2026). Challenging Data Aggregation Practices: A MAIHDA Study of Asian Student Outcomes in Introductory Physics.
title: AsianCrit and QuantCrit as a combined conceptual framework for disaggregated educational data analysis
description: The study draws on Asian Critical Theory (AsianCrit), which centers the racialization of Asian students, and Quantitative Critical Race Theory (QuantCrit), which holds that "numbers and quantitative methods are not neutral because they reflect human choices." AsianCrit tenets used include Asianization, strategic (anti)essentialism, and intersectionality; QuantCrit tenets include that numbers are not neutral and categories are neither natural nor inherent. "By integrating AsianCrit and QuantCrit, the study aligns its conceptual commitments with its methodological approach", guiding decisions about data disaggregation, model specification, and interpretation.
requirements: Researchers must make aggregation choices transparent and examine how racial categories and modeling choices can reproduce or conceal inequities
constraints: The analysis centers three AsianCrit tenets and two QuantCrit tenets the authors judged most relevant, not the full frameworks
target_learners: Asian (American) students in higher education
target_learning_goals: identifying and challenging inequities concealed by aggregated racial data
examples: The framework motivated disaggregating the pan-Asian category into subgroups such as Asian Indian, Chinese, White-Korean, and Filipino rather than using URM/non-URM groupings.
key_sources: Vy Le, Grace Angell, Jayson Nissen, Ben Van Dusen. (2026). Challenging Data Aggregation Practices: A MAIHDA Study of Asian Student Outcomes in Introductory Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.19049

article_title: Deep Learning Based Approach to Enhanced Recognition of Emotions and Behavioral Patterns of Autistic Children
citation: Nelaka K.A.R, Peiris M.K.V, Liyanage R.P.B. (2025). Deep Learning Based Approach to Enhanced Recognition of Emotions and Behavioral Patterns of Autistic Children. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07320
title: ASD children's facial-expression dataset collected from clinical, educational, and specialized database sources
description: The study uses a dataset of facial expressions of ASD children gathered from clinical settings, educational environments, and specialized databases. The images are heterogeneous in size, with "aspect ratios ranging from 0.75 to 1.33, significantly deviating from ImageNet standards", spanning roughly 150×200 to 800×600 pixels. This dimensional variability is the motivating problem for the autoencoder preprocessing pipeline and supports four-class emotion recognition.
requirements: Preprocessing to standardize variable-sized images to 299×299×3 before CNN classification
constraints: The article notes a lack of standardized ASD emotion datasets complicates comparative methodology evaluation
target_learners: children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
target_learning_goals: emotion recognition supporting tailored interventions
examples: The dataset was used to compare baseline direct resizing against autoencoder preprocessing for Xception and InceptionV3 classifiers
key_sources: Nelaka K.A.R, Peiris M.K.V, Liyanage R.P.B. (2025). Deep Learning Based Approach to Enhanced Recognition of Emotions and Behavioral Patterns of Autistic Children. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07320

article_title: Astro-Animation -- How Artists and Scientists Envision the Universe
citation: Laurence ARCADIAS, Robin H.D. CORBET and Emma BOOTH. (2024). Astro-Animation - How Artists and Scientists Envision the Universe. Mutual Images Research Journal.
title: Astro-Animation class and its freely available collection of 73 short animations
description: An undergraduate course at the Maryland Institute College of Art, co-taught by an animator and a NASA astrophysicist, with "two interlocking parts, one focused on astronomy and one on animation". Students work with NASA scientist mentors for a semester, visit NASA Goddard to present and screen films, and produce animations on topics such as black holes and gravitational waves with "underlying scientific rigour". The collection of 73 short animations is freely available and used by scientists, teachers, and outreach specialists.
requirements: Astronomy component taught by a scientist plus animation supervision and NASA scientist mentors for one semester
target_learners: undergraduate art college students (BFA animation)
target_learning_goals: astronomical concepts
scientific process and rigour
animation and visual storytelling
examples: Teams of three students randomly assigned to typically six scientist topics; films screened annually at NASA Goddard during Take Your Child to Work Day

article_title: Astro-Animation -- How Artists and Scientists Envision the Universe
citation: Laurence ARCADIAS, Robin H.D. CORBET and Emma BOOTH. (2024). Astro-Animation - How Artists and Scientists Envision the Universe. Mutual Images Research Journal.
title: Astro-Animation facilitator toolkit
description: A support resource developed by the project for workshop facilitators, "including step -by-step instructions, visual aids, and evaluation materials". It emerged from the public workshops and traveling exhibition strand of the project and was iteratively refined: the outcomes section reports that feedback led to clearer animation instruction, improved technical workflow, and better facilitation strategies. It is intended to let others run Astro-Animation-style art/science activities in informal settings.
requirements: Supports facilitators running short scientific presentations followed by hands-on animation activities
target_learners: workshop participants including teenagers and families from underserved communities
target_learning_goals: basic astronomical concepts
creative expression of scientific ideas through animation
examples: Toolkit adaptability was listed among key evaluation findings, with feedback leading to clearer animation instruction and improved technical workflow

article_title: Perspectives of Women and Men Students and Faculty on Conceptual and Quantitative Problem-Solving in Physics from Introductory to Graduate Levels
citation: Ghimire, A. and Singh, C. (2025). Perspectives of Women and Men Students and Faculty on Conceptual and Quantitative Problem-Solving in Physics from Introductory to Graduate Levels. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Perspectives+of+Women+and+Men+Students+and+Faculty+on+Conceptual+and+Quantitative+Problem-Solving+in+Physics
title: Explicitly reward all stages of the ASPIRE problem-solving heuristic (Analyze, Plan, Implement, Reflect, Evaluate) so expert-like problem-solving is valued beyond finding and manipulating equations
description: The article recommends that grading explicitly reward conceptual analysis, planning, and reflection alongside quantitative implementation, using the ASPIRE heuristic — "Analyze and Sift through the problem, Plan the solution, Implement the plan, Reflect on and Evaluate the solution process". The authors argue that "Explicitly rewarding all stages of the ASPIRE heuristic will signal to students that expert-like problem-solving involves more than finding and manipulating equations", and that this can support self-efficacy and identity development, particularly for historically underrepresented students.
requirements: Assessment structures must value conceptual aspects of problem-solving explicitly and in an integrated manner with quantitative aspects
constraints: In most traditional physics courses, homework, quizzes, and exams focus primarily on symbolic or numerical problems with only the implementation step important for grades
target_learners: introductory through graduate physics students, particularly women and historically underrepresented students in physics
target_learning_goals: integrated conceptual and quantitative physics problem-solving; self-efficacy and physics identity development
examples: The article reports that in traditionally taught courses students see only quantitative steps projected on the board and are graded primarily on implementation, and proposes the ASPIRE heuristic as the structured alternative
key_sources: Ghimire, A. and Singh, C. (2025). Perspectives of Women and Men Students and Faculty on Conceptual and Quantitative Problem-Solving in Physics from Introductory to Graduate Levels. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Perspectives+of+Women+and+Men+Students+and+Faculty+on+Conceptual+and+Quantitative+Problem-Solving+in+Physics

citation: Stubbs, C. W., Huang, D., Koh, J., Woods, M., & Plazas Malagón, A. A. (2025). Lessons Learned from Integrating Generative AI into an Introductory Undergraduate Astronomy Course at Harvard. https://github.com/astrostubbs/harvard-astro17-labs
title: GitHub repository of GAI-assisted Colab notebooks and instructor guide
description: A released repository (https://github.com/astrostubbs/harvard-astro17-labs) containing the course's Colab notebooks, associated data files, and a terse instructor's guide. It was produced at the end of term using the Claude Code command line GAI tool to clean up, test, and document the notebooks, an operation that took less than one hour. "The GitHub repository contains a dozen high-end Colab notebook/worksheets that were generated for this course", covering diffraction grating physics, observational extragalactic astronomy, and Hubble diagram fits using supernova luminosity distances.

instructors reusing the materials
target_learning_goals: model fitting to data
observational extragalactic astronomy skills

article_title: Knowledge Markers: An AI-Agnostic Concept for the Design of Programming Courses
citation: Christina Maria Mayr. (2026). Knowledge Markers: An AI-Agnostic Concept for the Design of Programming Courses. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06331
title: Knowledge markers (A/S/P): a lightweight, AI-agnostic course-level labelling scheme distinguishing Application, Structure, and Procedure knowledge
description: Knowledge markers are a lightweight, AI-agnostic course-level labelling scheme in which each learning unit carries one primary emphasis: (A) Application knowledge "refers to the ability to implement concrete solutions", (S) Structure knowledge to conceptual understanding and mental models, and (P) Procedure knowledge to systematic approaches such as debugging and verification. The article maps the markers onto Krathwohl's revised taxonomy as orientation and communicates them to students through a screw-tightening metaphor.
requirements: Labels must be communicated as part of the course culture, paired with explicit explanations and examples such as the screw metaphor.
constraints: A/S/P is intentionally coarse
It depends on consistent interpretation across authors
The marker denotes a primary intent, not exclusivity
target_learners: first-semester engineering students with little or no prior programming experience
instructors without formal didactic training
target_learning_goals: implementing concrete solutions (Application)
building conceptual understanding and mental models (Structure)
systematic debugging and verification (Procedure)

article_title: Asymptotic Behavior in High School Physics: physics 1 insights and discussions
citation: Kyle Kou Yuchang, Paul Zhang Yixing, and Victor Wang Shuang. (2025). Asymptotic Behavior in High School Physics: physics insights and discussions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29261
title: Asymptotic (limiting-case) analysis as a pedagogical framework for high school physics
description: The paper advances asymptotic analysis—examining how quantities behave as parameters approach critical values like zero or infinity—as a teaching framework that turns equations into physical intuition. It argues that "By focusing on these limiting cases, asymptotic analysis reveals fundamental principles governing physical phenomena," and uses limit reasoning to resolve paradoxes in collisions and circuits. The framework connects elementary topics to advanced ones such as impedance matching and perturbation theory.
requirements: Physics topics where parameters have meaningful limiting values (mass ratios, load resistance)
constraints: Demonstrated only on two canonical cases: multi-ball elastic collisions and internal-resistance circuits
target_learners: high school physics students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of momentum conservation
understanding of internal resistance and EMF
physical intuition about limiting behavior
examples: Three-ball collision analyzed via limits, impedance matching, and dimensional analysis; internal resistance analyzed via V = E − Ir in the limit R → ∞
key_sources: Kyle Kou Yuchang, Paul Zhang Yixing, and Victor Wang Shuang. (2025). Asymptotic Behavior in High School Physics: physics insights and discussions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29261

article_title: Generative AI in Higher Education Laboratory Learning: A Qualitative Case Study of Epistemic Scaffolding and Assessment Boundaries
citation: Matteo Tuveri, Alessandro Riggio. (2025). Generative AI in Higher Education Laboratory Learning: A Qualitative Case Study of Epistemic Scaffolding and Assessment Boundaries. University of Cagliari / INFN preprint.
title: AstroTutor constrained GenAI tutor
description: AstroTutor is a custom GPT-based tutor configured around course materials, the optical photometry activity and an instructional script specifying domain, purpose, response modes and limits. Its design was "intentionally conservative": it supported conceptual clarification, planner interpretation, diagnostic feedback and controlled operational help, but "was not designed to provide summative evaluation, certify the correctness of work or produce final reports for students". It was introduced as an optional support tool on the familiar ChatGPT platform, with students informed they remained responsible for verifying outputs and authoring reports.
requirements: Role-engineered framing via an instructional script limiting intended role
Students informed that it did not replace the instructor and that they remained responsible for verifying its outputs
constraints: Boundary limitation: the tutor was not intended to grade, certify, replace the instructor or complete the report
Controlled operational help: formulas, calculations and code allowed only when explicitly requested and accompanied by physical interpretation
target_learners: Master's-level astrophysics laboratory students
target_learning_goals: Understanding the physics behind laboratory methods
Interpreting the Observation Planner
Diagnostic feedback on plans and report sections
examples: Design constraints implemented included domain specificity, guided reasoning, interface interpretation, diagnostic feedback, controlled operational help and boundary limitation (Table 1).

article_title: From Tool Use to Technological Agency: LoopCAT as a Local-First, Open-Source Tool for Translation Technology Education
citation: Dogru, G., & Martín Mor, A. (2026). From Tool Use to Technological Agency: LoopCAT as a Local-First, Open-Source Tool for Translation Technology Education. https://loopcat.example.org
title: Assessment should reward defended refusal as much as AI adoption
description: The article argues that ethical participation includes deciding not to use a technology. "Assessment should not reward the mere frequency of AI use or assume that accepting automation is the desired outcome." Students should be able to defend both adoption and refusal in relation to a brief, evidence, and the people affected. Declining to transmit a confidential text or choosing an adequate non-AI workflow can demonstrate agency.
requirements: Assessment tasks must present genuine policy conditions and confidentiality constraints
constraints: This principle is proposed, not tested through classroom research
target_learners: translation students
target_learning_goals: ethical technology use
technological agency
justified decision-making
examples: Session 4 requires students to justify a local, hosted, or no-AI route under a simulated confidentiality constraint

article_title: Activity Report on the Ninth African School of Fundamental Physics and Applications (ASP2026)
citation: Kétévi A. Assamagan, Mounia Laassiri, Bobby Acharya, Christine Darve, Fernando Ferroni. (2026). Activity Report on the Ninth African School of Fundamental Physics and Applications (ASP2026). arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33943
title: ASP2026: a four-component hybrid physics school (students, teachers, policymakers forum, learners)
description: ASP2026, the ninth edition of the African School of Physics, ran July 5–19, 2026 at the University of Nairobi and CEMASTEA in Kenya as a hybrid event. "The scientific program at ASP2026 was arranged in four distinct components for university students, high school teachers, policymakers, high school pupils (learners)." Students followed two weeks of plenary and parallel lectures with hands-on computing, detectors and instrumentation sessions; teachers had a parallel in-person training workshop; a July 10 forum engaged policymakers; and a four-day outreach program served high school learners. ASP has run since 2010 as a biennial three-week event within a broader series of African physics activities.
requirements: Host country selected about two and a half years in advance through a bidding process; financial and in-kind support from institutes, the University of Nairobi and CEMASTEA covered travel, room and board, and equipment
constraints: Online participants reported lower satisfaction and desired in-person participation; parallel-session organization needed improvement
target_learners: African university students with at least three years of university education
Kenyan high school teachers
High school learners (grades 10–12)
African policymakers in research and education
target_learning_goals: Fundamental and applied physics topics including particle physics, accelerator physics, medical physics, computing, quantum computing, machine learning and instrumentation
Physics pedagogy and instructional planning for teachers
Encouraging high school learners to develop and maintain interest in physics
examples: Hands-on computing, detectors and instrumentation sessions for students; a teachers' workshop with pedagogy, IoT and physics experimentation sessions; learner outreach in electricity, particle accelerators and particle detectors
A policymakers forum including a panel on the African Strategy for Fundamental and Applied Physics

article_title: Ex-nihilo: Obstacles Surrounding Teaching the Standard Model
citation: Kevin A. Pimbblet. (2002). Ex-nihilo: Obstacles Surrounding Teaching the Standard Model. https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0209265v1
title: Taxonomy of astrophysics misconceptions by origin: internal, external, and combined causes
description: The article organises pupils' astrophysics misconceptions by origin, saying they "fall roughly into three camps": those caused by incorrect internal (mental) processes, those caused by incorrect external processes such as inaccurate information from teachers, parents and peers, and those caused by a combination of both. It cites a list of over 550 individual astrophysics misconceptions and notes pupils formulate their own ideas before formal education.
requirements: Formal education must systematically deal with self-generated misconceptions as it progresses; the article states they should be systematically dealt with during the course of time.
constraints: The article notes there is little in the way of strategies to deal with such misconceptions.
target_learners: Key Stage 4 science and physics pupils in England
target_learning_goals: Understanding the origin and evolution of the Universe (the Big Bang model)
examples: The article illustrates correction of an Aristotelian viewpoint through observational arguments including retrograde motion, the Galilean satellites, the phases of Venus, sunspots, and the supernova of 1604.

article_title: Teaching vs. learning: Changing perspectives on problem solving in physics instruction
citation: William J. Gerace & Ian D. Beatty. (2005). Teaching vs. Learning: Changing Perspectives on Problem Solving in Physics Instruction. 9th Common Conference of the Cyprus Physics Association and Greek Physics Association, Nicosia, Cyprus.
title: Assessment must serve rather than dictate learning, with frequent brief low-stakes formative assessment
description: The article argues that because "students use exams to determine what they should pay attention to", exams requiring equation manipulation and recognition of standard problem types will defeat any curricular reform aimed at conceptual understanding and metacognitive awareness. It therefore recommends formative assessment "to guide and enhance, rather than evaluate, learning", noting that "Formative assessments are frequent, brief, low-stakes, and designed to reveal thinking and gaps in knowledge rather than measuring ability", and that summative exams must be redesigned to reward conceptual and strategic analysis.
requirements: Instructor exams must be aligned with the conceptual, strategic, and metacognitive goals of reformed instruction
constraints: The article states high-stakes summative assessment approaches need rethinking as well, not only classroom formative practice
target_learners: high school and university physics students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding, qualitative and strategic analysis skills, and metacognitive awareness of learning
examples: The article describes formative assessments as brief, low-stakes probes that reveal thinking and knowledge gaps rather than measure ability

title: One-hour astronomer visit structure: slide show, hands-on activity, debriefing
description: Each visit focuses on a few simple concepts only and follows a fixed three-part structure: an introductory 10-minute slide show, 40 minutes of hands-on activity, and a final 10-minute debriefing and questions. address misconceptions about scientists

Reply to “Critical appraisal of “Proposal for the Hernia ASCEND Hugo™ RAS training pathway: acquisition of skills by comprehensive exercise‑based nimbleness and dexterity training””. title: The ASCEND framework: a Proficiency-Based Progression training pathway for robotic hernia surgery in which procedure-relevant errors are explicitly defined and systematically avoided before progression
description: The Hernia ASCEND Hugo™ RAS training pathway is a structured robotic hernia curriculum grounded in the Proficiency-Based Progression model. As the authors describe it, it is "founded on the Proficiency-Based Progression (PBP) model", in which "errors relevant to robotic hernia surgery (e.g., mesh malposition, vascular injury, or nerve entrapment) are explicitly defined and systematically avoided before progression". Learners advance by meeting defined proficiency milestones rather than by time served, and the pathway is described as modular and scalable across healthcare settings.

constraints: The initial report did not include outcome data; multicenter validation of ASCEND milestones against clinical endpoints is in progress
target_learners: surgeons training in robotic hernia repair (r-TAPP)
target_learning_goals: robotic surgical skills and proficiency in hernia repair without procedure-relevant errors
examples: The pathway was proposed for the Hugo™ RAS platform and its milestones are undergoing multicenter validation against clinical endpoints

citation: Luo Taizhen, Gong Yang, Dai Sidi, Xia Hua-an, Jiang Zhiyan, Gao Lingling. (2025). Questionnaire development: midwives' knowledge and attitude on liberal birthing position in 2nd stage. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07466-3
title: Use validated knowledge-and-attitude assessment results to design targeted training and continuing education for midwives
description: The article recommends that nursing administrators use the questionnaire to identify midwives' knowledge and attitude gaps and respond with targeted education. It states that "the assessment results can help identify any skill gaps and lead to the development of targeted training or continuing education programs," and that continuing education content should be designed according to pre-test results of the learners. The authors also suggest textbooks be organized around the questionnaire's four knowledge dimensions and include content addressing midwives' worries.

Administrative support for administering the assessment and acting on results
constraints: The authors note systemic factors such as hospital policies and human and equipment resources also affect practice and require separate study

nursing administrators
midwifery educators

positive attitudes toward liberal birthing position
midwifery core competencies
examples: The article suggests textbook design follow the four knowledge dimensions and include the worry contents, so that midwives can reduce worry and practice boldly once knowledge gaps are answered

article_title: Primary care nurses' performance in motivational interviewing: a quantitative descriptive study.
citation: Östlund Ann-Sofi, Kristofferzon Marja-Leena, Häggström Elisabeth, Wadensten Barbro. (2015). Primary care nurses’ performance in motivational interviewing: a quantitative descriptive study. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-015-0304-z
title: Assess MI performance with a validated fidelity instrument and provide training, feedback and supervision in clinical practice before evaluating MI outcomes

accurate self-assessment of one's own conversational skills

article_title: How female community health workers navigate work challenges and why there are still gaps in their performance: a look at female community health workers in maternal and child health in two Indian districts through a reciprocal determinism framework.
citation: Sarin Enisha, Lunsford Sarah Smith. (2017). How female community health workers navigate work challenges and why there are still gaps in their performance: a look at female community health workers in maternal and child health in two Indian districts through a reciprocal determinism framework. Human Resources for Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12960-017-0222-3
title: ASHA training curriculum and monthly meeting system as capacity-building components
description: The ASHA programme's capacity-building components include a training curriculum that "includes a section on gender sensitization, designed to be taught over 3 days", provision for refresher courses that are "not uniformly implemented across all states", and monthly meetings used to reiterate skills training. The article found the study-district meetings emphasized technical rather than inter-personal skills, and recommends they be systematized with sensitization given equal importance. article_title: Audio Universe: Tour of the Solar System
citation: Chris Harrison, James Trayford, Leigh Harrison, Nic Bonne. (2022). Audio Universe Tour of the Solar System: using sound to make the Universe more accessible. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.02110
title: Mapping astronomical properties to musical parameters: pitch for planet size, colour for stellar note, magnitude for appearance order, and water covering fraction for filter cut-off
description: This pattern maps physical properties of astronomical objects and data onto musical parameters so audiences can hear structure in the data. Smaller rocky planets were given higher pitches and gas giants lower pitches, with the Sun acting as a musical "pedal point"; stellar colour (B−V difference) selected one of five glockenspiel notes, with "The reddest stars are assigned the lowest notes and the bluest stars the highest notes"; brightness determined the order stars sounded; and Earth's water covering fraction by longitude controlled a low-pass filter cut-off frequency.
requirements: A consistent mapping must be chosen so the combined result is musically pleasing, and the same notes and instruments form the motif of the background music for consistency across the show.
constraints: The article notes the full-show version of the stars-appearing sequence did not use an exact accurate mapping of colour to pitch as described; the code was since updated for this accuracy mapping.
target_learners: general public planetarium and home audiences, including BVI audiences
target_learning_goals: perceiving astronomical properties (planet size, stellar colour and brightness, Earth surface composition) through sound
examples: Table 1 assigns the Sun Bb1 (Synthetic Mix), Mercury F6 (Flute), Venus Bb5 (Oboe), Earth Gb5 (Clarinet), Mars Db6 (Soprano Sax.), Jupiter Gb2 (Bass Trombone), Saturn Bb2 (Euphonium), Uranus Bb3 (Trumpet), Neptune F3 (French Horn) and the Moon Db6 (Piccolo).

article_title: Addressing the assessment challenge with an online system that tutors as it assesses
citation: Feng, M., Heffernan, N.T., & Koedinger, K.R. (2009). Addressing the Assessment Challenge with an Online System That Tutors as it Assesses. User Modeling and User-Adapted Interaction: The Journal of Personalization Research (UMUAI journal), 19(3), 243-266. http://www.doe.mass.edu/mcas/2002/results/summary.pdf
title: The ASSISTment system: online tutoring that assists while it assesses
description: The ASSISTment system is a web-based math tutoring system, first created in 2004, built from released 8th-grade MCAS test items. "The key feature of ASSISTments is that they provide instructional assistance while assessing students": students who answer an original question wrong must work through scaffolding questions, possibly with hints and buggy messages, until they get the problem correct. article_title: Developmental range of reflective judgment: The effect of contextual support and practice on developmental stage.
citation: Kitchener, K. S., Lynch, C. L., Fischer, K. W., & Wood, P. K. (1993). Developmental Range of Reflective Judgment: The Effect of Contextual Support and Practice on Developmental Stage. Developmental Psychology, 29(5), 893-906. https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1993-98188-001
title: Assess developing learners under both low-support and high-support conditions to capture the full developmental range of a skill
description: Because skill theory holds that observed competence varies with contextual support, a single spontaneous assessment underestimates what a learner can do. The article argues that "the same person exhibits differ- ent levels of performance under different assessment condi- tions and these differences are predictable ones." Pairing a low-support measure of functional level with a high-support, practice-supported measure of optimal level reveals both the lower and upper ends of the learner's developmental range, and the gap between them indicates what instruction and support could consolidate.
requirements: A high-support instrument that prompts the target skill (e.g., prototypic stage statements, memory prompts, practice opportunities) alongside a spontaneous low-support measure
constraints: Brief support-and-practice interventions probably will not produce optimal performance in all participants
target_learners: adolescents and adults developing reflective judgment
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of a learner's current and attainable reasoning level
examples: Participants were given prototypic stage statements, clarifying questions, memory prompts, and practice statements between testings, then scored significantly higher on the PRJI than on the RJI
key_sources: Kitchener, K. S., Lynch, C. L., Fischer, K. W., & Wood, P. K. (1993). Developmental Range of Reflective Judgment: The Effect of Contextual Support and Practice on Developmental Stage. Developmental Psychology, 29(5), 893-906. https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1993-98188-001

article_title: Processing capacity defined by relational complexity: Implications for comparative, developmental, and cognitive psychology
citation: Graeme S. Halford, William H. Wilson, Steven Phillips. (1998). Processing capacity defined by relational complexity: Implications for comparative, developmental, and cognitive psychology. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21, 803-865. https://www.psy.uq.edu.au/people/Department/gsh/index.html
title: Assess processing capacity with novel structures whose chunks have not been prelearned
description: Methodological principle from the chunking section: because learned chunks mask the parallel processing demand of a relation, "chunking can be inhibited by using novel structures for which chunks have not been learned." Familiar domains may still be used provided the specific orderings or bindings have not been prelearned as chunks, so the test measures the dimensionality of the relation itself rather than the efficiency of learned recodings.
requirements: Familiar domains can be used, but the specific orderings "will not have been prelearned as chunks."
constraints: Chunking develops through experience with constant mappings over time, so prelearned chunks must be avoided when measuring capacity.
target_learners: humans being assessed for relational processing capacity
target_learning_goals: measuring limits on parallel relational processing, such as transitive inference
examples: In testing transitivity, size relations between unknown persons can be used (e.g., John > Tom, Tom > Peter), a familiar domain with unprelearned orderings.
key_sources: Graeme S. Halford, William H. Wilson, Steven Phillips. (1998). Processing capacity defined by relational complexity: Implications for comparative, developmental, and cognitive psychology.
